(p-115) Surah Yunus (peace be upon him) is Meccan, and it has one hundred and nine verses.

﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ — with the ra pronounced emphatically (tafkhim) and vowelled with fatha. It is also read with imala (inclination of the vowel toward i), treating the original letter as though it had changed from a ya', and it is read with the intermediate sound (bayn bayn). As for its grammatical status: it may be a sequence of letters recited in the manner of enumeration, by way of challenge, according to one of the two views mentioned at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah; in that case it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). Or it may be a name of the surah, as is the consensus of most scholars, in which case its position is nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This surah is named 'Alif-Lam-Ra'." This is more apparent than making it nominative as the subject (mubtada'), because knowledge of the naming has not yet preceded, so the appropriate approach is to inform the listener of it, not to make it the title of the topic, since that depends on the addressee's prior knowledge of the attribution, as has passed. The demonstrative referring to it before its mention is because, by virtue of it being on the path of remembrance and about to be mentioned, it has come to be treated as present, as one says: "This is what so-and-so bought." Or it is accusative by the omission of a verb suitable to the context, such as: "Recite" or "Read." The word "tilka" (those) is a demonstrative referring to it. If "Alif-Lam-Ra" is considered as recited in the manner of enumeration, then the presence of its material, which is the aforementioned letters, has been treated as the mention of it, so it is pointed to, as if it were said: "These words composed of the kind of these letters laid out..." etc. If it is considered as a name of the surah, then the pointing to it has been emphasised after the emphasis on the specification of its name, or the command to mention it, or to recite it. The sense of distance in the demonstrative indicates the loftiness of its rank in grandeur. Its position is nominative as the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is the words of the Most High: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾.

On the view that "Alif-Lam-Ra" is the subject, then it is a second subject, or an apposition (badal) to the first. The meaning: these are particular verses of it, expressed by an independent noun. The purpose of stating that they are part of it is to describe them with the qualities for which it is well known to be characterised: the excellent attributes and perfect qualities.

By "the Book" is meant either the entire noble Qur'an, even though not all of it had been revealed at that time, either with regard to its determination and realisation in the knowledge of Allah, exalted and high, or in the Preserved Tablet, or with regard to its having been sent down all at once to the lowest heaven, as is well known. For the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah) was called by this name and by "Umm al-Qur'an" in the time of prophethood, while the collective individual whole had not yet been completed at that time. So each of "the Book" and "the Qur'an" must be considered according to one of the aforementioned senses.

Or it means the whole of the Qur'an revealed at that time, understood among people then. For just as it is applied to the individual whole, it is also applied to the whole of what was revealed in each era. Do you not see what is narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Prophet ﷺ would place two of the men slain at Uhud in a single garment, then he would say: 'Which of them had more memorisation of the Qur'an?'" So when he was pointed to one of the two, he would put him first in the grave. For what people understand of the Qur'an at that time, and what they preserve the differences in their memorisation of, is only the whole revealed at that time, without consideration of the realised individual whole in the knowledge of Allah the Glorified, or in the Tablet, nor of its having been sent down all at once to the lowest heaven.

﴿the Wise﴾, possessing wisdom. It is described thus because it comprises the various kinds of dazzling wisdoms and speaks them; or it is from the category of describing speech by the attribute of its speaker; or it is from the category of implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), based on likening the Book to a wise speaker of wisdom.

This is said, and the Book has been taken to refer to the surah itself, and the word "tilka" (those) is a demonstrative referring to the verses contained within it. They are treated as present, especially after mention of the surah containing them when explaining its name, or commanding its mention, or its recitation. It should then be that what is pointed to is each one of them, not all of them as a whole, since the whole is the very surah; so there would be no point in the annexation, nor any wisdom in restricting the attribute to the annexed noun, and the intended praise of the annexed by the qualities of perfection belonging to the annexee would not be achieved. Also, in stating that each of them possesses perfection there is more emphasis than in stating that the whole possesses it.

The understanding of "the Book" when used without qualification, although it is all of it according to one of the two aforementioned views, is nonetheless that its application to part of it is undoubtedly correct, and it is the familiar and well-known usage. Although the whole possesses the praiseworthy qualities mentioned on one of the two considerations, the wide recognition that each surah of it possesses what the whole possesses is undeniable, and upon this depends the realisation of praising the surah by its being part of the noble Qur'an; for if part of it were not described with the description of the whole and included under its ruling, that would not be possible. In this there is a strain and an artificiality that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 2:

﴿Is it a wonder for the people?﴾ The hamzah (the interrogative particle) is for denying their amazement and for expressing the listeners' astonishment at it, because it is misplaced. By "the people" is meant the disbelievers of Makkah. They were referred to by the generic noun (ism al-jins) without any mention of their disbelief, even though disbelief is the basis of their amazement, as is alluded to in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The disbelievers said﴾ ... etc. This was done to establish what they share with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to specify the basis of amazement in their claim, and then to show their error and expose the falsity of their claim by introducing denial and wonderment. The lam (preposition) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of ʿajaban. It has been said that it is connected to ʿajaban itself, by the well-known expansion regarding adverbial phrases (ẓurūf). It has also been said that when the verbal noun has the meaning of an active participle (ism al-fāʿil) or a passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl), it is permissible to place its complement before it. It has further been said that it is connected to kāna (was), and this is based on the view that the defective kāna (kāna al-nāqisah) signifies an event.

﴿That We revealed﴾: the anna clause is the subject (ism) of kāna, and its predicate (khabar) has been placed before it, to give importance to its matter, since it is the basis of the denial and wonderment, and to create suspense for what is delayed. Also, the subject contains a kind of detail, so preserving the original order would cause some disruption to the harmony of the parts of the speech. It is also read with the nominative ʿajabun (a wonder), taken as the subject, which is indefinite, and the predicate being ﴿that We revealed﴾, which is definite. This is because the particle anna with the verb is equivalent to a verbal noun definitely annexed to a definite noun. The preferred view in this case is to take kāna as complete (kāna al-tāmmah), and ﴿that We revealed﴾ as connected to ʿajabun, with an omitted particle of causation, meaning: "A wonder has arisen for the people because of 'that We revealed'," or "from 'that We revealed'," or as an apposition to ʿajabun. However, this does not direct the denial and wonderment toward its occurrence, but toward its being a wonder. The substitution (badal) is equivalent to removing the substituted element, but that does not mean abolishing it entirely. It was said "for the people" rather than "in the sight of the people" to indicate that they took it as a source of amusement for themselves. In this there is an additional censure of their condition that is not hidden.

﴿to a man from among them﴾: that is, to a human being of their own kind, as they said: "Has Allah sent a human being as a messenger?" Or from among their notables in terms of wealth, not from among their great men, as they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from one of the two towns?﴾ Both interpretations are of such evident falsehood that nothing more can be added to them. As for the first, sending an angel only occurs when the people to whom he is sent are angels, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Say: Had there been angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾. As for the common run of humanity, they are far from being fit for angelic communication. How could they be, when such communication is bound to affinity and similarity? Thus, sending an angel to them conflicts with the wisdom upon which the revolution of creation and legislation turns. What wisdom requires is that the angel be sent from among them to the elect, who are specially chosen for pure souls, supported with holy power, and connected to both the spiritual and the physical worlds, so that they may receive from one side and convey to the other side.

As for the second: the basis for selection to prophethood and messengerhood is precedence in possessing the aforementioned noble attributes and sublime qualities, and being foremost in attaining excellent virtues and acquiring lofty faculties, whether innate or acquired. None of them doubts that he (ﷺ) was in that regard at the furthest possible extreme and the ultimate limit of the highest degrees. As for precedence in worldly leadership and being foremost in attaining base worldly portions, it has no bearing whatsoever on that. Rather, it is mostly a hindrance to it. He (ﷺ) said: "If the world weighed as much as a gnat's wing with Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it."

﴿that you warn the people﴾: the anna is verbal (maṣdariyyah), because the complement of the anna may be an imperative, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that you set your face﴾. This is because the declarative and the imperative are equal in indicating the verbal noun, so it is permissible for an imperative or prohibition to be a complement, according to the occurrence of the verb. In that case, it is stripped of the meaning of command or prohibition, similar to how the verbal complement is stripped of the meaning of past or future. The requirement that the complement of the relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl) be declarative is only for the purpose of connecting it to describing definite nouns with sentences, not because of any deficiency in the imperative's indication of the verbal noun.

Or it is explanatory (mufassirah), since revelation in it carries the meaning of saying. It has also been permitted that it be the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy form (mushaddadah), with the omission of the pronoun of the matter and saying from the predicate, and the meaning is: "The matter is Our saying: warn the people." By "the people" is meant all people in general, not what was meant in the first instance. This is the reason for preferring the explicit noun over the pronoun. The second being identical to the first when a definite noun is repeated is not absolute.

﴿and give good news to those who believe﴾ in what We revealed and affirmed. ﴿that for them is﴾: that is, that for them there is ﴿a seat of truth﴾: that is, a prior precedence and an elevated station ﴿with their Lord﴾. The term "foot" (qadam) is used for it because precedence and reaching elevated stations are achieved through it, just as blessing is expressed by "hand," because it is given by it. It has been said: "a station of truth" (maqām ṣidq). The better view is that arriving at a station is achieved by the foot. Its annexation to truth indicates its certainty and firmness, and it draws attention to the fact that the basis for attaining the exalted ranks they have achieved is their truthfulness, since affirmation is never separated from truthfulness.

﴿The disbelievers said﴾: they are the ones who expressed amazement. Mentioning them here with the designation of disbelief is something for which there is no need to mention its cause. The omission of the conjunction is because it functions as an explanation of the sentence to which the hamzah of denial was attached, or because it is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf) based on a question, as if it were said: "What did they do after their amazement? Did they remain in doubt and disbelief, or did they settle on something?" So it was said: "The disbelievers said," in the manner of emphasis. ﴿Indeed, this﴾, meaning by it what was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of the wise Qur'an, which contains warning and good news, ﴿is clearly sorcery﴾: that is, evident. It is also read: "Indeed, he is a clear sorcerer," on the basis that the reference is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also read: "This is nothing but clear sorcery." This is an acknowledgment, without their realizing it, that what they witnessed is beyond human capacity and descends from the presence of the Creator of powers and decree. Yet they called it by what they said out of persistence in obstinacy, as is the habit of the stubborn contrarian and the practice of the silenced and defeated.

Surah 10, verse 3: "Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself above the Throne, arranging the affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him. Will you not then be reminded?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim):

﴿إنَّ رَبَّكُمُ﴾ ("Indeed, your Lord") is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) brought to demonstrate the falsehood of their aforementioned astonishment and of the false claim they built upon it, after the pointing to it with denial and wonder. In it is verified the truth of what they wondered at and the correctness of what they denied, by a general alerting to some of what indicates it from the affairs of creation and decree and the states of origination and governance. It guides them to knowledge of these with minimal reminder, since they acknowledge it without objection, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ ﴿They will say: "Allah." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And who arranges the affair?﴾ ﴿They will say: "Allah."﴾ That is, indeed your Lord and the Owner of your affair, at whom you marvel that He should send to you a man from among you with warning and good tidings, and you consider what was revealed to him of the Wise Book to be magic, is ﴿Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ and what is in them of the origins of existing things ﴿in six days﴾, that is, in six periods, or in the measure of six known days. For the very day, which is an expression for the time of the sun's being above the earth, cannot be conceived to occur when there is no earth or heaven. And in creating them gradually, along with complete power to create them at once, is evidence of choice and a lesson for observers, and an incitement for them to deliberation in states and stages. As for specifying that number exactly, it is a matter which the All-Knowing of the Unseen has kept to Himself, the knowledge of what it requires; exalted is His majesty and subtle is His wisdom. And the choice of the plural form for "heavens," according to what is well known, signals that they are bodies differing in natures and diverse in effects and rulings.

﴿Then He established Himself over the Throne﴾: the Throne is the encompassing body surrounding all other bodies; it was so named for its elevation, or by likeness to a king's throne, since commands and arrangements descend from it. It was said: it is the kingdom. The meaning of His, glorified is He, establishing Himself upon it is His dominion over it, or the establishment of His command. And from our companions: establishment upon the Throne is an attribute of His, glorified is He, without how; the meaning is that He, glorified is He, established Himself upon the Throne in the manner He intended, exalted above settling and resting. This is an explanation of the greatness of His kingdom and authority after the explanation of the magnitude of His dignity and the vastness of His power through the creation of those mighty bodies already mentioned.

﴿Arranging the affair﴾: tadbir (arrangement) is looking into the backs of affairs and their consequences so that they occur in the praiseworthy manner. What is meant here is decree in the most complete and perfect way. By "the affair" is meant the affair of the dominion of the heavens, the earth and the Throne, and other particular things originating little by little in various stages and countless modes of harmony and contrast in essences, attributes, times and periods. That is, He decrees what has been mentioned of the affair of existing things, of which what they marvelled at, the matter of resurrection and revelation, is one individual and a branch of its tree. He prepares the causes of each of them in origination and continuance at their specified times, and arranges their interests in the surpassing manner and fitting pattern, as wisdom requires and the interest demands. The clause is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (istawa). It has been permitted that it be a second predicate of (inna), or a resumed clause without grammatical place, built upon a question arising from mention of establishing upon the Throne, which indicates the enactment of the rulings of sovereignty. In any case, the choice of the present-tense form indicates the renewal and continuity of the arranging.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿There is no intercessor﴾ (p-119) is an explanation of His sole authority in decree and arrangement, and a negation of intercession in the most emphatic way, for negating every individual intercessor with the inclusive "min" implies negating intercession in the most complete way, as in His saying: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah.﴾ This, after His saying ﴿arranging the affair,﴾ runs in the same course as His saying: ﴿He protects, and none can be protected against Him,﴾ following His saying: ﴿Say: In whose hand is the dominion of all things?﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except after His permission﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of times: that is, there is no intercessor who intercedes for anyone at any time except after His permission, which is based on overwhelming wisdom. This is when the intercessor is among the chosen best, and the one for whom intercession is made is among those worthy of intercession, as in His saying: ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is right.﴾ In this is evidence of the greatness of His majesty, glorified is He, which is not hidden.

﴿That﴾ is a pointing to what is known by that greatness; that is, that One of great station, described by what has been mentioned of the attributes of perfection upon which the entitlement to divinity turns, ﴿is Allah﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿your Lord﴾ is an explanation of it, or a substitute for it, or a second predicate of the demonstrative noun. This comes after the explanation that their Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, etc., for the increase of affirmation and emphasis in reminding, and to make the command to worship follow from it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so worship Him﴾, that is: affirm His oneness, without associating with Him anything, whether an angel or a prophet, let alone a stone that neither sees nor hears nor harms nor benefits. And believe in what He has sent down to you. ﴿Will you not then be reminded?﴾ That is: do you know that the matter is as explained, and yet you do not remember that until you recognize the corruption of what you are upon, so that you refrain from it?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 4:

﴿To Him﴾, not to anyone else, either independently or in partnership, ﴿is your return﴾. That is, by resurrection (ba'th), as His saying, ﴿all together﴾, indicates. The word ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ (jamee'an, "all together") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive, because it is the grammatical agent in meaning. The meaning is: your return to Him will be as a gathered whole. The sentence serves as a reason (ta'lil) for the obligation of worship.

﴿The promise of God﴾ (wa'da Allah) is an absolute object (masdar mu'akkid li-nafsihi), meaning it emphasizes itself, because His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿To Him is your return﴾, is a promise from Him, glorified is He, of resurrection. Alternatively, it is governed by an implied verb, meaning "God promised." In either case, it is evidence that the intended meaning of "return" is return by resurrection, because death is far from being a promise, just as it is far from gathering.

﴿Truly﴾ (haqqan) is another absolute object emphasizing what the first one implies. ﴿Indeed He originates creation﴾ (innahu yabda'u al-khalq). It was also read as (yubdi'u). ﴿Then He repeats it﴾ (thumma yu'eeduhu). This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) by which the obligation of returning to Him, glorified and exalted is He, is given a reason. The ultimate purpose of origination and repetition is the recompense of the responsible persons for their deeds, whether good or evil. It was also read with a fatha (anna, "because"), that is, "because He..." It is permissible for it to be in the accusative, governed by what governed (wa'da Allah), meaning "God promised a promise: the origination of creation and then its repetition." It may also be in the nominative, governed by what governed "haqqan," meaning "it is established as a truth that the origination of creation..." and so on.

﴿That He may recompense those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾. That is, with equity (al-'adl). It is a circumstantial clause from the agent of yajzi, meaning "while being characterized by justice," or it is connected to (yajziya), meaning "that He may recompense them according to His justice and give them their rewards in full." This was stated in a general form to signal that it cannot be fully encompassed by enumeration. Or it means "according to their own equity and justice when they believe and engage in righteous deeds." This is the most suitable reading in light of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved, for them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾. Its meaning is: and He will recompense those who disbelieved on account of their disbelief. Repeating the predication makes the prepositional clause a predicate of the relative pronoun, in order to strengthen the ruling. The combination of the past and the future forms signifies their persistence in disbelief. Altering the noble arrangement signals that they fully deserve punishment, and that torment is far from being part of the final purpose of creation, whether in origination or repetition. It only befalls the disbelievers according to the consequence of their evil choice. As for the original purpose of this, it is reward.

This is the first verse of the commentary: Allah is the One who made the sun a source of radiance (ḍiyā'), and the moon a light (nūr).

﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance﴾ is an admonition to draw inference, through the traces of His handiwork in the two luminaries, to His existence, His oneness, His knowledge, His power and His wisdom. This follows the admonition to draw inference from what has already passed, namely the origination of the heavens and the earth, His istiwā' (establishment) upon the Throne, and other things. It is also an explanation of some of the individual instances of the governance (tadbīr) that was indicated in general terms, and a guidance to the point that since their affairs related to their livelihood have been governed with this wondrous governance, then His governing their interests related to the Hereafter, by sending the Messenger, sending down the Book, clarifying the paths of guidance and specifying the abysses of perdition, is all the more fitting and more deserving.

The verb "ja'ala" (made), if taken in the sense of creating and originating, then "ḍiyā'an" (a radiance) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of its object, meaning: He created it while it was possessed of radiance, with an elided modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf); or it is "ḍiyā'an maḥḍan" (pure radiance) for emphasis. If it is taken in the sense of making into (tasyīr), then "ḍiyā'an" is its second object, meaning: He made it a radiance according to one of the two aspects mentioned, but not after it had been devoid of that state; rather He originated it thus, as in their saying: "Narrow the mouth of the well and widen its bottom." The word "ḍiyā'" is a verbal noun like "qiyām", or a plural of "ḍaw'" like "siyāṭ" of "sawṭ"; its yā' is changed from a wāw because of the kasra before it. It has also been read "ḍi'ā'" with two hamzas and an alif between them, with the lām placed before the 'ayn (a metathesis).

﴿And the moon a light﴾: the discussion of it is the same as the discussion of the sun. Radiance (ḍiyā') is stronger than light (nūr). It has been said: that which is radiant by its essence is ḍaw', and that which is luminous by an accident is nūr. Therefore there is in it an indication that its light is derived from the sun.

﴿And He determined for it stages﴾: that is, He determined for it and prepared it, or its course was determined through stages, or He determined it as one having stages, by including in "taqdīr" (determining) the meaning of "taṣyīr" (making). The specification of the moon with this determination is because of the swiftness of its motion, the observability of its stages, the connection of the rulings of the Sharī'ah with it, and its being the chief reference in the chronology of the Arabs. The pronoun has been made to refer to each of the two luminaries. The stages are twenty-eight; the moon descends into one of them each night, neither overstepping it nor falling short of it, according to a determination that is level and does not vary. It travels through them from the night of its first appearance to the twenty-eighth. When it is in its last stage it becomes thin and bent like a bow; then it remains hidden for two nights or one night when the month is short. The sun's stay in each of these stages is thirteen days. These stages are the positions of the stars to which the Arabs attributed the rain-bringing "anwā'" (star-risings), and they are: al-Sharaṭān, al-Buṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabaran, al-Ha'ah, al-Han'ah, al-Dhirā', al-Nathrah, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabhah, al-Zubrah, al-Ṣarfah, al-'Awwā', al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zibānī, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawlah, al-Na'a'im, al-Balda, Sa'd al-Dhābiḥ, Sa'd Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ūd, Sa'd al-Akhbiyah, Far' al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Far' al-Dalw al-Mu'akhkhar, and al-Rishā', which is the belly of the fish.

﴿That you may know﴾: either by the succession of night and day, which are governed by the rising and setting of the sun; or by considering the descent of each of the two luminaries into those stages; ﴿the number of the years﴾ in which there is a scientific purpose connected with establishing your religious and worldly interests; ﴿and the reckoning﴾: that is, the reckoning of times in months, days, nights, and other things to which some of the aforementioned interests are attached. The specification of "number" with "years" and of "reckoning" with "times" is because in counted years no meaning distinct from the orders of numbers has been considered, as has been considered in the reckoned times. The verification of this is that reckoning (ḥisāb) is the enumeration of that which has a discrete quantity by the repetition of its like, such that from a certain group of them there results a definite limit which has a particular name and an independent ruling, like the year that results from twelve months, each of which results from thirty days, each of which results from twenty-four hours, for example. Counting (ʿadd) is merely the enumeration of a thing by the repetition of its like, without considering that from this there results something of that kind. Since in counted years there was not considered the resulting of a definite limit having a particular name other than the names of the orders of numbers, and an independent ruling, the number was attached to them; and the resulting of the orders of numbers from tens, hundreds and thousands is a conventional matter that does not benefit the counted thing in any way. Whereas in reckoned times there was considered the resulting of those orders which have special names and independent rulings, and reckoning, which indicates that, was connected to them. The year, in terms of its being realized in itself, is among the things to which reckoning relates; what counting relates to is a group of them, and its relation within that to each one of that group is not from the aspect mentioned, namely the aspect of its resulting from a number of months, each of which results from a number of days, each of which results from a group of hours. For that is the function of reckoning. Rather, it is from the aspect that it is a single member of that counted group, without anything else being considered along with it. The placing of the number before the reckoning, although the order between their objects in existence and non-existence is the reverse, is either because the knowledge related to the number of years is a comprehensive knowledge of what reckoning relates to in detail, even if the aspect is not the same; or because the number, insofar as no other matter has been considered in it, as has been verified above, is in the position of the simple relative to the compound, with respect to the reckoning in which that has been considered.

﴿Allah did not create that﴾: that is, what has been mentioned of the sun and the moon, in the states that have been described; and in it there is a notification that the meaning of making them in those states and conditions is nothing but creating them thus, as has been indicated. And it does not detract from this that the moon's receiving light from the sun is a new occurrence, for what is meant by making it a light is making it such that it is characterized by light when the conditions of being so characterized are actually present.

﴿Except with truth﴾: this is an exceptive clause (istithnā' mufarragh) from the most general of the states of the agent or the object. That is: He did not create that connected with anything of things except connected with truth, observing the requirement of perfect wisdom; or it is observed in it. This is what was indicated in general terms, namely the knowledge of the states of the years and times, on which their affairs of dealings and acts of worship depend.

﴿He details the signs﴾: that is, the cosmic signs (al-āyāt al-takwīniyyah) mentioned; or all signs, so that the signs mentioned enter among them in the first place; or He details the revealed signs (al-āyāt al-tanzīliyyah) that draw attention to that. It has been read with the nūn of majesty (nūn al-'aẓamah). ﴿For a people who know﴾: the wisdom in the origination of created beings, so that they may draw inference from that to the affairs of their Originator, exalted is He; or they know what is within the folds of the revealed signs, and so they believe in them. The specification of the detailing to them is because they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day﴾ is another general admonition concerning what has been mentioned, namely: in their succession, and in each of them being a replacement (khilfah) for the other, according to the rising and setting of the sun, which follow the movements of the heavens and the stillness of the earth. Or (it refers to) their difference in themselves, in that each of them increases as the other decreases, and decreases as the other increases, according to the variation in the state of the sun in relation to us, in nearness and distance, according to the seasons. Or (it refers to) their difference and variation according to places: either in length and shortness, for the lands near the North Pole (p-122) have longer summer days and shorter summer nights than the lands far from it; or in themselves, for the sphericity of the earth requires that at some times in some places it is night while in the opposite place it is day.

﴿And what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth﴾ of kinds of created things ﴿are signs﴾, great or numerous, indicating the existence of the Creator, may He be exalted, and His unity, the perfection of His knowledge, His power, and the far-reaching nature of His wisdom, of which among its requirements is what they denied: the sending of the Messenger ﷺ, the sending down of the Books, the Resurrection and the recompense. ﴿For a people who are mindful of God﴾: He specified them with this because the impetus to reflection and contemplation is nothing but the fear of God, may He be exalted, and caution against the consequence. Thus they are the ones who recognize that all created beings are signs, to the exclusion of others. ﴿(And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, while they turn away from it).﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us﴾ is an explanation of the outcome for those who denied the Resurrection and turned away from the clear signs (al-bayyinat) that point to it, after it has been established that the return of all things is to Him, the Exalted, and that He will restore them after their origination for recompense, reward and punishment, and after a detailing of some of the verses that bear witness to this. The meaning of "meeting Him" is either returning to Him, the Exalted, through the Resurrection, or the meeting of the reckoning, as in His saying, Mighty and Exalted: ﴿Indeed I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾. Whichever it is, there is, together with the shift to the divine name (damir al-jalala), a magnification of the matter that is not hidden.

The meaning of "not expecting" is not expecting in any sense, which encompasses both lacking hope and lacking fear, for the absence of each of them does not require the absence of belief that what is hoped for or feared will occur. That is: they do not expect the return to Us, or the meeting of Our reckoning, which leads either to good reward or to evil punishment. So they do not hope for the first, and this is what His saying, Mighty and Majestic, points to: ﴿and are content with the life of this world﴾, for it indicates preferring the lowly and base over the high and precious, like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾. And they do not fear the second, and this is what His saying, Exalted, points to: ﴿and are at rest in it﴾, that is, they settled in it with the settling of one who has no departure from it, secure from the arrival of distressing things, not bringing to mind what would grieve them of Our punishment.

It has been said: the meaning of "hope" is its literal sense, and the meaning of "meeting" is a good meeting. That is: they do not hope for a good meeting with Us through resurrection and revival into eternal life, and they were content, in exchange for it and for the various noble honours in it, with the lowly, perishing life of this world, and they were at rest in it, that is, they settled into it, bent upon it, confining the full resolve of their aims to its pleasures and adornments, without any diverting force turning them away or any inclining force restraining them. The choice of the preposition bi (with) over ila (to), which indicates mere arrival and reaching, is to signal complete attachment and lasting companionship and intimacy. Restricting "hope" to fear alone is rejected by the word "contentment with the life of this world," for it indicates what was mentioned: abandoning the higher and taking the lower. The choice of the past form in the last two relative clauses is to indicate certainty and establishment, just as the choice of the future form in the first is to indicate the continuation of not hoping.

﴿And those who are heedless of Our signs﴾, which are detailed in the pages of the cosmos as some of them have been pointed to, or Our revealed signs that alert to being taken as evidence, agreeing with them in indicating the truth of what they do not hope for of the meeting that follows from resurrection, and the falsehood of what they were content with and at rest in from the life of this world, ﴿are heedless﴾, not reflecting upon them at all even if they are alerted to this and reminded with all kinds of calamities, because of their absorption in what diverts them from them, of the countable conditions. The repetition of the relative pronoun is to use it as a means to make its clause a nominal sentence, indicating the continuity and permanence of the heedlessness they are in. And treating the descriptive difference as if it were a difference of essence is to signal that the last attribute differs from the first attributes and is independent in entailing punishment.

This said, as for what has been said, that the conjunction is either because the two attributes differ and to alert that the threat is upon combining complete oblivion of the signs with immersion in desires such that the Hereafter never comes to mind at all, or because the two groups differ, with the first being those who denied the Resurrection and desired only the life of this world, and the latter being those whom love of the immediate distracted from reflecting on the deferred, then it is a statement far from soundness, so reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 8:

﴿Those﴾ who are described by what has been mentioned of the evil attributes, ﴿their abode﴾, that is, their dwelling and their resting place from which there is no escape for them, ﴿is the Fire﴾, not what they were content with of the worldly life and its delights. ﴿Because of what they used to earn﴾ of the inner deeds that are counted, and what follows from them of kinds of disobedience and misdeeds; or [it means] because of their earning of them. The combining of the past and the present forms is to indicate continuous, renewing persistence. The preposition "bi-" (because of) is connected to the meaning of the last clause, which occurs as a predicate of the demonstrative noun, and it together with its predicate is the predicate of "inna" (indeed) in the Exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not hope for meeting Us...﴾ and so on.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ i.e., who perform faith (al-iman), or who believe in what the signs (al-ayat) attest to, which the heedless have neglected, or in everything that must be believed in, so that this is included in it in an initial inclusion (indiraj awwaliyy). ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ i.e., the deeds that are righteous in themselves and befitting to faith. The mention of the modified noun (al-mawsuf) has been omitted because the phrase has come to function as nouns (jariyanuha majra al-asma'). ﴿Their Lord guides them﴾ The shift to the third person (al-iltifat) has been preferred, to honour them by the attribution of "Lord" and to indicate the cause of the guidance ﴿by their faith﴾, i.e., He guides them, because of their faith, to their abode and destination, which is Paradise. It has not been mentioned, relying on its being evident and the soul's being led to it, especially when considering what preceded concerning the abode of the disbelievers, and what their evil deeds led them to, and the witnessing of what befell them by allusion and explicit statement. In the noble composition there is an indication that mere faith and righteous deeds do not suffice for reaching Paradise, but after that there must be divine guidance, and that disbelief and sins are sufficient for entering the Fire. Furthermore, there is no dispute that what is meant by faith, which has been made a cause of that guidance, is their particular faith accompanied by righteous deeds, not faith devoid of them, nor what is more general than both. However, this has no bearing on evidence contrary to what the People of the Sunnah wal-Jama'ah hold, namely that faith devoid of righteous deeds leads to Paradise in general, and its possessor is not eternal in the Fire. For the explicit meaning of the noble verse is that faith joined with righteous deeds is a cause of guidance to Paradise; as for whether everything that is a cause of it must be likewise, there is definitively no indication in it or in anything else for this. How could there be? The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing, for them is security, and they are guided﴾ speaks against that. For what is meant by wrongdoing (al-zulm) is polytheism (al-shirk), as the exegetes have unanimously held, and the meaning is: they did not mix their faith with associating partners. Even if it is taken in its apparent sense, it would still include in guidance one who believed but did not do righteous deeds, then died before he committed a forbidden act or abandoned an obligatory duty. (p-124)

﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾ i.e., before them, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾. Or they flow while they are on raised thrones and arranged couches. The clause is either a new sentence (mustaʼnafah), or a second predicate (khabar thani) for "inna", or "tajri" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of "yahdihim", on the assumption that the one guided to is what they desire in Paradise, as has been said. It has also been said: He guides them and makes them steadfast to walk the path that leads to reward and Paradise.

His saying "rivers flow beneath them" serves as an explanation and elucidation, for holding fast to the rope of happiness is in the status of having arrived at it. It has also been said: He guides them to the perception of wondrous realities according to the practical faculty, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah will bequeath to him the knowledge of what he did not know."

﴿In gardens of bliss﴾ is another predicate, or another circumstantial clause from it (the subject), or from the rivers, or it is connected to "tajri" or to "yahdi". Thus the one guided to is either their dwellings in Paradise, or what they desire therein.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 10, verse 10:**

﴿Their call therein﴾ means their supplication (du'a'uhum). It is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the sentence). The phrase of Almighty and Majestic He, (fīhā), "therein," is connected to it. The words of Exalted He, ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾, are its predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate). That is, their supplication is this utterance. It is a complement (ma'mul, the element governed by a verb or particle) of an omitted verb (muqaddar, an implied element) that may not be made explicit.

The meaning is: "O Allah, we glorify You with glorification." They may say this when they witness, therein, the wondrous signs of His power and the results of His mercy and compassion, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which have not occurred to the heart of any human. This is to sanctify His exalted station above the taints of incapacity and deficiency, and to declare His generous promise free from the marks of breaking it.

﴿And their greeting therein﴾: the greeting (taḥiyya) is an honouring with a noble state. Its origin is "May Allah give you a good life." That is, it is what some of them say to one another, or it is the greeting of the angels to them, as in the words of Exalted He: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace﴾. Or it is the greeting of Almighty and Majestic He to them, as in the words of Exalted He: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. ﴿Peace﴾ means safety from every disliked thing. ﴿And the last of their call﴾ means the conclusion of their supplication ﴿is that: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ That is, they say this as an attribution of praise to Him, Almighty and Majestic, with attributes of honour after describing Him with attributes of majesty. That is, their supplication is confined to what has been mentioned, since they have no awaited request that they would thread into the string of supplication.

"An" (أنْ) here is the lightened form (mukhaffafa, the light form) of "anna" (أنَّ), the heavy form (muthaqqala, the heavy form). Its original is "annahu al-ḥamdu lillāh," and the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the dummy pronoun) has been omitted, as in the verse of the poet:

*Indeed, everyone who goes barefoot or shod is doomed.*

It was also recited as (anna al-ḥamda lillāh), with the heavy form and the accusative ḥamd. The placing of the mention of their greeting between their supplication and its conclusion, in the narration, is perhaps for the purpose of ending the narration with praise, seeking blessing, though the greeting is not entirely extraneous. The claim that the order of occurrence is also like this, namely that when they entered Paradise and witnessed the greatness and majesty of Allah, Exalted, they glorified Him and described Him with attributes of majesty, and then the angels greeted them with safety from calamities and success with various honours, or the Lord of Might greeted them with that, so they praised Him, Exalted, and extolled Him, is rejected by the attachment of "the last" to their supplication. It has been allowed that the intended meaning of "supplication" is worship, as in the words of Exalted He: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and from what you call upon﴾, etc., to indicate that there is no obligation (taklif) in Paradise. That is, their worship is nothing but that they glorify Him and praise Him. That is not worship in the strict sense, rather they are inspired to it and speak it out of delight. And the specification of the conclusion does not support this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 11:

﴿And if God were to hasten for the people﴾: they are those who do not hope for the meeting with God, the Exalted, because they deny the Resurrection and what follows from it of reckoning and recompense. It points to some of the grave sins they commit as a consequence of this, namely their seeking to hasten what they were threatened with of punishment, out of denial and mockery. Their mention by the generic noun is because the hastening of good for them does not depend on the attribute mentioned, since not all of this is by way of gradual respite (istidraj). That is: if God were to hasten for them ﴿the evil﴾ that they were seeking to hasten, [they would be destroyed]. They used to say: ﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾, and the like.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿their hastening for good﴾ is put in the accusative because it is a similative infinitive (masdar tashbihi, an infinitive of manner), placed in the position of the infinitive of its governing verb. This indicates that hastening is taken into account on the side of the compared element (al-mushabbah), just as hastening is taken into account on the side of the element compared to (al-mushabbah bihi), and it implies the swiftness of His response to them, so that their hastening for good is itself His hastening it for them. The full sense is: and if God were to hasten for them the evil at their seeking it, hastening it for them in a manner like His hastening the good for them at their seeking it. So what was omitted was omitted, relying on the remaining words to indicate it.

﴿the term would have been decreed for them﴾: the appointed time that was set for their punishment would have been fulfilled for them, and they would have been destroyed and annihilated completely, without being granted a moment's respite. The choice of the passive form (al-mabni lil-maf'ul) follows the customs of divine majesty, while also giving notice that the agent is determined. It was also read in the active form, as in the reading "laqadayna" (We would have decreed). The choice of the future (mudari') form in the conditional, although the meaning is past, is to convey that the non-fulfilment of the term is due to the continuing absence of hastening. The negated present tense placed in the position of the past is not explicit in indicating the negation of the continuation of the act; rather it may indicate the continued negation of it according to the context, as has been verified in its proper place. Know that the basis of meaning in a conditional sentence is that the consequent be something distinct from the antecedent in itself and following from it in existence, as in His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿If he were to obey you in many matters, you would surely be in distress﴾ (49:7), for distress (al-'anat), that is, falling into hardship and ruin, is something distinct from his obedience (ﷺ) to them and follows from it in existence. Or the consequent may be a complete individual of the antecedent, distinguished from the rest by something particular to it, as in the omitted answers in such verses as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ (6:30), and His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾ (6:27), and His saying: ﴿If only you could see when the guilty ones﴾ (32:12), and their like; that is, you would see a tremendous and dreadful matter or something similar to that. And as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If God were to take people to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ (35:45), when the answer is interpreted as total annihilation. For this is a complete individual of the absolute notion of taking to task, which has been expressed by what admits of no greater expression of severity and dreadfulness, so its placement is fitting in the context of the consequent of absolute taking to task.

As for what we are concerned with here, namely the decreeing (al-qada'), it is not something distinct from the hastening of evil in itself, and this is evident. Rather it is either that very thing or a particular instance of it, like its other particulars, without any distinction over the rest, since what is not included in the concept of hastening evil, such as severity and terror, has not been taken into account in its concept. Therefore its following from it, in existence or in non-existence, adds no further benefit that justifies making it a consequent of it. So the truth is that the antecedent is not the mentioned hastening itself, but rather the will for it, which entails the mentioned decreeing in existence or non-existence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If He were to take them to task for what they have earned, He would hasten the punishment for them﴾ (35:45 cf. 16:61), that is: if He were to will to take them to task. For the hastening of punishment for them is itself taking them to task, or a particular of its particulars not distinguished from the rest, so there is no further benefit in stating its following from it, in existence or non-existence. The benefit lies only in stating its following from the will for it, as mentioned. Also, in the consequent's following from the will of the antecedent there is something that is absent in its following from the thing itself: an indication of emphasis and of the magnitude of the matter, and an indication that affairs are dependent upon His will, exalted is He, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms.

﴿So We leave those who do not hope for Our meeting﴾: with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), which indicates emphasis in the threat. It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied element that the conditional sentence indicates, as if it were said: "But We do not do that, since wisdom requires otherwise, so We leave them, granting respite and gradual enticement," ﴿in their transgression﴾, which is their not hoping for the meeting and their denial of the Resurrection and recompense, and what follows from that of their evil deeds and their vile sayings, ﴿wandering blindly﴾, that is: they waver and are bewildered. Thus placing the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun gives a kind of explanation of the transgression by what is contained in the relative clause, and it indicates that it is the cause of the leaving and of the gradual enticement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 12:

﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing.﴾ That is: harm of any kind befalls him, whether sickness, poverty, or other hardships, befalling him lightly (يسيرة). ﴿He calls upon Us﴾ to remove it and relieve it. ﴿Lying on his side﴾ (لجنبه) is a circumstantial clause (حال) referring to the subject of (دعا), as evidenced by the two circumstances coordinated after it, and the lam here carries the meaning of (على), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They fall down upon their chins (للأذقان)﴾. That is: he calls upon Us being upon his side, i.e., lying prone. ﴿Or sitting, or standing﴾: that is, in all states, both those mentioned and those not mentioned. The mention of these three is specific because a person is customarily never free of them. Or it means: he calls upon Us in all states of his illness, with (الضر) being specifically the sickness intended, lying down, unable to sit; sitting, unable to rise; and standing, unable to move.

﴿But when We remove from him the harm that touched him﴾, immediately after he called upon Us, as the particle (ف) indicates, ﴿he passes on﴾ (مر), that is, he goes on and persists in his former way which he followed before the harm touched him, forgetting the state of hardship and affliction. Or (مر) means he passes by the position of supplication and entreaty and turns away with his side. ﴿As if he had never called upon Us﴾: that is, as if he had never called upon Us. It is lightened and the pronoun of the matter (ضمير الشأن) is omitted, as in his saying:

؎ as if there had never been between al-Hajun and al-Safa

The comparative clause is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (حال) from the subject of (مر), that is: he passes by, likened to one who never called upon Us. ﴿To a harm﴾: that is, to the removal of a harm ﴿that touched him﴾. This is a description of the species with regard to the condition of some of its individuals who are characterized by these attributes.

﴿Thus﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (مصدرية), and (ذلك) is a reference to the verbal noun of the following verb, with the sense of distance included for magnification, and the particle (الكاف) is superfluous (مقحمة), to indicate the increased grandeur of the referent, an insertion that is hardly ever left out in the Arabic language or in any other. Among this is their saying: "Someone like you does not stint," in place of: "You do not stint," that is: like that wondrous adornment ﴿it was made attractive to the extravagant﴾: that is, to those characterized by the blameworthy attributes mentioned, and their extravagance is because God, exalted is He, gave them faculties and perceptions only so that they would direct them to their proper ends and employ them for what they were created for, namely the sciences and righteous deeds. When they directed them to what is not fitting, and these were their capital, they destroyed them, and they were extravagant in an evident extravagance. The adornment is either from God, glorified is He, by way of abandonment and forsaking (التخلية والخذلان), or from Satan through whispering and enticement.

﴿What they used to do﴾: of turning away from the remembrance and the supplication, and immersion in desires. The connection of this noble verse with what precedes it is that in each of them there is a respite for the disbelievers by way of istidraj (الاستدراج) after deliverance from the evil that was decreed in the first, and from the harm that was established in the second.

﴿Certainly We destroyed the generations﴾, that is, the generations of old, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and their likes. The "min" (from) in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿before you﴾ is connected to "destroyed," meaning: We destroyed them before your time. The address is to the people of Makkah, in the manner of the shift of grammatical person (al-iltifat) for the sake of intensifying the severity of the threat, after reinforcing it with the oath of emphasis. ﴿When they wronged﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) for the destruction, meaning: We destroyed them when they committed wrongdoing by denying and persisting in error and misguidance, without delay.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and their messengers came to them﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "wronged," with "qad" implied. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿with clear proofs﴾ are connected to "came to them," with the "ba'" (with) being for transitivity (ta'diyah), or they are connected to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause from "their messengers," indicating their excessive wrongdoing and their extreme obstinacy. That is: they wronged by denying, while their messengers had come to them with clear signs indicating their truthfulness, or they were accompanied by them at a time when there was no room for denial.

It has been permitted that His words, Exalted is He, "and their messengers came to them" be a conjunction (atf) upon "wronged." According to Sibawayh it then has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), and according to others its place is the genitive (jarr), because it is conjoined to what is genitive by the addition of the temporal element to it. Wrongdoing is not restricted to denial, so there is no need to excuse this by saying that the order of mention need not follow the order of occurrence, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration﴾ ... etc. Rather, it is to be understood as covering all kinds of wrongdoing, and denial is derived from His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and they would not have believed﴾ in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, for the lam is for emphasizing the negation. That is: it was not valid nor proper for them to believe, due to the corruption of their readiness and God's abandonment of them, since He knew that the favours would not benefit them. According to the first view, the sentence is a conjunction upon "wronged," since it is a report of the initiation of denial, while this is with persistence upon it. According to the second, it is a conjunction upon what it was conjoined to. It is said that it is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) between the verb and what runs in the place of its figurative verbal noun (masdar tashbihi), namely His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Thus﴾, for the recompense referred to is an expression of its verbal noun, meaning: like that dreadful recompense, that is, the severe destruction which is complete annihilation ﴿We recompense the guilty people﴾, meaning every guilty group. In this is a severe warning and a firm threat to the people of Makkah, since they share with those destroyed the crimes and sins which are denying the Messenger and persisting upon it, and it confirms the content of what preceded in His words, Exalted is He: "And if God hastened for people the evil as they hasten for the good." It was also read with the yaʼ (third person), in shift to the third person (al-iltifat ila al-ghaybah). It has been permitted that the intended "guilty people" are the people of Makkah, in the manner of placing an apparent noun in place of a pronoun of address, to signal that they are the foremost in criminality, and this is utterly rejected by His words, Exalted is He, "

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 14:

﴿Then We made you successors in the earth after them﴾ For this clearly indicates that it is the beginning of an addressing of their affairs, and that what is explained in it is only the initial stages of their conditions, in order to test the manner of their deeds, in a way that gives the sense of inclining them towards faith and obedience. Thus it is impossible that this should follow the explanation of the final outcome of their affairs and the address that pronounces a definitive verdict of their destruction on account of the completeness of their criminality. The meaning is: Then We made you successors in the earth after the destruction of those generations whose reports you hear and whose traces you witness, a succession of one who tests, ﴿so that We may see﴾ that is, so that We may deal with you as one who looks on, ﴿how you act﴾. So this is a figurative metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah). And "kayfa" (how) is in the accusative as an adverb of manner (masdariyyah) governed by "ta'malun" (you act), not by "nazhura" (We see), because the interrogative meaning contained in it prevents its governing verb from preceding it. That is: what kind of deed. Or it is in the accusative of circumstance (hal), that is: in what state you do the deeds befitting succession, of the attributes of goodness, like His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿that He may test you, which of you is best in deed﴾. In this there is an indication that the intended purpose and the original aim of the succession is only the manifestation of the good qualities of righteous deeds, while evil deeds are far from proceeding from them, especially after they have heard the reports of the destroyed generations and witnessed the traces of some of them, let alone that their manifestation should be counted among the ultimate cause (al-'illah al-ghaʾibah) of the succession. (p-128) It has also been said: it is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi), that is: what deed you do, good or evil, so that We may deal with you according to it. In that case, the word "kayfa" carries no indication that what is considered in the recompense is the aspects and qualities of the deeds rather than their essences, as is the view of the one who holds that position; rather, it is then used figuratively to mean: "what thing".

The shift from addressing them to the third person ("when it is recited to them") is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), turning away from them and directing the address to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It enumerates their offences, which opposed what was intended of them through the vicegerency (istikhlaf): denying the Messenger, disbelieving the clear signs, and other things, "like the practice of those before them of the destroyed generations." The present tense of the verb indicates the renewal of their answer, which recurs with the renewal of the recitation. ﴿Our signs﴾ indicate the truth of monotheism (tawhid) and the falsity of polytheism (shirk). The attribution (idafah) honours what is attributed and encourages belief in it and warns against denying it. ﴿clear﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier: they are clear in indicating that. Mentioning the verb of recitation in the passive, with ﴿Our signs﴾ as its subject rather than the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as the active agent, indicates that there is no need to specify the reciter, and signals that their speech concerns the recited text itself and not the one reciting it.

﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us say﴾: the relative pronoun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that what is in the relative clause is the cause of the great [offence] attributed to them, and that they dared to say it only because they did not fear His punishment on the Day of Meeting, due to their denial of it and of what is among its preliminaries, namely the resurrection. It also censures them for this. That is, they said to the one who recites these verses to them, who is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he is not mentioned here to indicate that he is definite: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this﴾. They pointed by "this" to the Qur'an containing those signs, not only to the signs themselves, intending to remove the whole from between them. That is: bring another book that we may read, one that contains nothing of what we find unlikely, such as the resurrection, the reckoning and the recompense, and what we dislike, such as the censure of our gods, their faults, and the threat against worshipping them.

﴿Or change it﴾: by altering its arrangement, by putting in place of the verse containing those things another verse free of them. They said this out of guile and in hope of his cooperation, so that they might use it to compel him and to mock him.

﴿Say﴾ to them: ﴿It is not for me﴾, that is, it is not proper or suitable for me, and I am not able at all, ﴿to change it of my own accord﴾, that is, on my own initiative. This is a verbal noun used as an adverb of time and place, and it is also read with the letter tā' vocalised with a fatha.

The restriction of the answer to demonstrating the impossibility of what they proposed first, rather than their second proposal, indicates that the impossibility of their first proposal is so evident that there is no need to explain it. Moreover, addressing it, though it is futile, may be regarded as a kind of indulging the foolish, since such a proposal would not come from people of sense. Also, what proves the impossibility of the second proves the impossibility of the first all the more.

﴿I follow only﴾, that is, I follow nothing in what I bring and leave aside, ﴿what is revealed to me﴾ without any alteration to it whatsoever. This is in the sense of restricting his state (ﷺ) to following what is revealed to him, not restricting his following to what is revealed to him, as is apparent from the wording, as if it were said: "I do nothing except follow what is revealed to me." The detailed treatment of this matter has already been given in the commentary on Surat al-An'am. This is a justification of the opening statement, for one whose duty is to follow revelation in the form in which it is, certainly does not act independently of it in anything. In this there is also an answer to the objection of abrogation (naskh), i.e. that some verses abrogate others, and a rejection of their insinuation against him (ﷺ) by this question, namely that the Qur'an is his own speech. For this reason, the change in the answer is qualified by the phrase ﴿of my own accord﴾. He also called it a great disobedience entailing a great punishment, in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a mighty Day﴾. This is a justification of the content of what precedes it, namely the impossibility of alteration and the restriction of his (ﷺ) command to following revelation. That is: I fear, if I disobey Him, the Exalted, by undertaking what is not mine to do, namely altering it of my own accord, and by turning away from following revelation, the punishment of a mighty Day, which is the Day of Resurrection, or the Day of Meeting which they do not expect. In this there is an indication that they deserved it by this proposal.

The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah), together with its attribution to his (ﷺ) pronoun, serves to magnify the matter of disobedience and to show the perfect purity of the Prophet (ﷺ) from it. The mention of the Day with nunation of magnification (al-tanwin al-tafkhimi), and its description as great, serves to magnify and make dreadful the punishment in it. There is no room to interpret their proposal as an alteration and bringing of another Qur'an by way of revelation, by explaining His words, ﴿It is not for me to change it of my own accord﴾, as meaning that it is not easy for me to change it by seeking it through revelation. [Such an interpretation is rejected] for "I follow only what is revealed to me" without any contrivance of seeking or otherwise on my part. The justification mentioned rejects this, not because the proposal then contains no disobedience at all, as has been supposed. For seeking the alteration of revealed verses, in accordance with what the legislative wisdom requires, by replacing some with others, especially at the prompting of the disbelievers' proposal, is undoubtedly a disobedience. Rather, it is because this proposal does not contain the disobedience of fabrication, although that is the one intended by what is mentioned in the justification. Do you not see that the two noble verses after it are explicit that their proposal was to bring other than the Qur'an and to alter it by way of fabrication, and that their claim in the first place was also of this kind?

And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 16:

﴿Say: "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you through me."﴾ This is a confirmation of the truth of the Qur'an and of its being from Allah the Exalted, following the demonstration of the falsity of what they proposed to bring, and of its impossibility in both expression and meaning. The command was introduced in a separate, independent form, although it falls under the previous command, in order to show the utmost care for its matter and to announce its independence in concept and style. For it is a proof that it is by the command and will of Allah the Exalted, as will come. What preceded was merely a report of the impossibility of what they proposed. The object of "willed" (shā'a) is omitted, indicated by the conditional clause, and nothing more, as has been said. For the object of the will is only omitted when it occurs in a conditional clause and its object is implied by the consequent, and when its connection to it is not strange, as in the verse:

"Had I willed to weep blood, I would have wept it."

Here it was not omitted, because the final condition is absent. Also, what necessitates the consequent, namely the non-recitation of it by him, ﷺ, to them, is only the will of Allah the Exalted regarding him, not His will regarding something other than the Qur'an.

The meaning: all matters are contingent upon the will of Allah the Exalted, and I have no share in them whatsoever. Had He willed that I not recite it to you, not by my own choice to refrain from reciting it, but by His not sending it down to me and not commanding me to recite it, as the preference of "recitation" over "reading" indicates, then I would not have recited it to you.

﴿Nor would He have made it known to you through me﴾: that is, nor would He have informed you of it through my agency. The consequent, namely non-recitation and non-informing, is false, so the antecedent is negated, namely the will for non-recitation. It is clear that the will for non-recitation necessarily entails the absence of the will for recitation, so the negation of the former necessarily entails the negation of the latter; and the negation of the absence of the will for recitation occurs only through the establishment of the will for recitation. Thus it is established that his recitation of the Qur'an, ﷺ, is by the will and command of Allah the Exalted. We have restricted the informing to being through him, ﷺ, because the absence of informing in general is not among the necessary consequences of the condition, which is the will for his non-recitation, ﷺ, and therefore it may not be placed in the chain of the consequent.

The attribution of non-informing to Him, the Exalted, which indicates that informing is attributed to Him, the Exalted, is a notice that he, ﷺ, has no role in that, as the context requires.

It has been read as "wa-lā adra'tukum" and "wa-lā adrakum" with a hamza in both, according to the dialect of those who say a'taʾtu and arḍa'tu for a'ṭaytu and arḍaytu; or it is from al-darʾ, meaning "repelling", that is: nor would I have made you adversaries who repel me with disputation through my reciting it to you. It has also been read as "wa-lā andharatukum bihi" ("nor would I have warned you with it"), and it has been read as "la-adrakum" with the lām of the response, that is: had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, and He would certainly have informed you of it through the tongue of another, in the sense that it is the truth from which there is no escape; had I not been sent with it, another would certainly have been sent with it. Or in the sense that He, the Exalted, bestows favour upon whom He wills, and has singled me out with this honour.

﴿For I have dwelt among you a lifetime﴾: this is a justification for the necessary connection that entails the recitation being by the will and command of Allah the Exalted, as explained above; but not by way of inferring it from his, ﷺ, non-recitation before by reason of His will for him, but by way of citing as evidence what they witnessed from him, ﷺ, during that long period, of matters that demonstrate the impossibility that the recitation should come from him, ﷺ, without revelation. "A lifetime" ('umuran) is put in the accusative by analogy with a time adverb. The meaning: I have remained among you for a long span of time, the amount of forty years, during which you have known all the details of my circumstances and have full knowledge of what is with me.

﴿before it﴾: that is, before the descent of the Qur'an, I did not engage in anything connected with it, neither from the standpoint of its inimitable composition, nor from the standpoint of its meaning, which reveals the secrets of realities and the rulings of the laws.

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾: that is, will you not consider this, and so not reason the impossibility of its issuing from one like me, and the necessity of its being sent down from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise? For this is not hidden from one who has sound reason.

The truth from which there is no escape is that whoever has even a small measure of intellect, if he reflects on his affair, ﷺ, and that he grew up among them this long period without associating with scholars in any matter, nor referring to them in any art, nor mixing with eloquent people in discourse and debate, nor engaging with them in composing sermons and poetry, and then brought a Book whose eloquence overwhelmed every skilled eloquent speaker, and whose rhetoric surpassed every refined orator, whose composition rose above every prose and verse, and whose content contained the wonders of all kinds of knowledge, revealing the secrets of the unseen from behind the veils of concealment, speaking of the reports of what has been and what will be, confirming what lies before it of the revealed Books and watching over them in their general and detailed rulings, there remains in his heart no trace of doubt that it is a revelation sent down from Allah. This is what the consensus of the majority agrees upon.

However, the more fitting approach, given that the answer in what preceded was based on the mere impossibility of his issuing any alteration or substitution, because that would be a disobedience entailing a great punishment, and his condition being limited to following revelation and refraining from arbitrary opinion, without addressing there or here whether the Qur'an in itself is beyond human capacity or whether he, ﷺ, is unable to bring its like, is to adduce here, in support of the claim, what befits that from his continuous circumstances during that extended period, of his complete purity from anything that might suggest the issuing of lying or fabrication from him against anyone whatsoever, as its following with the condemnation of the one who fabricates against Allah the Exalted indicates.

The meaning: I have remained among you before the revelation, never imposing upon anyone by arbitrary decree, nor by dispute, nor have I hovered around any speech containing a trace of doubt, let alone what contains lying or fabrication. Will you not consider and so not reason that one whose constant state throughout this distant era is such, it is impossible that he would fabricate against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and impose upon all creation commands and prohibitions entailing the seizure of wealth, the shedding of blood, and the like; and that what he brought is a clear revelation (p-131), a sending down from the Lord of the worlds. And His words, Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 17:

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari), whose meaning is negation: that is, there is no one more unjust than him, in the sense that he is more unjust than every wrongdoer. Although the construction of the expression conveys the denial that anyone could be more unjust than him, without addressing the denial or negation of equality, for when it is said, "Who is more excellent than so-and-so?" or "There is no one more knowledgeable than him," it is necessarily understood that he is more excellent than every excellent person and more knowledgeable than every knowing person. The addition of His words, exalted is He, "a lie" (kadhiban), although invention (iftira') is never anything but that, serves to indicate that what they attributed to Him implicitly, and imposed upon him (ﷺ) explicitly, is, in addition to being an invention against Allah exalted is He, a lie in itself. For an invention may be a lie only in its attribution, as when the sin of Zayd is attributed to 'Amr. This is an intensification, on his part (ﷺ), of his avoidance of what has been mentioned of inventing against Allah, glorified is He.

﴿Or denies His signs﴾, and so disbelieves in them. This is a wronging of the polytheists through their denial of the Qur'an and their attributing it to him (ﷺ). The particle fa' (فاء) (here "so" or "then") serves to order the discourse upon what preceded regarding the Qur'an being by the will and command of Allah exalted is He. Thus there is no room for taking the invention here to mean the invention of attributing a son and a partner.
