That is: since the matter is as such, whoever invents against Allah exalted is He by fabricating speech and saying, "This is from Allah" — or who substitutes some of His signs exalted is He for others, as you permit this regarding me, and likewise whoever denies His signs exalted is He as you do — is more unjust than every wrongdoer.

﴿Indeed, He﴾: the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n), placed as the subject of "inna," and the predicate is the clause that follows it. The basis for placing it in this position is the claim of its fame, which renders its mention unnecessary. The benefit of introducing the sentence with it is to indicate the grandeness of its content, along with the added effect of fixing it more firmly in the mind. For the pronoun is not understood at first except as an ambiguous matter of importance, so the mind remains awaiting what follows it, and thus it becomes firmly established upon its arrival with especial firmness. It is as though it were said: "Indeed, the matter is this, namely: ﴿The criminals will not succeed﴾," that is, they will not escape from what they fear, nor attain what they seek. The intended meaning is the category of criminals, so that the inventor and the denier are included in it by primary inclusion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 18:

﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which neither harms them nor benefits them.﴾ This is a narration of another transgression of theirs, from which their first transgression arose. It is conjoined to His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ (the verse), coordinating one narrative with another. "Min dūni" (besides) is connected to "ya'budūna" (they worship), and its place in i'rab is the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its subject, meaning: going beyond Allah, glorified is He, not in the sense of abandoning His worship entirely, but in the sense of not being content with it and making it a companion to the worship of idols, as the context of the noble arrangement reveals. ﴿That which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ means: that which by its nature has no power to harm or benefit, namely the idols, which are inanimate objects. "Mā" is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun. The negation of harm is placed first because the least of the requirements of worship is the averting of harm, which is the first of benefits. Worship is a newly arising matter preceded by non-existence, which is the very place where harm is suspected; so, since the idols cannot inflict harm, there is no cause for bringing worship into being. It has been said: they neither harm them if they abandon worshipping them, nor benefit them if they worship them. The people of al-Ta'if worshipped al-Lat, and the people of Makkah worshipped al-'Uzza, Manat, Hubal, Isaf and Na'ila.

﴿And they say: "These are our intercessors with Allah."﴾ It is narrated from al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, al-Lat will intercede for me." It has been said: they believed that the one who governs each region is a particular spirit among the spirits of the celestial spheres. So they designated for that spirit a particular idol among the idols and occupied themselves with its worship, while their true aim was that spirit. Then they believed that this spirit, in the presence of the Supreme God, is occupied with His worship. It has also been said: they used to worship the stars, so they set up specific idols for them and occupied themselves with worshipping them, intending thereby the worship of the stars. It has been said: they inscribed specific talismans upon those idols, then drew near to them through them. It has also been said: they set these idols in the forms of their prophets and their great ones, and they claimed that whenever they occupied themselves with worshipping these images, those great ones would intercede for them with Allah, exalted be He.

﴿Say﴾ in rebuke to them: ﴿Do you inform Allah of what He does not know?﴾ That is: do you tell Him of something that has no existence at all, namely that the idols are your intercessors with Allah, exalted be He? For if it had any existence, the Knower of the unseen would know it. In this there is reproach and mockery of them and of what they claim, of the impossibility that scarcely falls within the bounds of soundness and possibility. It is read " atunabbi'ūna" with lightened pronunciation.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿in the heavens or in the earth﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the omitted returning pronoun in "ya'lamu", serving to emphasise the negation, because what does not exist in them is, by custom, non-existent. ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him﴾: above their association, which entails that false saying, or above their partners whom they believe to be their intercessors with Allah, exalted be He. It is read "tushrikūna" with the second person, as being part of the speech commanded to be said; and on the first reading it is a concluding parenthetical remark from His part, glorified and exalted be He.

﴿Mankind was but one community﴾ is an explanation that tawhid (affirming the oneness of God) and Islam (submission to God) are an ancient religion (milla) upon which all people were unanimous, both by innate nature (fitra) and by revealed law (tashri'). The polytheism (shirk) and its branches are ignorances invented by the misguided, in opposition to the majority and in breaking the unity of the community.

As for taking their (the people's) "taking" (ittikhadhihim) to mean that they agreed upon misguidance during the interval (fatra) between prophets, and their disagreement being about what they had of following and persistence in it, this has no possibility. That is, the meaning is: mankind, from the beginning, was entirely united upon the truth and tawhid without any disagreement. This lasted from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until Qabil (Cain) killed Habil (Abel). It was said: until the time of Idris, peace be upon him. It was said: until the time of Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him. It was said: from the time of the Flood, when God left none of the disbelievers upon the earth, until disbelief appeared among them. It was said: from the time of Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, until 'Amr ibn Luhayy spread the worship of idols. Thus, by "mankind" is meant the Arabs specifically, and this is the most fitting reading, given that the noble verse follows the mention of what was reported of them of blunders and the declaration of the exalted status of Majesty above such things.

﴿Then they differed﴾: some of them disbelieved and others remained upon what they were upon, so each of the two groups opposed the other. This does not mean that each of them devised a separate religion from among the religions of disbelief, opposing the religion of the other, for the discourse is not about that kind of disagreement, since each of them would then be a falsifier, and it is inconceivable that judgment be passed between them by preserving the one upon truth and destroying the one upon falsehood. The resultative fa' (al-fa' al-ta'qibiyya, the "fa" indicating sequence) does not contradict the extension of the period of agreement, since the intended meaning is to show that disagreement occurred immediately after the end of the period of agreement, not immediately after the beginning of the agreement.

﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾: concerning the postponement of the judgment between them, or the postponement of the decisive punishment between them until the Day of Resurrection, for it is the Day of Decision, ﴿surely the matter would have been decided between them﴾ immediately, ﴿concerning that about which they differ﴾, by distinguishing truth from falsehood, preserving the one upon truth and destroying the one upon falsehood. The use of the imperfective form (yakhtalifun, "they differ") is to depict a past situation and to indicate continuity.

(p-133) ﴿And they say﴾ — this recounts another of their offences, coordinated with His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they worship﴾ (verse 18). The verb is in the present tense to bring before the mind the image of their shameful statement and to indicate its continuity. The speakers are the people of Makkah.

﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ They meant: a sign of the kind they had proposed. As though, from their extreme rebellion and corruption, and their utmost persistence in obstinacy and stubbornness, they did not count the clear proofs sent down upon him ﷺ as being of the category of signs, and proposed others instead, even though there had been sent down to him manifest signs and abundant miracles that would compel them to submit and accept, if they had been people of intellect.

So say to them in reply: ﴿Surely the unseen belongs to Allah﴾ — the lam here denotes exclusive knowledge, not exclusive power to create; for the unseen and the seen are equal in that exclusivity. The meaning is: what you have proposed, and claimed to be a necessary consequence of prophethood, and made your faith contingent upon its descent, is among the unseen matters specific to Allah, exalted is He, and I have no knowledge of it. ﴿So wait﴾ for its descent; ﴿surely I am with you among those who wait﴾ — that is, for what Allah will do to you for your audacity in committing such a great act as denying the signs and proposing others. Taking "the unseen" to mean the impediment to sending down the proposed signs is ruled out by the arrangement of the command to wait upon the unseen being exclusively His, exalted is He.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 21:**

﴿And when We let people taste mercy﴾, meaning health and abundance, ﴿after hardship has touched them﴾, meaning it has mixed with them until they felt the harm of its effect on them. Attributing the touching to the hardship, after attributing the causing to taste to the divine name (*damir al-jalala*, the pronoun referring to Allah), is one of the Qur'anic courtesies, as in His saying: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ and its like. It was said: Allah imposed on the people of Makkah a drought for seven years, until they nearly perished. Then He showed them mercy with rain, and they began to revile His signs, to oppose His Messenger (ﷺ), and to plot against him. This is His saying: ﴿then they have a scheme against Our signs﴾, meaning by slandering them, disregarding them, and devising ways to repel them. The first ﴿إذا﴾ (*idha*) is conditional, and the second is its response; it is as if it were said: they suddenly encountered the effect of the scheme from them. The indefiniteness of (*makr*, scheme) is for emphasis, and ﴿في﴾ (*fi*, "against") is related to the stable predicate (*al-istiqrar*) to which the preposition *lam* is attached. ﴿Say: Allah is swifter in scheming﴾, meaning: His punishment is quicker in reaching you than what you do in repelling the truth. Calling the punishment "scheming" is because it occurs in response to their scheming, whether in existence or in mention. ﴿Indeed, Our messengers﴾, who guard your deeds, and the attribution is for honour, ﴿record what you scheme﴾, meaning your scheming, or what you scheme, and this is a confirmation of retribution against them and an alert that what they plotted to hide is not hidden from the guardians (*al-hafazah*, the recording angels), let alone from the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. The form of the future tense (*sighat al-istiqbal*, the imperfect verb form) in both verbs indicates continuity and renewal. The sentence is a justification from Him, Exalted, for the swiftness of His scheming, glorified is He, and is not part of the spoken discourse, like His saying: ﴿Even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾. The recording of the messengers of what they scheme is among the beginnings of the nullification of their scheming and the complete failure of its effect, and in this there is an exaggeration beyond description. The shift in address, turning it away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward them, is for intensifying the rebuke. It was also read in the third-person form (*lafz al-ghaybah*), in which case it is a justification for what was mentioned, or for a command.(p-134)

**Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 10, verse 22:**

﴿He it is who enables you to travel﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new clause that continues the discourse without grammatical attachment), brought to explain another of their offences, which is based on what has passed just before, namely the variation in their condition according to the variations that befall them of ease and hardship. That is: He enables you to travel, a continuous enabling, both during the act of travel and before it, ﴿on land﴾, on foot and on riding animals. It is also read (*yanshurukum*), "He spreads you," from *al-nashr* (dispersal), and from it is His saying, Exalted and Mighty is He: "Then, behold, you are human beings who scatter abroad" (Q 30:20).

﴿and at sea, until when you are in the ships﴾. "Ships" (*al-fulk*) is the plural of *falak* on the pattern of *usud*, the plural of *asad* (lion), not on the pattern of *qufl*. The endpoint of the "enabling" is not the beginning of their boarding the ships. Rather, the whole conditional clause is the intended meaning, as is indicated by the choice of the verb "to be" (*al-kawn*), which implies continuity, over "to board" (*al-rukub*), which implies occurrence. ﴿and they sail with them﴾: the ships sail with them, "them" referring to those in them. The shift to the third person (*iltifat*, a change of grammatical person in mid-discourse) is to signal their bad condition, which calls for turning away from them. It is as though He is describing their evil states to others, in order to make them marvel at them and to elicit their denunciation and censure. It has been said that there is no *iltifat* here. Rather, the meaning of His words, "until when you are in the ships," is "when some of you are in them," since the address is to all, and among them are those who travel on land. The pronoun in the third person then refers back to that implied genitive (*mudaf muqaddar*, an understood noun in construction), as in His words: "Or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by a wave" (Q 24:40), that is: or like those in darkness in a deep sea, which a wave covers.

﴿with a favourable wind﴾, gentle in its blowing and suited to their aim, ﴿and they rejoice in it﴾, in that wind, because of its goodness and its suitability. ﴿there comes upon them﴾ is the answer of *idha* (when). The pronoun in the accusative refers to the favourable wind; that is, it (the violent wind) overtakes it and takes control of it from a direction opposite to it. The blowing in agreement with it is not usually called the arrival of another wind, but rather a strengthening of the first wind. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the ship (*al-fulk*). The first view is more apparent, because it entails the second without the reverse being true: blowing in the direction of the gentle wind counts as an arrival in relation to the ship, but not the gentle wind itself, and moreover it does not necessarily involve the clashing of waves that requires their coming from every place. Also, the awe-inspiring effect in describing its taking control of what they rejoiced in and attached the ropes of their hopes to is greater.

﴿a violent wind﴾, that is, possessing violence (*'asf*). It has been said that *'usuf* (violence) is specific to wind, so there is no need for a distinguishing marker (for the feminine). It has been said that *al-rih* (wind) may also be masculine. ﴿and the waves come to them﴾ on the ship ﴿from every place﴾, that is, from the places from which waves usually come. There is no improbability in its coming from all sides as well, since its coming need not be only from the direction of the blowing wind. It may come from other directions according to causes that happen to arise for it. ﴿and they think they are encompassed﴾, that is, they are destroyed, since this is a figure of speech for destruction, originally based on an enemy surrounding a tribe, or all routes of escape being blocked to them. ﴿they call upon God﴾ is a substitute for "they think" (*badal*), a substitution of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*), because of the connection and necessary relation between the two. Or it is a resumptive sentence based on a question that naturally arises in the mind, as though it were said: "What did they do?" and the answer is: "They called upon God." ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, without associating with Him any of their gods, not merely dedicating the supplication to Him, Exalted is He, but also worship. For by merely dedicating supplication to Him, Exalted is He, they would not be sincere to Him in religion.

﴿If You deliver us from this﴾. The *lam* is an introductory *lam* (*lam al-muwatta'a*, preparing for an oath), on the understanding of an implied verb of saying, meaning: saying, "By God, if You deliver us from this," ﴿from this﴾ predicament, ﴿we will surely be﴾ absolutely and forever after that ﴿among the grateful﴾ for Your blessings, of which this blessing being requested is one. It has been said that the clause is the object of "they called" (*da'awa*), because supplication is a kind of speech. The first view is preferable because the second requires that their supplication be restricted to that alone. In His words, "we will surely be among the grateful," there is an emphasis in indicating that they are steadfast in gratitude, persevering in it, and counted among those described as grateful and firmly rooted in it, which is not conveyed by saying "we will surely give thanks" (*la-nashkurannal*).

Then, when He delivered them, behold, they committed injustice on the earth without right. The fa' here indicates the swiftness of their response. [They] "behold, they were transgressing" (yabghūna) in the earth, meaning they encountered corruption in it and hastened to it, racing one another in it and exceeding the limits of corruption they had previously been in. The word derives from the saying "bagha al-jurh" (the wound transgressed), when it spreads in corruption. The addition of "in the earth" indicates that their transgression encompassed all its regions. The present tense (ṣīghat al-muḍāriʿ) indicates renewal and continuity. His saying, "without right," is an emphasis on what transgression (al-baghy) already implies. Or its meaning is: it is without right in their own view as well, in that it is manifest injustice whose ugliness is hidden from no one, as in His saying, "and they kill the prophets without right" (3:112). As for what has been said, that it is a precaution against transgression with right, such as the ghazis destroying the abodes of the unbelievers, cutting down their trees, and burning their crops, the noble composition does not support this, because it is based on transgression meaning the spoiling of a thing's form and the nullification of its benefit, not the meaning mentioned, which suits the state of the corrupters.

"O mankind" is a turning of the address to those transgressors, for intensifying the threat and exaggerating the warning. "Your transgression" is what you engage in, and it is the subject (mubtada'). His saying, "is only against yourselves," is its predicate (khabar), meaning: it is against you in reality, not against those whom you transgress against, even if it is thought to be so. His saying, "the enjoyment of the worldly life," is an explanation that the immediate benefit in it is a thing of no account, swiftly passing away, and lasting in its ruin. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasising a verb that is implied by way of resumption (isti'nāf), meaning: you enjoy the enjoyment of the worldly life. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun standing in the place of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: enjoying the worldly life. The governing element is the stability (istiqrār) contained in the predicate, not the transgression itself, because that would lead to separating the verbal noun from its complement by the predicate, and one does not predicate of a relative pronoun until its relative clause is complete. You are aware that restricting their transgression to being against themselves by the condition of their enjoying the worldly life has no meaning worth considering. It has also been said that it is an adverb of time, like "the arrival of the pilgrim" (maqdam al-ḥājj), meaning the time of the enjoyment of the worldly life, and what has passed applies to it exactly.

It has also been said that it is an object of a verb indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: you seek the enjoyment of the worldly life. It is not hidden that this does not indicate transgression in the sense of seeking, and making the verbal noun also bear that meaning disturbs the eloquence of the noble composition, because the resumption is to explain the evil end of what was reported of them concerning transgression, interpreted as excessive corruption, which suits their state. So what relation is there between it and transgression in the sense of seeking? Making the first [term] also bear that meaning is something that must be averted from the sanctity of the revelation.

It has also been said that it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: for the sake of the enjoyment of the worldly life, and the governing element is the stability mentioned. In this there is the point that what is caused by the mentioned [factor] is the transgression itself, not its being against themselves. It has been said: "against themselves." It has been said that the governing element in it is a verb indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: you transgress for the sake of the enjoyment of the worldly life, with the sentence being a resumption. It has been said that it is a direct object (mafʿūl ṣarīḥ) of the verbal noun, and "against yourselves" is a superfluous adverbial phrase (ẓarf laghw) connected to it. By "the selves" is meant the kind, and the predicate is omitted due to the length of the speech. The estimation is: "Your transgression against the sons of your kind for the enjoyment of the worldly life is to be feared, or its manifest corruption, or something like that." In this there is what has passed concerning its being based on what is not fitting to the context, namely that transgression means seeking.

Indeed, if its accusative were taken as a cause (ʿilla), meaning: "Your transgression against the sons of your kind for the sake of the enjoyment of the worldly life is to be feared," as one of them chose, it would have some validity in general. But the truth required by the eloquence of the revelation is only the first. It was also read as "enjoyment" (matāʿu) in the nominative, as the predicate, and the adverbial phrase is connected to the verbal noun, or it is a second predicate, or a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is the enjoyment of... etc., as in His saying, "except an hour of a day, a notification" (46:35), meaning: this is a notification.

So "themselves" in the first way means the sons of their kind. It was expressed thus only to stir their compassion for them and to urge them to abandon preferring the mentioned enjoyment over their rights. There is no room for taking it literally, because their transgression being a burden upon them is not established in their view, as is required by what is reported of them, and it has not yet been stated so that it might be made part of the speech, and its being an enjoyment made the intended point of the statement. Moreover, the notion of it being a burden upon them is detrimental to it being an enjoyment, let alone it being one of the origins of its establishment for the subject, as is apparent from the context.

As for their transgression against the sons of the kind, its establishment is known among them, and it contains the origins of enjoyment: taking wealth, dominating people, and other things. As for the last two ways, there is no reason to deviate from the literal meaning, for the subject is either the transgression itself or the pronoun referring to it in its own right, not insofar as it is a burden upon them, as in the case where the adverbial phrase is connected to the verbal noun. So reflect.

It was read as "enjoyment" (matāʿan) in the accusative, and "the worldly life" (al-ḥayāta) in the accusative. As for the accusative of "enjoyment," it is as has passed. As for the accusative of "the life," it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for "enjoyment." It has been said that it is a direct object of "enjoyment," if its accusative is not as a verbal noun, because an emphatic verbal noun does not govern.

It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Do not deceive, nor help a deceiver; do not transgress, nor help a transgressor; do not break [a pledge], nor help one who breaks it." And he used to recite it.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "Three things, whoever has them, they will return upon him: transgression, breaking [a pledge], and deception." God the Exalted says: "Your transgression is only against yourselves" (10:23), "and they plot only against themselves" (6:123), "whoever breaks [his pledge] breaks it only to his own detriment" (48:10).

And from him ﷺ: "The swiftest of good in reward is the maintenance of kinship ties, and the swiftest of evil in punishment is transgression and a perjurous oath." It is also narrated: "Two things God hastens for [a person] in this world: transgression and disobedience to parents." And from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "If one mountain transgressed against another mountain, the transgressor would be crushed."

"Then to Us is your return" is coordinated with the implied resumed sentence that has passed, as if it were said: "You enjoy the enjoyment of the worldly life, then you return to Us." The construction was changed to a nominal sentence with the prepositional phrase fronted, to indicate permanence and restriction. "Then We will inform you of what you used to do" in the world, persistently in transgression. This is a threat of recompense and punishment, like the saying of a man to one who threatens him: "I will inform you of what you did." In this there is a hidden subtlety built upon a noble wisdom: that everything that appears in this creation, of substances and accidents, appears in a form different from its true form, by which it will appear in the afterlife. Sins, for example, are deadly poisons which in this world have appeared in a form that the souls of the disobedient find pleasing; likewise acts of obedience, though they are the most beautiful of beauties, have appeared to them in disliked forms. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said: "Paradise is surrounded by disliked things, and Hellfire is surrounded by desires." So transgression in this creation, although it appears in a form that transgressors desire and the misguided find pleasing because of the enjoyment they get from it, in terms of taking wealth, avenging themselves on enemies, and the like, yet that is not enjoyment in reality; rather it is harm from where they do not reckon. This becomes clear to them only when what they were doing of transgression is brought forth in the form of its true reality, which is contrary to the form they were seeing it in. This is what is meant by the mentioned "informing." And God, glorified and exalted, knows best.

(p-137) ﴿Indeed, the likeness of the life of this world﴾ is a resumptive statement, brought to explain the state of the worldly life, the brevity of the period of enjoying it, and the nearness of the promised return. Its strange condition, wondrous in its nature and unique in its likeness, has been compared, owing to its strangeness, within the category of parables, in the swiftness of its passing and the cutting off of its bliss after its arrival and people's deception by it, to the condition of the varieties of plants on the earth in the sudden disappearance of their splendour and freshness and their going away as debris, leaving no trace at all after they had been tender and fresh, their parts intertwined with one another, the earth adorned with their colours, and strengthened after their weakness, so that people became eager and thought they were safe from calamities. The thing compared to (al-mushabbah bihi) is not what the kaf (ka) entered upon in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿like water which We sent down from the sky, so the plants of the earth mingled with it﴾; rather it is what is understood from the statement as a whole, for it is a compound simile (al-tashbih al-murakkab).

﴿Of what men and cattle eat﴾, from the herbs, crops and fodder. ﴿Until, when the earth takes on its adornment﴾: the earth, in its adornment through what is upon it of the various kinds, forms and colours of plants, is made to take on its ornament in the manner of a metaphor for a bride who has taken on the colours of garments and adornments, and so has adorned herself with them. The verb (ازَّيَّنَتْ) originally is تَزَيَّنَتْ, and it was assimilated (idghām). It has also been read according to the original form, and it has been read (وَأزْيَنَتْ) like أغْيَلَتْ without i'lal (vowel-change of weak letters). The meaning: it became possessed of adornment; and (ازْيانَّتْ) is like (ابْياضَّتْ).

﴿And its people think that they have power over it﴾: able to harvest it and gather its produce. ﴿Then Our command comes upon it﴾: this is the answer to (إذا, "when"), meaning: the calamities and afflictions that destroy it struck its crop, ﴿by night or by day, and We make it﴾: that is, its crop, and evil is what is upon it, ﴿into stubble﴾: that is, like what has been reaped from its root, ﴿as though it had not flourished﴾: as though its crop had not flourished; the genitive noun is omitted for emphasis. It has also been read with the verb in the masculine form. ﴿Yesterday﴾: that is, previously, within a near time, for "yesterday" is a proverbial expression for this; as if it were said: it had not flourished a moment ago. ﴿Thus﴾: that is, like that wondrous detailing ﴿We detail the signs﴾: that is, the Qur'anic signs, of which these signs alerting to the states of the worldly life are part; that is, We clarify and explain them. ﴿For a people who reflect﴾ upon their intricacies, and who stand upon their meanings. The restriction of its detailing to them is because they are the ones who benefit from it. It is also permissible that by the signs is meant what was mentioned within the parable of the created and perishing things, and by detailing them is meant their being made to change in the order described, in existence and annihilation, for they are signs and indications by which whoever reflects upon them is guided to the states of the worldly life, in its present state and its end.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 25:

﴿And God calls to the Abode of Peace﴾. This is an encouragement of people toward the everlasting life of the Hereafter, following their being encouraged away from the transient life of this world. That is, He calls all people to the abode of safety from every hateful thing and calamity, which is Paradise. It is mentioned by this name in order to contrast it with the world, which is described by what corresponds to this name, namely that it is a place exposed to calamities. Or [it means]: He calls to the abode of God Most High, and the restricting of the honorific attribution to this noble name is to draw attention to that. Or [it means]: He calls to an abode in which God - or the angels - greet those who enter it, or in which some of them greet others.

﴿And He guides whom He wills﴾ to His guidance from among them ﴿to a straight path﴾ that leads to it, which is Islam and provisioning oneself with piety. In the generalizing of the call and the restricting of guidance to His will is evidence that the command is other than the will, and that whoever persists in misguidance, God has not willed his right guidance.

For those who did good: that is, their deeds, meaning they performed them in the fitting manner, which is their descriptive goodness, entailing their intrinsic goodness. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it by his saying: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." ﴿The best (reward)﴾: that is, the best recompense. ﴿And more﴾: that is, what exceeds that recompense, out of bounty, in accordance with His saying, exalted is His name: ﴿and He will give them more of His bounty﴾. It was also said: the best (reward) is like their good deeds, and the increase is ten times their like, up to seven hundred fold and more. It was also said: the increase is forgiveness from Allah and good pleasure. It was also said: the best (reward) is Paradise, and the increase is the meeting (with Allah). ﴿And no darkness shall cover their faces﴾: that is, it shall not cover them, ﴿qatar﴾ (darkness), a dust in which there is blackness. ﴿Nor humiliation﴾: that is, any trace of disgrace or the dimming of dejection. The meaning: there shall not befall them what befalls the people of the Fire, or what would necessitate that of grief and bad condition. The indefiniteness (of the words) is for belittling, that is, any part of these two. The sentence is resumed to explain their safety from hardships, following the explanation of their success in attaining their desires. The second (clause), although it implies the first, is mentioned as a reminder of what Allah, exalted is He, delivers them from by His mercy. Placing the object before the subject is for the sake of emphasis, showing that what is safeguarded from being covered is the noblest of their organs, and for creating suspense for the delayed element: when something that should be placed first is delayed, the soul remains anticipating its arrival, and when it arrives, it settles there with greater firmness. Also, the subject contains a kind of detailed specification, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿From them come forth pearls and coral﴾, and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And there has come to you in this the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers﴾.

﴿Those﴾: a reference to those mentioned, in view of their being characterized by the attributes mentioned. The distance implied in the demonstrative is to indicate the elevation of their rank and the loftiness of their station, that is: those who are described with the beautiful qualities mentioned, who are successful in attaining the rewards and who are saved from hardships. ﴿They are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide eternally﴾ without cessation, remaining forever without departure.

﴿والَّذِينَ كَسَبُوا السَّيِّئاتِ﴾ [And those who earned evil deeds]: that is, shirk and sins. This is a subject (mubtada') with an omitted modifier (al-mudaf) understood. Its predicate (khabar) is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ بِمِثْلِها﴾ [the recompense of an evil is its like]. That is, the recompense of those who earned evil deeds is that one evil is requited with one like it, and no more is added to it, unlike what is added for a good deed. The change of construction, where it does not say "and for those who earned the evil deeds, the worst (al-sūʼā)", is to observe the complete distance and contrast between the two groups. The mention of "earning" (al-kasb) indicates that this is only because of the evil of their conduct and due to their crime against themselves. Or the relative clause is conjoined to the first relative clause, as if it were said: "And for those who earned evil deeds is a recompense of an evil like it," as in your saying: "In the house is Zayd, and in the room is ʿAmr." This also indicates that what is meant by the increase (al-ziyada) is grace (al-fadl).

﴿وَتَرْهَقُهم ذِلَّةٌ﴾ [and humiliation will cover them]. And what humiliation! As the magnifying tanwin (tanwin al-tafkhim) indicates. In attributing the covering (al-rahaq) to their selves rather than their faces, there is an indication that it encompasses them, enveloping them all. It is read ﴿يَرْهَقُهُمْ﴾ with the letter ya' (yarhaquhum) [a variant reading (qira'a)]. ﴿ما لَهم مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنَ عاصِمٍ﴾ [they will have no protector from God]. That is, no one will protect them from His wrath and His punishment, exalted is He. Or: they will have from Him, exalted is He, no one who will protect them as there is for the believers. In the negation of a protector there is an exaggeration in negating protection that is not hidden. The sentence is independent (mustaʾnafa), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (tarhaquhum).

﴿كَأنَّما أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهم قِطَعًا مِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ [as if their faces were covered with pieces of the night], due to the extreme blackness and darkness of it. ﴿مُظْلِمًا﴾ [dark] is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the night," and the governing element in it is (ughshiyat), because it is the governing element in (qitaʿan), which is qualified by the prepositional phrase and its object, and the governing element of the qualified noun governs the qualifier. Or the meaning of the verb is in (min al-layl). It is read (qiṭʿan) with the letter ṭāʾ vowelless, and it means a portion of the night. He said:

"Open the door and look at the stars: how many pieces of the dark night are upon us?"

So it is permissible for (muzlimān) to be an adjective of it, or a circumstantial clause from it. It is read (kaʾannamā yughshī wujūhahum qiṭaʿun mina al-layli muẓlimun), and the sentence, like what precedes it, is independent, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (tarhaquhum).

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ [those] — that is, those described by the blameworthy attributes mentioned — ﴿أصْحابُ النّارِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ [are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever]. Since this noble verse concerns the disbelievers, as evidenced by the context and the preceding verses, there is no basis in it for the Wa'idiyya (the school that holds to the doctrine of threat).

﴿And on the Day We gather them all﴾ is a new sentence, brought in to explain another of their dreadful conditions. Its placement in the recitation, although it comes after some of the conditions described earlier in terms of their occurrence, serves to indicate that each of the preceding and following points is independent in its consideration. Had the external order been observed, the whole would have been counted as one matter, as has already been mentioned in the story of the Cow. For this reason it has been separated from what precedes it. The word "Day" (yawm) is in the accusative as the object of an implied verb: "Warn them" or "Remind them." The pronoun in "We gather them" refers to both groups, those who did good and those who earned evil deeds, because this is what is immediately understood from the Most High's words ﴿all together﴾. The second group is singled out in His words ﴿Then We will say to those who associated partners﴾, meaning: We will say to the polytheists among them. This is also because rebuking and threatening them before all witnesses is more terrible, and the statement that all are gathered is more fitting for the awesomeness of the Day. The description of their association (with God) is singled out within the relative clause from among the other evil deeds they earned, because the rebuke and reproach are founded upon it, together with what it indicates that it is the greatest of their crimes and the principal of their evil deeds. It has also been said that the reference is to the second group alone, so that placing the relative pronoun in the place of the pronoun is for the reason mentioned just above.

﴿Stay where you are﴾: "makanakum" is in the accusative because it is originally an adverb of place for a verb which has been replaced by it, not because it is an ism al-fi'l (a verb-like noun, a noun functioning as a verb) whose vowel is an indeclinable vowel (harakat bina'), as is the view of al-Farisi (Abu 'Ali al-Farisi). That is: "Keep to it until you see what will be done to you." ﴿You﴾ is an emphasis of the pronoun that has moved to it from its governing verb, to take its place. ﴿And your partners﴾ is coordinated with it. It has also been read in the accusative, on the basis that the waw means "together with." ﴿Then We separated them﴾ comes from (zilta) "I removed the thing from its place," I remove it; that is, I removed it. The doubling of the letter is for intensification, not for transitivity. It has also been read as "fazayalna," with the same meaning, like "kallamtuhu" and "kalamtuhu." It is coordinated with "We will say." The choice of the past tense form indicates the certainty that is established and assured, for the sake of increasing the rebuke and the regret. The fa' indicates that the separation and its beginnings occurred immediately after the address, without any interval, to show (p-140) the complete looseness of the relationship and connection between the two groups. That is: We separated them and cut off their associates and the ties that had existed between them in the world. But this is not from both sides; rather it is from the side of the worshippers alone, since it is not possible that the partners include the devils, as will come. Thus their hopes were disappointed and the bonds of their desires were broken, and total despair of obtaining from their side what they had hoped for came upon them. Although this state was known to them from the moment of death and of being afflicted with punishment, this degree of certainty was only attained at the time of direct witnessing and face-to-face encounter. It has also been said that the intended meaning of separation is physical separation: that is, We kept them apart after gathering them in the place of standing, and after their partners disowned them and their worship, as in His words ﴿Where are those you used to associate ﴾ ﴿besides God? They will say: They have strayed from us﴾. The waw in His words ﴿And their partners will say﴾ is then a circumstantial waw, with "qad" understood, according to those who require it, and without it according to others; it is not a conjunctive waw as in the first interpretation, because the dialogue requires the presence that is lost through separation. The ordering of the separation in this sense after the command to remain in place does not carry the same subtle point mentioned above as it does under the first meaning, such that the external order would need to be changed in order to observe it. For separation after the dialogue is necessarily so, whereas the severing of associates and ties is not like that; rather its beginning occurs from the moment of gathering, and indeed some of its stages occur before it. What occurs at the time of dialogue is only its extreme limit, as has been indicated. Therefore no account is taken of the change in placing it first. Especially since the subtle point mentioned is observed. And even if it is granted that all its stages come after the dialogue, observing that subtle point is sufficient to call for placing it first. It is also permissible for the waw to be circumstantial on this interpretation as well. By "the partners" is meant, it has been said: the angels, 'Uzayr, the Messiah, and others among the people of knowledge whom they worshipped. In this there is support for the pronoun referring to all of them.

And their saying ﴿You did not used to worship us﴾ is an expression of their disowning of their worship, and that in reality they worshipped only their own desires and their devils who misled them, because these are what commanded them to associate others with God, rather than them. It is like their saying ﴿Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them﴾ … the verse. It has also been said: God, who made everything speak, will make the idols speak, so they address them with this in place of the intercession they used to expect.

"So Allah suffices as a witness between us and you; indeed, We were heedless of your worship" (﴿فَكَفي بِاللَّهِ شَهِيدًا بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَكُمْ﴾ فَإنَّهُ العَلِيمُ الخَبِيرُ ﴿إنْ كُنّا عَنْ عِبادَتِكم لَغافِلِينَ﴾): that is, heedless of your worship of us. The omission of the object here serves to make it evident and to indicate the complete extent of the heedlessness regarding it. Heedlessness is an expression for not being pleased with it; otherwise, the angels' lack of awareness of their being worshipped is not apparent. This rules out the possibility that by "the partners" is meant the devils, as has been said; for their being pleased with their associating others with Allah is beyond doubt, even if they did not compel them to it. Here, inna is the lightened form of inna, and the lam is the lam that distinguishes it (from the negation).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 30:

﴿Hunalika﴾ means: in that dreadful station, or at that time, using the adverb of place for time (tabluu), i.e., tests and experiences ﴿every soul﴾, whether believing or disbelieving, happy or wretched, ﴿what it has sent forward﴾ of deeds, and it witnesses it in its reality, followed by its effects of benefit or harm, good or evil. As for what it knows of its own state from the moment of death and of being tried with punishment in the barzakh, that is something general (mujmal). It is also read as (nabluu), with the first-person plural of majesty and (kull) in the accusative, with ma being a substitution for it, meaning: we deal with it as one who tests it and learns its states of happiness and misery, by testing what it has sent forward of deeds. It may also be meant: we afflict with trial, i.e., punishment, (p-141) the one who is disobedient because of what it has sent forward of evil, so that "ma" is in the accusative by removal of the preposition. It is also read as (tatlu), meaning: follows, because its deed is what guides it to the path of Paradise or to the path of Hellfire, or it reads in the book of its deeds what it has sent forward of good or evil. ﴿And they are returned﴾: the pronoun refers to those who associated partners, being coordinated with (zayyalna), and what is coordinated with it. His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿hunalika tabluu﴾ ... etc., are an interjection in the midst of the narration, confirming its content.

﴿To Allah﴾, i.e., to His recompense and punishment, ﴿their true Lord (mawlahum al-haqq)﴾, i.e., the one whose lordship is established and true, not what they took as a false lord. It is also read as (al-haqqa) in the accusative as praise, like their saying: "Praise be to Allah, worthy of praise," or as an emphasizing infinitive.

﴿And what they used to invent went astray from them﴾: it was lost and vanished, i.e., its loss and error became manifest, not that it had been non-errant before that; or it went astray in their belief too, ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾ concerning their gods interceding for them, or what they used to claim, that they were gods.

This being so, making the pronoun in (ruddu) refer to the souls indicated by "every soul," coordinated with "tabluu," and that the shift to the past tense serves to indicate certainty and settledness, and that choosing the plural form signifies that their return to Allah will be in a collective manner, does not fit with the mention of the attribute of truth in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿their true Lord﴾, for that is an allusion to those who are returned, as has been indicated. And even if it is sufficed to say that this is an allusion to some of them, or the truth is taken to mean justice in reward and punishment, then His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and what they used to fabricate went astray from them﴾, which admits of no room for correction at all, since the pronouns in it are all three referring to the polytheists, necessarily entails a disjunction; and restricting "every soul" to the polytheist souls, despite the generality of the trial for all, is rejected by the context of emphasizing the terror of the situation. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 31:

﴿Say﴾: i.e., to those polytheists whose conditions have been related, and clarifying what their deeds lead to, as an argument for the truth of monotheism (tawhid) and the falsehood of the associationism (shirk) in which they are. ﴿Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾: i.e., from both of them together, for sustenance is obtained through heavenly causes and earthly materials; or from each of them, as an expansion upon you. It has also been said that "min" (from) explains the word "man" (who), with the omission of a modifier, i.e., from the people of the heaven and the earth.

﴿Or who owns hearing and sight﴾: "am" (or) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and what it contains of the word "bal" (rather) serves to turn away from the first interrogation, yet not in the manner of refutation but in the manner of transition, diverting the speech to another interrogation; this is to draw attention to its sufficiency for what is intended, i.e., who is able to create them both and shape them upon this wondrous natural disposition (fitrah), or who protects them from afflictions despite their multitude and the swiftness with which they are affected by the slightest thing that touches them. ﴿And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living﴾: i.e., and who gives life and causes death, or who produces the animal from the sperm-drop and the sperm-drop from the animal. ﴿And who manages the affair﴾: i.e., and who undertakes the management of the affairs of the whole world; this is a generalization after the specification of some of what falls under it, the apparent matters being mentioned explicitly. ﴿Then they will say﴾ without hesitation or delay ﴿"Allah"﴾, since there is no room for obstinacy given its utmost clarity; and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "Allah does what has been mentioned of these acts, not another." ﴿Then say﴾ at that point, as a rebuke to them, ﴿"Will you not then fear [Allah]?"﴾ The hamzah (interrogative particle) is for denying the non-occurrence of taqwa (God-consciousness), in the sense of denying the actual reality, as in "Do you strike your father?", not in the sense of denying the occurrence, as in "Shall I strike my father?" The fa' (then) is for coordination with an implied element to which the noble composition extends, i.e., "Do you know that, and yet you do not protect yourselves from His punishment that has been mentioned to you, by what you engage in of associating with Him what shares with Him nothing of the attributes of divinity that have been mentioned?"

﴿Fa-dhalikum﴾ is a summing-up (fadhlakah) of what came before. That is: "That [is] the One whom you have acknowledged as possessing the attributes mentioned," with "dhalikum" as the subject (mubtada'). The words ﴿Allah﴾ are its predicate (khabar). ﴿Rabbukum﴾, meaning "your Lord, the One who owns you and manages your affairs absolutely," is either a substitute (badal) for it or an explanatory apposition (bayan). ﴿Al-Haqq﴾ ("the Truth") is an adjective of it, meaning: "your Lord, whose lordship is established and whose divinity is realised, with a realisation free of any doubt." ﴿Fa-madha﴾ may be read in two ways. Either the whole phrase "dhalikum" is treated as one single noun, in which the interrogative has come to dominate the demonstrative, or "dha" is a relative pronoun (mawsul) meaning "alladhi" ("that which"). The meaning is then: "What is it that [lies] after the Truth?" That is, what lies beyond it, by way of metaphor (isti'arah). The word "al-haqq" is repeated explicitly either because the intended meaning of the second "al-haqq" differs from the first, or to strengthen the affirmation and to achieve a complete contrast between it and error (dalal). The interrogative is a denial (inkari), meaning a denial of the occurrence and its negation: there is nothing beyond the Truth except ﴿error﴾, which no one chooses. Therefore, since it is established that worshipping the One described with the mentioned beautiful attributes is true, it becomes clear that whatever lies outside it, such as the worship of idols, is pure error, because there is no intermediate position between the two. It is called error, even though it is an act of the bodily limbs, on account of its being founded upon an erroneous belief. This opinion holds when "the Truth" refers to monotheism (tawhid). If, however, "the Truth" refers to the first meaning, then "error" refers to the idols themselves and not to their worship. The meaning is: "What lies after the Lord, the true One whose lordship is established, except error?" That is, the falsehood that is lost and perished. It is expressed by the verbal noun (masdar) for the sake of emphasis, as if it were the very essence of error and loss. This is more fitting with His words, ﴿and what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾, according to the second interpretation.

﴿Fa-anna tusrafun﴾ is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari), meaning a denial of the reality and a declaration of its improbability, together with a note of wonder at it. It contains an emphasis that the direction of the denial toward the act itself does not have. This is because every existing thing must necessarily exist in some state, with certainty. So when all states of its existence are negated, its existence is negated by way of demonstrative proof (burhani), as has been mentioned many times. The particle "fa" indicates that the denial follows from what precedes it. That is: "How are you turned away from the Truth, from which there is no escape, which is monotheism, to error, away from the clear path, which is associating partners with God and worshipping idols? Or from the worship of your true Lord, whose lordship is established, to the worship of falsehood, whose error and loss you have heard of in the Hereafter?" The choice of the passive form of the verb indicates that turning away from the Truth to error is not something that a rational person does by his own will. Rather, it happens only when an external force diverts him by compulsion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 33:

﴿Thus﴾ i.e., just as the lordship of Allah the Exalted has been established (ḥaqqat al-rubūbiyya lillāh), or just as there is nothing after the truth but error (al-ḍalāl), or that they are turned away from the truth. ﴿The word of your Lord has been justified﴾ — its wisdom and decree — ﴿against those who defied﴾, i.e., who rebelled in disbelief and went beyond its utmost limits, ﴿that they will not believe﴾. It is either a substitute (badal) for "the word" or an explanation (ta'līl) of its being justified (ḥaqqiyya). What is meant by it is the promise of punishment (al-'idda bi-l-'adhāb).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 34:

﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners﴾ (p-143) is another argument for the truth of monotheism (tawhid) and the falsity of associating partners with God (shirk), by showing that their partners are far from deserving divinity, through explaining that the distinctive attributes of the divine (khawass al-ilahiyyah) belong exclusively to Him, glorified and exalted, in both the initiation of creation and its return. The clause is not joined by a conjunction to what precedes it, to signal that it stands independently in establishing the matter sought. The question is for rebuke and compulsion. The restoration (i'adah) and its realization have been placed upon it, because its place is clear and its proof is evident, in the position of the initiation of creation, and so it has been strung in its thread, where it is said: ﴿Who originates creation and then restores it?﴾, signifying that the two are mutually entailed in existence and in knowledge, which necessitates acknowledging them. Their obstinacy and stubbornness hinder them from this.

Then he (ﷺ) was commanded to explain to them who does this, and it was said to him: ﴿Say: "God originates creation and then restores it."﴾ That is: He alone does both, whatever the case may be, not that the Prophet (ﷺ) stands in for them in this, as has been said, because the command-word is not the same as the answer that is intended from them, even though it entails it, since the matter asked about is not "Who originates creation and then restores it?" as in the Exalted saying: ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say: "God."﴾ So that the word commanded would be identical with the answer intended from them, and he (ﷺ) would be standing in for them in that. Rather, what is sought is the existence of one among their partners who does the initiation and the restoration. Thus the answer required from them is "No" and nothing else.

Indeed, he (ﷺ) was commanded to include it in his statement, to signal that it is the only possible answer and that it is established, and to indicate that they do not dare to state it openly for fear of rebuke and being silenced, not out of obstinacy and contentiousness. So reflect. The repetition of the sentence in the answer in full, without its predicate being omitted, as in the previous answer, is for greater emphasis and confirmation.

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ Ifk means diverting and turning away from something, and it may be specifically applied to turning away from an opinion, which is the more fitting for this context. That is: how are you turned from the truth to falsehood? The discussion of it is as mentioned under (tusrafun).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 35:**

﴿Say: "Is there any of your associates who guides to the truth?"﴾ This is another argument against what was mentioned before. It is brought as a further charge against them after the first charge, and as a further silencing after the first silencing. Its separation from what precedes it is due to the indication, already mentioned, that it stands on its own. ﴿Who guides to the truth?﴾ That is, in any way at all. The lowest degree of being worthy of worship (ma'budiyya) is that the one worshipped guides his worshippers to what is good for their affairs. As for specifying the path of guidance, restricting it to the setting up of proofs, the sending of messengers, and the granting of success in reflection and contemplation, as has been said, this undermines what the situation requires of complete rebuke and obligation. The inability to guide in one particular way does not entail inability to guide in general. The verb "hada" is used with "ila" (to) because it implies the sense of reaching a destination. It is also used with the lam (li-) to indicate that the destination is the ultimate aim of the guidance, and that the guidance was not directed toward it by mere chance. For this reason, it is used with the lam in what is attributed to God Most High, where He says: ﴿Say: "God guides to the truth."﴾ That is, He alone guides to it, to the exclusion of anyone else. This is through what has been mentioned: the setting up of evidences and proofs, the sending of messengers, the sending down of books, the granting of success in reflection and contemplation, and other kinds of guidance. The discussion of the command to ask and answer is as it was explained earlier.

﴿Is then the one who guides to the truth﴾, who is God, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿more worthy to be followed, or the one who does not find guidance [yahiddi]?﴾ The Arabic word is read with a kasra on the ha'. Its original form is "yahtadi", which was assimilated (idgham). The ha' was given a kasra because two unvowelled letters came together. It is also read with a kasra on the ya', as a following of the vowel of the ha'. It is also read with a fatha on the ha', by transferring the vowel of the ta' to it. That is, he does not find guidance by himself, let alone guide others. There is in this a degree of emphasis that is not hidden. The negation of finding guidance is stated, although what is understood from what preceded is the negation of giving guidance, because the negation of giving guidance usually entails the negation of finding it. Whoever has found guidance to the truth (p-144) is not free, in some measure, from guiding others, and the least of this is that he serves as an example for them, so that one who sees him follows his way without realizing it. The fa' (then) is for the sequencing of the question upon what has preceded: the clear establishment of God's guidance, and the absence of guidance in their associates, which is understood from the restriction (qasr) and from the absence of an answer that indicates the answer "none." This necessarily compels them to the true answer. It is not that the question is directed toward sequencing, as occurs in some contexts, for that is specific to the rhetorical (inkari) question, as in God's words: ﴿Is then the one who follows the good pleasure of God﴾ ... and so on, and similar. The hamza (interrogative particle) is placed later in the logical order, but it is placed first in the wording to show its established precedence in requiring the front position. This is the view of the majority. So much so that if the question had used the word "ay," the hamza would certainly have been delayed. Do you not see God's words: ﴿Which of the two groups is more deserving of security?﴾ after establishing what compels the polytheists to answer from their own situation and the situation of the Messenger of God, (ﷺ).

It is read as "la yahdi" (does not guide), meaning "la yahtadi" (does not find guidance), because it comes intransitively, or it means "does not guide others." The form of the comparative may be taken in its literal sense, with the object of comparison omitted, as Makki preferred. The reckoning is: "Is the one who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed than the one who [does not guide], or the one who does not guide is more worthy..." and so on. Or it may be in the sense of "worthy" (haqiq), as Abu Hayyan preferred. In either case, the interrogation is for the purpose of imposing an obligation, and "an yuttaba'a" (that he be followed) is in the place of an accusative or genitive after the removal of the preposition, according to the well-known disagreement. That is, "bi-an yuttaba'a" (by being followed).

﴿Except one who is himself guided﴾ is an exceptive construction lacking its object (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of states. That is, he does not find guidance, or does not guide others, in any state, except in the state of being guided by God to find guidance, or to guide others. This is the state of their associates among the angels, the Messiah, and 'Uzayr, peace be upon them. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Or the one among the idols who does not find his way to a place, so that he moves to it, unless he is moved to it, or unless God Most High moves him from his state until He makes him a responsible living being and then guides him." It is also read as "illa an yahdiya" (unless he guides), from the causative form (tafil) for emphasis.

﴿What is the matter with you?﴾ That is: what is the reason for you in taking these as associates with God, glory be to Him and exalted. The interrogation is a rebuke by way of denial. In it there is a wonder at their condition. God Most High's words: ﴿How do you judge?﴾ - that is, by what clear reason requires its falsehood - are a denial of their false judgment, an expression of astonishment at it, and a reproach to them for it. The fa' (then) is for the sequencing of both denials upon what has become clear regarding the obligation to follow the one who guides to the truth. If you say: the rebuke by the earlier interrogation appears only regarding someone who reverses its correct answer, judging that the one who does not guide is more worthy to be followed than the one who guides, whereas they do not judge their associates more worthy of that to the exclusion of God, glory be to Him and exalted, but rather that both deserve it together, with the superiority of His side, since they say: "These are our intercessors with God." I say: their judgment that He, Exalted, deserves to be followed in a shared manner is itself a judgment on their part that He does not deserve that in an exclusive manner. Thus they became judges that their associates deserve it to the exclusion of God Most High, without realizing it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 36:**

﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أكْثَرُهُمْ﴾ (﴿And most of them do not follow﴾) is an independent sentence (*mubtada'*, an inceptive clause), not included within the scope of the preceding command. It is directed from the Exalted One Himself to explain their lack of understanding of the content of the clear proof that silenced them and left them with no reply (*alqamahum al-hajar*). That proof makes it obligatory to follow the Guide to the truth, and it condemns the falsity of their judgment. They are not affected by it because they have not been guided to the path of knowledge at all. The meaning is that most of them, in their beliefs and their discussions, follow only (*illa zannan*, ﴿except conjecture﴾) a weak conjecture, without giving attention to any single item of knowledge. Much less do they follow the paths of sound evidence that guides to the truth and is built on certain and correct premises, so that they would understand its content, recognize its soundness, and recognize the falsity of their own erroneous judgments that contradict it. Thus rebuke and binding argument are established against them. Therefore, "following" (*ittiba'*) here means belief in general, covering both what accompanies acceptance and submission and what does not. The restriction (*qasr*, exclusivity) refers to what was indicated above: that among them there is no following of any single item of knowledge, and no attention paid to it. The reason for specifying this following to "most of them" is to indicate that some of them do follow knowledge and thereby recognize the truth of monotheism and the falsity of polytheism, but they do not accept it out of arrogance and obstinacy. Thus, in their case, there is an effect from the aforementioned proof, even if they do not display it. That they are more unbelieving and more numerous than the first group does not contradict what is understood from the implication of the speech, according to common usage, that those are in a worse state than others. The criterion is the bad state in terms of understanding and perception, not in terms of disbelief and punishment.

Or: ﴿And most of them do not follow﴾ means: most of them do not follow, throughout the duration of their lives, ﴿except conjecture﴾, and they never abandon it. The negative particle that enters upon the present-tense verb indicates the continuation of the negation according to the context. Therefore "following" here means submission and compliance. The restriction is with respect to time. The reason for specifying this following to "most of them", despite the participation of the obstinate ones in it, is to hint at what will later come from some of them: following the truth and repentance, as will come later.

It has been said: the meaning is: ﴿And most of them do not follow﴾ in their affirmation of God Most High ﴿except conjecture﴾ that is not supported by any proof in their possession. It has also been said: ﴿And most of them do not follow﴾ in their saying to the idols that they are gods ﴿except conjecture﴾. The word "most" here means all of them, so reflect carefully. It has also been said: the pronoun in (*akthаruhum*, "most of them") refers to people in general, so there is no need for this complication.

﴿Indeed, conjecture does not avail against the truth﴾: that is, against certain knowledge and correct belief that corresponds to reality, ﴿anything﴾ in terms of providing sufficiency. It is permissible for (*shay'an*, "anything") to be the object (*maf'ul bihi*), and (*min al-haqq*, "against the truth") to be a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) from it. The sentence is a resumptive new sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining the status of conjecture and its invalidity. In it there is an indication of the obligation of knowledge in the fundamentals of faith (*usul*) and the impermissibility of relying on blind imitation (*taqlid*). ﴿Indeed, God is All-Knowing of what they do﴾: this is a threat against them for their ugly deeds, and it includes, initially, what is related about them of turning away from decisive proofs and following corrupt conjectures. It has been read as (*taf'alun*, "what you do") with a shift to direct address (*iltifat*) in order to intensify the threat.

The commentary begins here, on their rejection of the Qur'an, following their rejection of the rational proofs contained within it. That is: it was not valid or proper that ﴿this Qur'an﴾, which is filled with the varieties of guidance that merit following, among which are those clear proofs declaring the truth of *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness) and the falsehood of *shirk* (associating partners with God), ﴿should be fabricated apart from God﴾. That is, it should be a fabrication by created beings, meaning something fabricated by them. It is named with the verbal noun (*masdar*) for emphasis (*mubalaghah*). ﴿But it is a confirmation of what is before it﴾ of the divine books whose truth is attested, that is, confirming them. How could it not be, since its inimitability, which places it beyond their capacity, makes it a standard by which they are measured and a witness to their soundness? Its being in the accusative is as the predicate of *kana* (was), which is understood. It has also been permitted that it be the reason (*'illah*) for an elided verb, whose implied sense is: "But God sent it down as a confirmation of..." and so on. It was also read in the nominative by positing an implied subject, that is: "But it is a confirmation of..." and so on.

﴿And a detailed explanation of the Book﴾ is conjoined to it, in the accusative and the nominative, that is: and an elaboration of what has been written and established of realities and laws. ﴿In which there is no doubt﴾ is a third predicate falling under the rule of the corrective clause (*istidrak*), that is, free of doubt. Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "the Book," even though that word is in a genitive construction, since it is in meaning an object. Or it is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) with no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rab*). ﴿From the Lord of the worlds﴾ is another predicate, that is: coming from the Lord of the worlds. Or it is connected to (*tasdiq*) or to (*tafsil*), or to the verb that is given as the reason for these two. "There is no doubt in it" is then a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiradh*), as in your saying: "Zayd, there is no doubt about it, is generous." Or it is a circumstantial clause from "the Book," or from the pronoun in (*fihi*). The context of the noble verse, following the prohibition against following conjecture, is to explain what must be followed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 38:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ That is: rather, do they say, "Muhammad (ﷺ) has invented it"? The interrogative hamzah (alif of interrogation) is for denying the reality of the claim and deeming it far-fetched. ﴿Say﴾ — as a rebuke to them and a demonstration of the invalidity of their corrupt assertion: "If the matter is as you claim, ﴿then produce a sura like it﴾," that is, in eloquence, excellence of composition, and strength of meaning, in the manner of fabrication; for you are like me in Arabic and eloquence, and you are more practised than I am in arrangement and expression. It was also read as (bi-sūratin mithlihi) with an idafah, meaning: with a sura of a book like it. ﴿And call upon﴾ for support and assistance ﴿whomever you can﴾ to call upon and seek help from, of your gods whom you claim to be helpers for you in important matters and calamities, and the sources of your support, to whose opinions you resort in everything you do and everything you leave undone, ﴿besides Allah﴾. The phrase ﴿besides Allah﴾ is connected to (call upon), and (dūn) functions as an exception particle; its detailed treatment has already passed in His, the Exalted, words: ﴿and call your witnesses besides Allah﴾. That is: call upon other than Him, the Exalted, whomever of His creation you can, for none is able to do it. Excluding Him, glorified is He, from the ruling of invocation serves to specify their disavowal of Him, the Exalted, and their being on the brink of opposition and hostility, not to indicate that He alone has power over what they were charged with; for that would give the impression that, had they called upon Him, the Exalted, He would have answered them in it. ﴿If you are truthful﴾, that is: in your claim that I fabricated it, for that entails the possibility of producing its like, and that in turn entails your own capability to do so. The answer is omitted, since what is mentioned indicates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 39:

﴿Nay, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge of it﴾ This is a transition (idrab) and a shift away from demonstrating the invalidity of what they said about the Mighty Qur'an, by means of the challenge (tahaddi), to demonstrating it through an explanation that it is a speech arising from their ignorance of its sublime status. So "ma" (what) is an expression for the whole of it, not for what it contains of mention of the Resurrection and recompense and what opposes their religion, as has been said, for it is among what must be kept far from the sanctuary of the Revelation. That is: they hastened to deny it with the most hasty haste, without reflecting upon it, or considering the evidences it contains that point to its being as it has been described just now, and without knowing that it is not something that could have a counterpart which the created being could produce. The expression "by what they did not encompass in knowledge of it" (rather than saying "they denied it without encompassing its knowledge" or something similar) is to indicate their complete ignorance of it, and that they did not know it except under the heading of not knowing it, and that their denial of it was only because of their not knowing it, since attaching the judgment to the relative pronoun indicates that what follows the relative clause is a cause for it.

﴿And its interpretation has not yet come to them﴾ This is a conjunction with the relative clause (ṣila), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the relative pronoun. That is: they have not yet come to understand its interpretation, and its refined meanings, which indicate the loftiness of its status, have not reached their minds. The expression of that by "the coming of its interpretation" is to indicate that its interpretation is directed toward minds and drawn into them by itself. Or: the interpretation of what it contains of informing about the unseen has not yet come to them, until it becomes clear whether it is true or false. The meaning is that the Qur'an is miraculous in terms of its composition and meaning, and in terms of its informing about the unseen. They hastened to deny it before they reflected upon its composition and pondered its meaning, or awaited the occurrence of what it informed of concerning future matters. The negation of the coming of the interpretation with the word "lamma" (not yet), which indicates expectation, after the negation of encompassing its knowledge with the word "lam" (not), is for emphasizing the blame and intensifying the reproach, for the shamefulness of denying a thing before knowing it when its coming is expected is more heinous than denying it before knowing it absolutely. The meaning: it was incumbent upon them to pause until the time of the occurrence of what was expected, but they did not do so. As for whether what was expected has occurred since then, and whether they persisted in their former state even then, there is no reference to that here. Citing as evidence for it the continuation of the blame, or the claim that their saying "he fabricated it" was a denial after reflection, arises from a lack of reflection, so reflect. How could it be otherwise, since they did not say it after the challenge but before it? The claim that it was preceded by the challenge mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah is refuted by the fact that that surah is Madani and this one is Makki. What indicates it is rather what will be recited to you of His Exalted saying: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it and among them are those who do not﴾ ... etc.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus﴾ ... etc., is a description of their condition described and an explanation of the punishment it leads to. That is: like that denial, founded on first impression and rashness without reflection and deliberation, ﴿those before them denied﴾, that is: they committed denial, or they denied what was denied of the miracles which appeared at the hands of their prophets, or they denied their prophets. ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, who are those before them among the deniers. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that the denial was wrongdoing, or to indicate that it is the cause of what befell them of evil consequence, and to include these wrongdoers in their company in sin and threat by a primary inclusion. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And among them﴾ ... etc. describes their state after the expected ta'wil (the realization or fulfilment of what the Qur'an announces) has come. At that point they can be divided into those who believe in it and those who do not, since it is impossible to believe in something without knowledge of it, and all of them shared in denying and disbelieving it before that. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge﴾ [10:39]. That is: among these deniers there are those ﴿who believe in it﴾ when they come to know it fully, when its ta'wil (its realization) arrives, and when its truth becomes manifest, after they had tried to oppose it and exerted their powers against it, only to find themselves diminished before it; or after they witnessed the occurrence of what it had reported, just as it had reported, time and again. The meaning of believing in it is either: (a) merely affirming its truth, i.e., they accept it in their own minds and know that it is true, but they are stubborn and arrogant. These are the ones indicated by restricting the following of conjecture to most of them, which implies that they know the truth according to the first interpretation, as was pointed out earlier. Or: (b) true faith, i.e., they will believe in it and repent of disbelief. These are the ones indicated by the aforementioned restriction, according to the second interpretation, as being those who will follow the truth, as has already been explained.

﴿And among them is one who does not believe in it﴾: i.e., he does not affirm it in his own mind, just as he does not outwardly affirm it, owing to his extreme dullness which prevents him from comprehending its knowledge properly, even though he is above the level of those who have no comprehension of it at all.
