Or owing to the feebleness of his intellect and the disorder of his discernment, and his inability to purify his knowledge from the admixture of conjectures and illusions to which he has become accustomed, so he remains in the doubt he was in. This degree of comprehension and arrival of ta'wil is sufficient to counter what preceded, namely complete lack of comprehension. These are the ones intended earlier by His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture﴾ [10:36], according to the first interpretation. Or: they will not believe in it in the future, but will die upon their disbelief, whether stubbornly or in doubt. These are the ones who persist in following conjecture according to the second interpretation, without submitting to the truth or yielding to it.

﴿And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters﴾: i.e., of both groups according to the first interpretation, not only of the stubborn ones, as has been said, because they both share the root of corruption, which entails that they share in the threat (of punishment). Or, according to the second interpretation, of those who remain persistent in disbelief, namely the stubborn and the doubtful among them.(p-148)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 41:

﴿And if they deny you﴾, i.e., if they persist in denying you and insist upon it, as has been reported of them after the establishment of proof through the challenge. ﴿Then say: "For me is my work, and for you is your work."﴾ i.e., disassociate yourself from them, for you have given them due warning. This is like His Exalted saying: ﴿And if they disobey you, then say: "Indeed, I am free from what you do."﴾ The meaning is: for me is the recompense of my work, and for you is the recompense of your work, whether it be true or false. The singular "work" (ʿamal), though attributed to them, is used on account of the unity of its kind (al-ittihad al-naw'i) and in order to observe the perfection of the contrast. ﴿You are free from what I do, and I am free from what you do.﴾ This is an emphasis on what the lam of exclusivity (lam al-ikhtisas) conveys, namely that the recompense of an action does not pass to other than its doer; i.e., you will not be held accountable for my work, nor will I be held accountable for your work. And because of what it may suggest of mutual abandonment and of not confronting them, it has been said that this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 42:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ is an explanation of their being sealed upon their hearts, such that there is no path to their faith. The pronoun referring to the word (man) ("who") is in the plural, out of regard for the meaning, just as it is in the singular in what follows, out of preservation of the apparent wording. Perhaps this is to indicate the large number of listeners, on the basis that listening does not depend on what sight depends upon, namely facing, the absence of a veil, and light. That is: "And among them are people who listen to you when you recite the Qur'an and teach the laws."

﴿Then can you make the deaf hear﴾: the hamza of interrogation is for denial, and the fa' is conjunctive. The combination of the two is not for the sequential ordering of the denial of making them hear upon their listening, as is the view of Sibawayh and the majority (on the basis that the hamza is placed before the fa' because it requires initial position, as is established in its proper place). Rather, it is for denying that hearing follows upon it, as is customary. However, this is not by way of coordination with the verb mentioned, because that would lead to a corruption of meaning, since it is either a relative clause (silah) or a descriptive clause (sifah). In either case, coordinating with it would require that the coordinated element fall within its scope and that the denial be directed at it from that standpoint, and there is no doubt of its corruption. Rather, it is by way of coordination with an implied element understood from the implication of the composition, as if it were said: "Do they listen to you, then you make them hear?" This is not a denial of their listening, since that is a certain matter, but a denial of the occurrence of hearing following upon that and its consequence according to the general custom. Indeed, it is even a negation of its possibility, as indicated by placing "the deaf" in the position of their pronoun and describing them as lacking reason, through His words, exalted is He: ﴿And even if they were not reasoning﴾. That is: even if their deafness were joined by the absence of their reason, because a deaf person who has reason may perhaps grasp when a sound reaches his ear canal; but when the loss of hearing and reason together is combined, then the matter is complete.

﴿And among them are some who look at you﴾, that is, who witness the clear proofs of your prophethood. ﴿Would you then﴾, that is, after that, ﴿guide them?﴾ The phrase ﴿guide the blind﴾ was used to express the denial of their guidance and to present it as something in the realm of the impossible. This is emphasized by the words ﴿even though they do not see﴾, meaning: even if the lack of sight were joined by the lack of insight. The purpose of sight is reflection (i'tibar) and discernment (istibsar), and the foundation of these is insight (basirah). This is why the blind person who has insight makes shrewd guesses and perceives what the sighted fool does not perceive. Since foolishness and blindness are combined in them, the door of guidance has been closed to them.

The answer to "law" (lau, "even if") in both clauses is omitted, because of the indication of the Almighty's words ﴿make the deaf hear﴾ and ﴿guide the blind﴾ upon it. Each of the two is conjoined to an implied clause that corresponds to it in meaning, and both are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object of the preceding verb. That is: "Would you make the deaf hear even if they were reasoning, and even if they were not reasoning? Would you guide the blind even if they were seeing, and even if they were not seeing?" That is, in every supposed condition. The first of each pair has been omitted in this construction in a regular manner, because the second clearly indicates it. For when a thing is realized in the presence of a preventing factor, or a strong preventing factor, it is all the more so realized in its absence, or in the presence of a weak preventing factor. The emphasis found in the conjunctive "law" and "in" (even if) revolves around this subtle point. The discussion of the Almighty's words ﴿even though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ and its like has already passed several times.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 44:

﴿Indeed, God does not wrong people﴾. This indicates that what is related about them, namely their failure to find the path of truth and the inoperativeness of their faculties of perception, is not due to any matter traceable to God, the Mighty and Majestic, such as creating them deficient in faculties or the like. Rather, it comes from them. That is, He does not diminish for them ﴿anything﴾ of what their religious and worldly welfare, and their primary and ultimate perfections, depend upon, namely the foundations of their perceptions and the means of their knowledge through the outward and inward faculties, and the guidance to truth through sending messengers and revealing scriptures. Rather, He completes all of that for them, without any deficiency whatsoever.

﴿But people﴾ (it is also read with the lightening of the particle "lakinna" and with the nominative "al-nas") — the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to add specification and affirmation. That is: but they, by not using their faculties for what they were created for, by turning away from accepting the call to truth, and by denying the messengers and scriptures, ﴿wrong themselves﴾. That is, they diminish what they diminish, namely they neglect the foundations of their perfection and the means of their guidance. The object is not mentioned because the aim is to restrict wronging to themselves, not to specify what the wronging relates to. The expression of their act as "diminishing", although it is in fact a complete forfeiture and total nullification, is for the sake of observing its counterpart (qarina) aspect. As for the words of the Mighty and Majestic, "themselves" (anfusahum): either it is an emphasis of "people", in which case it has the status of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) in the words of the Exalted: ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers﴾, restricting wrongdoing to them. Or it is the object of "yazlimun" (they wrong), as in all other occurrences, and its being placed before the verb is merely for the sake of giving it prominence while observing the verse-ending rhyme (fasila), without intending to restrict being wronged to them, according to the view of those who do not consider fronting to imply restriction. This would be like the Qur'anic statement: "We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves." As for the view of those who consider it to imply restriction, perhaps the preference for restricting the wronging (to themselves) rather than restricting the wrongdoer status to them is for the sake of emphasizing the nullity of their acts and the feebleness of their minds, since of the two matters, when the doer and the object are one, the more ugly, the more rejected by reason, the more repugnant to nature, and the more obligatory to avoid for everyone is being wronged, not being the wrongdoer. Moreover, restricting the former to them necessarily entails what the apparent state requires regarding restricting the latter to them, since if none of the people wrongs anyone except himself, it follows that no one wrongs him except himself; for if someone else wrongs him, that other would have to be a wrongdoer toward someone other than himself, whereas it is presupposed that no one wrongs anyone except himself. Thus the first restriction is sufficient without the second, while observing the benefit mentioned.

The form of the present tense (al-mudari') indicates continuity, both in negation and affirmation. For when the negative particle enters upon the present tense, it indicates, according to the context, the continuation of negation, not the negation of continuation. Do you not see that your saying "ma Zaydan darabtu" (I did not strike Zayd) indicates the restriction of the negation, not the negation of restriction? The purpose of the noble verse is to establish the argument, and it may also be intended as a warning. Thus the negated present refers to the future, and the affirmed present indicates continuity. The meaning is that God does not wrong them by punishing them on the Day of Resurrection in any degree of wrong; but they wrong themselves with a continuous wronging, for their persistent engagement (p-150) in evil deeds, which necessitate punishment, is itself their wronging of themselves. On both interpretations, the noble verse is a concluding appendix (tadhyil) to what precedes it.

[And the Day He gathers them] is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb. It is read with the nun (نُون, "We gather them") as iltifat (a shift from one grammatical person to another). The meaning is: "Mention to them, or warn them of, the Day He gathers them."

[As if they had not remained] means: as though they had not remained, [but only] a little of the day. [A little of the day] is a figure of speech (mathal) for extreme brevity. The time is specified as "of the day" because its hours are more easily recognized than the hours of the night. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the object pronoun. The meaning is that He gathers them resembling, in their outward appearance to people, those who did not remain in this world and did not enjoy its bounties except for that small amount. For whoever has lived in it for ages and enjoyed its pleasures would not be without some trace of blessing and some signs of delight, which contrast with their state of shabby appearance and bad condition.

Alternatively, the meaning is: those who did not remain in the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection) except for that same short period. In that case, the purpose of the restriction is to show how completely easy the gathering is in relation to God's power, even after a long age, and to expose the falsehood of their disbelief and denial, as in their saying ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?﴾ and similar statements. Or the purpose is to show the complete correspondence between the two states of existence in their forms and shapes, since the brevity of the stay in the barzakh is one of the causes of no alteration or change. Then His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They will recognize one another﴾ serves as an explanation and confirmation of this, because mutual recognition after a long lapse of time turns into mutual unfamiliarity.

According to the first interpretation, the sentence is a new independent statement: some of them recognize others, as though they had been separated only briefly. This is the case at the very beginning of their emergence from the graves, when they are still in the same familiar state they were in among themselves. Then recognition ceases because of the overwhelming terrors that bewilder and the difficult conditions that befall them, which change forms and shapes and transform them from one state to another.

﴿Those who denied the meeting with God have certainly lost﴾ is a testimony from God, glorified and exalted, to their loss, and an expression of wonder at it. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in (they recognize one another), with the implied meaning of "saying." The use of the relative pronoun to refer to them, although the context calls for a pronoun, serves to condemn them through what is contained in the relative clause, and to indicate that it is the cause of what befell them.

If "the meeting with God" means the reckoning and recompense in general, or a good meeting, then "loss" means a bad bargain. The meaning is: they made a bad deal in their trade and dealings, exchanging disbelief for faith and misguidance for guidance. The meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they were not guided﴾ is that they did not know the conditions of trade or follow its proper ways. If "the meeting" means a bad meeting, then "loss" means destruction and misguidance, that is, they went astray and were destroyed through their denial, and they were not guided to the path of salvation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 46:

﴿Whether We show you﴾ its original form is "in nurika," and "ma" is an added particle (zā'ida) to emphasize the meaning of the conditional (sharṭ), and for this reason the verb is emphasized with the nun (nūn al-ta'kīd). That is: by Your victory, by Our showing you ﴿some of what We promise them﴾, i.e., what We have promised them of punishment, and We hasten it in your lifetime so that you see it. The shift to the form of the future tense (al-istiqbāl) serves to bring the image before the mind (li-istiḥḍār al-ṣūrah), or to indicate renewal and continuity; that is, We promise them a renewed promise, as wisdom requires, of warning after warning (inḏār ghibb inḏār). In singling out "some" for mention there is a symbol of the promise through showing them part of what was promised, and indeed He showed it to him on the day of Badr. ﴿Or We take you (tatawaffayannaka)﴾ before that, ﴿then to Us is their return﴾, i.e., however the situation turns, We will have shown you some of what We promised them first; then to Us is their return, in this world and the Hereafter, and We will certainly fulfill what We promised them.

(p-151) It is said: what is mentioned is the answer (jawāb) to the second conditional, as if it were said: "then to Us is their return, and We will show it to you in the Hereafter," and the answer to the first is omitted because it is evident, i.e., "then that is so."

﴿Then Allah is Witness over what they do﴾ of the evil deeds that were related about them. The meaning of "witness" (shahādah) is either its consequence and result, which is His punishing them, or its establishment and performance by making the limbs speak. The manifestation of the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalālah) serves to bring in awe, to instill reverence, and to emphasize the threat. It is also read "thammah" (there), i.e., "there."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 47:

﴿For every community﴾ among the past nations ﴿there is a messenger﴾ who is sent to them with a particular law (shari'a), suited to their circumstances, to call them to the truth. ﴿So when their messenger comes﴾ and conveys to them what he was sent with, but they deny him and oppose him, ﴿judgment is passed between them﴾, that is, between each community and its messenger, ﴿with justice﴾, meaning with fairness. It is decreed that the messenger and those who believe in him are saved, and that those who deny them are destroyed, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ in that judgment which necessitates their punishment, because it is a consequence of their own deeds.

Or: ﴿for every community﴾ of the nations there is, on the Day of Resurrection, a messenger to whom it is attributed and by whom it is called. ﴿So when their messenger comes﴾ to the place of standing to bear witness against them concerning disbelief and faith, in accordance with His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And the prophets and the witnesses will be brought, and judgment will be passed between them﴾.

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ This is hastening toward what they had been promised of punishment, in the manner of mockery and denial, as the answer indicates. It is not a request to specify the time of its coming in the form of a challenge (*ilzam*, binding the opponent to a claim), as in Surat al-Mulk: ﴿If you are truthful﴾, meaning: that it will come to us. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) and to the believers who recite to them the verses containing the aforementioned promise. The answer to the conditional is omitted, relying on what precedes it, as it is omitted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So bring us what you promise us, if you are among the truthful﴾. For hastening carries the force of a command to bring it quickly, so it is as if it were said: "Let it come to us quickly, if you are truthful." And because of what it implies, that its coming is through the agency of the Prophet (ﷺ), it was said:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 10, verse 49:**

﴿Say: I have no power over harm or benefit for myself﴾. That is: I am not able to do either of them in any way whatsoever. The mention of harm first is because the context of the verse (*nazm*, the arrangement of the discourse) is to demonstrate his inability with respect to it. As for mentioning benefit, it serves to widen the scope, as a completion of the inability. What occurs in Surah al-A'raf, where benefit is mentioned first, serves to signal its importance, and the context there is its context. The meaning is: I do not have power over any of my affairs, to repel or to bring about, even though that is closer to occurring. So how could I have power over your affairs, to the point that I would cause the coming of your promised punishment?!

﴿Except what Allah wills﴾. This is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*): that is, "but rather, whatever Allah wills occurs." Taking it as a connected exception, meaning "except what Allah wills that I should possess," is refuted by the context of disavowal (*tabarru'*), which precludes that he, peace be upon him, should have any part in bringing about the promise. For that would require explaining that the matter in dispute is one that Allah does not will him to possess, peace be upon him. Making *ma* refer to some of the familiar states that are attached to voluntary actions, which are delegated to the servants, so that the meaning becomes: "I do not possess for myself any harm or benefit except what Allah wills that I possess of them, of harm and benefit that follow from my voluntary actions, such as the harm and benefit that follow from eating and drinking, in their absence and their presence," is a manifest forced interpretation (*ta'assuf*).

Allah's saying, the Exalted: ﴿For every nation there is a term﴾, is an explanation of what was left vague in the exception, and a restriction of the absoluteness in the preceding decree, which suggests that the thing decreed is an accomplished matter, not dependent on anything other than the coming of the Messenger and the nation's denial. That is: for every nation, from among those between whom and their Messenger a judgment has been passed, there is a specific term that belongs to them alone and does not extend to another nation, appointed for their punishment, which descends upon them when that term arrives.

﴿When their term comes﴾. If the term is taken to mean a specific limit of time, then the meaning of its coming is clear. If it is intended as the extent of time it reaches, then its coming is an expression of its ending, since at that point its coming is fully realized. If the pronoun refers to the nations implied by "every nation," then the explicit mention of "term" as an annexed noun serves to convey the intended meaning, which is that each nation reaches its own specific term. Its coming to them specifically, from among the nations, through the acquisition of the term by annexation, is conveyed generally by the sense of plurality, as if it were said: "When their terms come to them, such that each of those nations is reached by its own specific term." If, however, it is taken as specific to each nation, as is the apparent meaning, then the explicit mention in place of the pronoun serves to increase the affirmation, and the annexation to the pronoun serves to convey complete specification, that is: when its specific term comes to it.

﴿Then they shall not delay﴾ from that term ﴿for an hour﴾. That is: not even a little of time, since "an hour" is an image for the utmost smallness of it. That is: they will not delay from it at all. The form *istif'al* (the verb form "yasta'khirun") signals their inability to do so despite seeking it. ﴿Nor shall they advance﴾, that is, they will not move ahead of it. This is conjoined to "yasta'khirun," but not to show that advancing is absent, even though it is possible in itself as delaying is. Rather, it is for the emphasis of the absence of delay, by placing it in the category of what is rationally impossible. As in His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾. For one who dies a disbeliever, although it is manifest that he has no repentance at all, has been placed in the same category, regarding the non-acceptance of repentance, as one who postpones it until the arrival of death, signaling that the existence of repentance at that time and its non-existence are entirely equal, as was mentioned in Surah al-A'raf.

It has also been allowed that the coming of the term be understood as its approach, to the extent that advancing in some degree is possible, like the day on which their destruction was appointed at a specific hour of it. But there is no added benefit in restricting the absence of delay to its approach. The mention of the absence of delay is given precedence over the absence of advancing because the more important purpose is to show that they will not escape the punishment even for an hour, and that is by delaying. As for what occurs in Allah's saying, the Exalted: ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay﴾, where advancing is mentioned first in the wording, this is because the purpose there is to explain the secret of postponing their punishment despite their deserving it, as is indicated by His, mighty and majestic be He, saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope divert them; but they will come to know﴾. So what matters most in that place is the explanation of the absence of advancing, as was mentioned there.

﴿Say﴾ to them, after you have explained the manner in which God's *sunnah* (the established divine way and practice, sunnat Allah) operates among the nations in general, and have alerted them that their punishment is a decreed and inevitable matter, which awaits only the arrival of its appointed term. This is a notice of its complete imminence, and a treatment of it as though it had actually arrived: ﴿Tell me﴾, that is, inform me, ﴿if His punishment comes upon you﴾, the punishment you are hastening, ﴿by night﴾, that is, at a time of sleeping and being occupied with sleep, ﴿or by day﴾, that is, while you are engaged in your affairs, in accordance with the term determined for you by the will (*mashi'ah*), which follows wisdom, just as it was determined for the other destroyed nations. The words of His, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten thereof?﴾ form the answer to the conditional clause, with the *fa'* (the particle of consequence) omitted, as in your saying: "If I come to you, what will you feed me?" The word ﴿the criminals﴾ is placed in the position of the pronoun in order to emphasize the denial, by showing how incompatible their condition is with hastening it, (p-153) for it is fitting that a criminal should perish from fear of the coming of the punishment, let alone hasten it. The conditional clause is linked to *ara'aytum* (﴿Tell me﴾), and the meaning is: inform me, if His punishment comes upon you, what is the thing that you hasten from Him, glorified is He? A thing cannot be hastened after it has come. The purpose of this is to exaggerate the denial of their hastening it, by removing it from the sphere of possibility, and by treating its hastening in the state of impossibility as though it were hastening after its arrival, on the basis of treating the certainty of its arrival and its imminence as though it were its actual arrival, as has been indicated. This denial is in the position of a prohibition, as in the saying of the One, exalted is He: ﴿The command of God has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ (Qur'an 16:1), except that the treatment there is explicit, while here it is implicit. This is like the saying of one who says to his debtor, who is pressing him for his right: "Tell me, if I give you your right, what will you then demand from me?" He intends to exaggerate the denial of the demand by placing it in the same category as demanding after giving, on the basis of treating its certainty as if it were the thing itself.

And the words of His, exalted and majestic is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 51:

﴿Then, when it has befallen you, [will you] believe in it?﴾ This is a denial of their belief in the punishment after its actual descent, and it is included together with what precedes it, namely the denial of their urgent demand for it after its coming in a judgmental sense, under the statement that was commanded. That is: after the punishment has befallen you and actually descended upon you, do you believe in it at a time when belief no longer benefits you? It is a denial of their delaying it until this point, and an announcement that it entails remorse and regret, so that they may desist from the obstinacy in which they are, and turn toward making amends before the time is lost. Thus the fronting of the adverbial phrase serves restriction (qasr). It has also been said that (what is it that the guilty seek to hasten?) is connected to (Tell me, "if...") and the answer to the conditional is omitted, meaning: they will regret the hastening, or recognize its error. The conditional clause is a parenthetical insertion that confirms the content of the interrogation.

It has also been said that the answer is His saying, exalted is He: "Then, when it has befallen you..." etc., and the first interrogative is a parenthetical insertion. The meaning is: Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you, do you believe in it after its occurrence at a time when belief no longer benefits you? Then the particle of delay (thumma) was used to indicate remoteness, then the conditional particle was added to indicate that the remoteness stands on its own, since the first is like a preparation for it. And (idha) was used reinforced with (ma) as an intensification of the sense of occurrence and an increase in ignorance-highlighting, and that they did not believe except after belief no longer benefited them at all.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Now?﴾ is a resumption from His side, exalted is He, not included under the quoted saying, and it is brought to confirm the content of what preceded, with the presumption of speech. That is: it will be said to them at their belief after the descent of the punishment: "Now you believe in it?" as a denial of the delay and a rebuke for it, by clarifying that it was not due to a lack of prior warning, nor to reflection and contemplation regarding its matter, nor to any other thing that might be considered an excuse for delay; rather, it was by way of denial and urgent demand for it in a manner of mockery. It was also read (Ālān) with the hamza omitted and its vowel placed on the lam.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you used to hasten it﴾, that is, in denial and mockery, is a clause that came as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of (you believed) which is understood, to intensify the rebuke and reproach, and to increase the reproach and dismay. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the verb is for observing the rhyme (fawasil), not for restriction.

His saying, exalted is He:

Then it is said: ... etc., is an emphasis on the rebuke and reproach through the threat of punishment and retribution, and it is conjoined to what was implied before "now" (al-An). ﴿To those who did wrong﴾, i.e., they placed disbelief and denial in the place of faith and affirmation; or they wronged themselves by exposing themselves to punishment and destruction. The placing of the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun serves to censure them by what is contained in the relative clause (al-sila) and to signal that this is the cause of what befell them. ﴿Taste the punishment of eternity﴾, the painful one that lasts forever. ﴿Are you recompensed﴾ today ﴿except for what you used to earn﴾ in the world of the various kinds of disbelief and sins, among which is what has passed of (p-154) hastening (al-istి'jal).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 53:

﴿And they ask you for information⦆ i.e., they ask you to inform them (istikhbar), saying, in the manner of mockery or denial: ﴿Is it true?⦆ "Ahaqq" is a predicate (khabar) placed before the subject (mubtada'), which is the pronoun "huwa", for emphasis on it. This is supported by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is true⦆. Alternatively, "ahaqq" is the subject (mubtada'), and the pronoun is raised by it, standing in place of the predicate (khabar), and the clause is in the position of an accusative (nasb) governed by "yastanbi'unaka" (they ask you). It has also been read as "aḥaqqa huwa" (Is it the truth?), as an allusion that it is false, as if it were said: "Is it the truth and not the falsehood, or is it that which you have named the truth?"

Say to them, without turning to their mockery, overlooking what they intended, and building the matter upon the foundation of wisdom: ﴿Yes, by my Lord⦆. "Iy" (ey) is among the particles of affirmation, meaning "yes" in an oath specifically, just as "hal" means "qad" in interrogation specifically; for this reason it is joined with its "waw" (wa). ﴿Indeed, it⦆, i.e., the punishment promised, ﴿is true⦆, certainly established without doubt. The answer has been emphasized with the most complete forms of emphasis according to the intensity and strength of their denial. It has been further affirmed and confirmed by the words of the Mighty of Name: ﴿And you cannot escape⦆, i.e., you cannot escape the punishment by fleeing, and it will certainly overtake you. This is either coordinated (ma'tuf) with the answer to the oath, or it is a new sentence (musta'naf) brought to explain their inability to escape, along with what it contains of the aforementioned affirmation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 54:

﴿And if every soul that had wronged⁠ ﴾ through polytheism (al-shirk), or through transgression against others, or other kinds of wrongdoing—even once, as the description being a verb (fi'l) implies—﴿whatever is on the earth﴾, that is, whatever is in the world of its treasures, its wealth and its benefits, all of it, however much it may be, ﴿would ransom itself with it﴾, that is, would make it a ransom for itself from the punishment; from iftada, which has the meaning of fada (to ransom). ﴿And they will conceal⁠ ﴾, that is, the souls indicated by "every soul," and the shift to the plural form, although the generality is already realized in the singular form as well, is to convey the gravity of the matter, since the concealing is done together and collectively. This was not taken into account in what preceded in order to realize what is intended by assuming that everything on earth belongs to each one of the souls. The choice of the masculine plural form is either to treat the word "soul" as referring to a person, or to give precedence to the masculine referents over the feminine ones. ﴿the regret⁠ ﴾ over what they had done of wrongdoing, that is, they hid it and did not show it—but not out of patient endurance and self-restraint (hayhat wa-la-ta hina sabr, "far-fetched, and there is no time for patience"), but because they were stunned ﴿when they saw the punishment⁠ ﴾, that is, at the moment of witnessing, from the horror of the situation and the severity of the terrors that they had not expected, so they were not able to speak a word. So "lamma" (when) here means "when" and is in the accusative governed by "asarru" (they concealed), or it is a conditional particle whose response has been omitted because of what precedes it. It has also been said: their leaders, from among those whom they misled, concealed it out of shame before them and fear of their reproach; but the matter is too grave for anything other than fear of the punishment to overtake them there. It has also been said: "they concealed the regret" means they made it sincere, because concealing it is making it sincere; or because the secret of a thing is its essence, where one hides it and guards it jealously, so there is a mockery of them in this. It has also been said: they showed the regret, from the saying "asarra al-shay'" and "ashharahu," meaning "he displayed it," when his patience was exhausted and his self-control failed.

﴿And it will be judged between them⁠ ﴾, that is, the judgment is carried out between the wrongdoers among the polytheists and others from the categories of wrongdoers, by making the truth manifest, whether it concerns the rights of God, glorified is He, or the rights of people from falsehood, and each group is treated in the manner befitting it. ﴿with justice⁠ ﴾, with equity. Restricting wrongdoing to transgression and taking the judgment to mean merely adjudication between wrongdoers and the wronged, without addressing the state of the polytheists—who are the greatest of wrongdoers—is not supported by the context; for its implication is either that wrongdoing refers to polytheism, or to what enters into it at the first level. ﴿And they⁠ ﴾, that is, the wrongdoers, ﴿will not be wronged⁠ ﴾ regarding what is done to them of punishment; rather, it is among the requirements of their wrongdoing and its necessary consequences.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 55:

﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is: whatever exists in them, either as part of their reality or outside them but established within them. The word "mā" (whatever) is used to give precedence to non-rational beings over rational ones. This is an affirmation of God's perfect power over all things, and a demonstration that everything is included under His dominion, which He disposes as He wills, bringing into existence and annihilating, rewarding and punishing. ﴿Surely the promise of God﴾: the use of the Glorious Name here serves to magnify the importance of the promise and to indicate the reason for the ruling. The word "promise" (wa'd) may be understood either in the sense of what is promised (al-mawʿūd), that is, all that has been promised, whatever it may be, so that the punishment they sought to hasten is included in it, as is what was mentioned in the course of describing their condition, included in the first instance; or in its verbal sense (al-maṣdar), that is, His promise of all that has been mentioned. Accordingly, the meaning of His words ﴿is true﴾ (aḥaqq) on the first interpretation is: established and certain to occur without doubt; and on the second: conforming to reality. The opening of both clauses with the two particles of alerting and affirmation (alā and inna) serves to register their content, which confirms the content of the preceding noble verses, and to draw attention to the necessity of keeping it in mind and safeguarding it. ﴿But most of them﴾ — because of the deficiency of their intellects, the dominance of heedlessness over them, and their understanding only through familiar sensory conditions — ﴿do not know﴾ this, so they say what they say and do what they do.

He gives life and causes death ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ in this world, without anyone having any part in that; ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ in the Hereafter, through resurrection and gathering.

﴿O mankind﴾ is a shift (iltifat, a change of address) and a return to drawing them toward the truth and inducing them to accept and follow it, after warning them of the perils of misguidance through the stark admonitions recited to them, which declare the evil of their final outcome. It also indicates that all of this is directed toward their welfare and benefit. ﴿There has certainly come to you an admonition﴾: *mawizah*, *wa'z* and *'izah* all mean reminding of consequences, whether by deterrence and warning or by inducement and encouragement. The word "from" (*min*) in His words, ﴿from your Lord﴾, is either initial (*ibtida'iyyah*), linked to "has come to you," or partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), linked to an omitted element that serves as a qualifier of "admonition," meaning: an admonition that is one of the admonitions of your Lord. In the mention of the title of Lordship (*rububiyyah*) there is an excellence of placement that is not hidden.

﴿and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾: that is, it is a book comprising these benefits and advantages. It reveals the states of actions, their good and their bad, encourages the former and deters from the latter. It clarifies the true knowledge which is a healing for what is in the breasts of the spiritual ailments, such as ignorance, doubt, polytheism, hypocrisy, and other deviant beliefs. It is a guide to the path of truth and certainty by directing to reasoning from the signs set up in the horizons and in the souls. Its coming is a mercy for the believers, since through it they were delivered from the darkness of disbelief and misguidance into the light of faith, were freed from the levels of the fires, and ascended to the degrees of the gardens. The indefiniteness in all of these (*tankir*) is for magnification.(p-156)

"Say" (qul) is a shift in address, directing the speech to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so that he would command the people to seize upon the grace and mercy that are in the Mighty Qur'an. ﴿By the grace of God and by His mercy﴾. What is meant by these two is either what is in the coming of the Qur'an of grace and mercy, or the category (jins) of them; and both are included in it in the primary sense. The preposition (ba') is connected to an omitted verb, and the original sentence is: "Let them rejoice in the grace of God and His mercy." The repetition of the preposition before "His mercy" serves to indicate that each is independently sufficient to warrant rejoicing. Then the prepositional phrase was placed before the verb to convey restriction (qasr). Then the fa' was introduced upon it to convey the sense of causation, so it became: "By the grace of God and His mercy, then let them rejoice." Then it was said: ﴿So by that let them rejoice﴾, for emphasis and affirmation. Then the first verb was omitted because the second indicates it. The first fa' is conditional (jaza'iyyah), and the second serves to indicate causation. The original is: "If they rejoice in anything, then by that let them rejoice, and not in anything else." Then the fa' was introduced to indicate causation, then the condition was omitted. The sense of distance in the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) indicates the great degree of the grace of God Most High and His mercy. It is also permissible that what is meant by "the grace of God and His mercy" is: "then let them strive," and "so by that let them rejoice." It is also permissible for the preposition to be connected to "has come to you," meaning: "An admonition has come to you by the grace of God and His mercy; so by that, i.e., by its coming, let them rejoice." It was recited as (fa-li-tafrahu) [with the lam of command and the ta' of the second person plural]. Ubayy recited (fa-ifrahu) [in the imperative]. And from Ibn Ka'b: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Say: By the grace of God and His mercy﴾, and said: 'By the Book of God and Islam.'" It was also said: His grace is Islam, and His mercy is what He promised for it. That is, what has been mentioned of the grace of God and His mercy ﴿is better than what they gather﴾ of the debris of this world. It was recited as (yajma'un) [with ya', third person plural]... meaning: "So by that let the believers rejoice; it is better than what you gather, O you addressed."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 59:

﴿Say: Have you considered﴾, i.e., tell me, ﴿what Allah has sent down to you of provision﴾. The word ما (ma) is in the accusative position, governed either by what follows it or by what precedes it. The lam (in لكم, "to you") indicates that the intended meaning of "provision" is what is lawful for them. Describing it as "sent down" is because it is decreed in the heaven, and it is brought into existence, or what its existence or continuance depends upon, through heavenly causes such as rain and the stars, in ripening and coloring. ﴿Then you made from it﴾, i.e., you made part of it ﴿unlawful﴾, i.e., you judged that it is unlawful ﴿and lawful﴾, i.e., you made part of it lawful, meaning you judged it to be lawful, although all of it is lawful. This is their saying: ﴿These are livestock and tilth, forbidden (hijr)﴾ ... to the end of the verse, and their saying: ﴿What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾, and the like. The unlawful is mentioned first because the effect of the making appears in it and the rebuke revolves around it.

﴿Say﴾: a repetition to emphasize the command of questioning, i.e., tell me. ﴿Has Allah permitted you﴾ in that making, so that you are complying with His command, Exalted is He? ﴿Or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾ The "or" (أم) is connected, and the interrogation is for confirmation and rebuke, since knowledge of the final alternative is certain. It is as if it were said: "Or has He not permitted you, but you fabricate against Him, glorified is He?" The glorious Name is made explicit and placed before the verb, indicating the complete ugliness of their fabrication and emphasizing the rebuke after an emphasis, while observing the rhyme-endings. It is also permissible that the interrogation is for denial, and the "or" is disjunctive (منقطعة). The meaning of "bal" (بل) in it is a turning away and a transition from rebuke and reprimand by denying permission to what its interrogative hamza conveys of rebuke for fabricating against Him, glorified is He, and confirming it. Placing the prepositional phrase before this may be for restriction (القصر), as if it were said: "Rather, is it upon Allah alone, Exalted, that you fabricate?!"(p-157)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 60:

﴿And what will be the thought of those who fabricate lies against Allah?﴾ This is a statement sent down from Him, the Exalted, to explain the terror of what they will encounter. It is not included under the saying that was commanded (to be spoken). The expression of them with the relative pronoun (alladhina) in the place where a pronoun would be expected serves to cut off the first possibility of the disjunction, and to record upon them the fabrication (iftira'), and the addition of "lie" (al-kadhib), although fabrication cannot be anything but a lie, serves to show the complete ugliness of what they devised and that it is a lie in their own belief as well. The word "ma" (what) is interrogative, placed as a subject (mubtada'), with zanna (thought) as its predicate, and its two objects are omitted.

As for the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, it is an adverbial complement of the thought itself, meaning: what is their thought on that day, the day of the presentation of deeds, words, and the requital for them, measure for measure. The intent is to magnify and make terrible its dread, by the terror of what is connected with it of what will be done to them on that day. It has been said that it is an adverbial complement of what their thought is connected to today of matters that will occur on the Day of Resurrection, treating it, and what is in it of states, because of the complete clarity of its matter in being fixed and established, as if it were something already accepted by them. That is: what is their thought regarding what will happen on the Day of Resurrection? Do they suppose that they will not be questioned about their fabrication, or will not be recompensed for it, or will be recompensed with an easy recompense, and for that reason they do what they do? Nay, indeed they will be in the most severe punishment, because their disobedience is the most grievous of disobediences, and who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? It has been read in the past tense form, meaning: they thought on the Day of Resurrection. The use of the past form is because it is certain to occur, so it is as if it has already happened.

﴿Indeed Allah is surely Full of Bounty﴾, that is: great, whose true reality cannot be comprehended, ﴿to mankind﴾, that is: all of them, in that He bestowed upon them the intellect that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and between the good and the ugly, and showed them mercy by sending down the Books and dispatching the Messengers, and clarified for them the secrets that the intellects cannot independently grasp, and guided them to what concerns them regarding the affairs of livelihood and the Hereafter. ﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾ for that magnificent blessing, so they do not direct their powers and faculties to that for which they were created, nor do they follow the proof of reason in what it independently determines, nor the proof of the Law in what can be known only by it. He has graciously shown them the explanation of what they will encounter on the Day of Resurrection, yet they do not pay heed to it, so they fall into what they fall into. Thus this is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for what preceded, establishing its content.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 61:

﴿And you are not engaged in any matter﴾ i.e., in any affair, from "sha'antu sha'nahu," meaning I intended his intention; it is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul). ﴿And you do not recite from it﴾: the pronoun refers to the affair (sha'n), and the adverbial phrase (zarf) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., a recitation that is from the affair, since it is the greatest of his affairs, upon him be peace; or it refers to the Revelation (tanzil), and the pronoun preceding its mention is for the glorification of its status. The "min" here is either for the starting point (ibtida'iyya), or partitive (tab'idiyya), or it refers to God, Mighty and Majestic, and the "min" is for the starting point. The "min" in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿from any Qur'an﴾ is redundant (za'ida) for the emphasis of the negation, or it is for the starting point according to the first aspect, and explanatory (bayaniyya) or partitive according to the second and third.

﴿And you do not do any deed﴾ is a generalization of the address after its specification to the leader of all; and in each of the two situations what befits it has been observed: first, the deeds mentioned are those that carry grandeur and majesty, and second, what encompasses both the great and the small.

﴿except that We are witnesses over you﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of the states of those addressed by the three verbs, i.e., you are not engaged in any of them in any state except that We are observers, watching over it and guarding it. ﴿when you are immersed in it﴾ i.e., you plunge into it and rush into it. The basic meaning of "ifada" is rushing forth in abundance or with force. And since by the previous verbs is meant the continuous, lasting state coinciding with past time as well, the past form was chosen in the exception, and in the adverb the word "idh," which conveys the present with the meaning of the past, was used.

﴿And not absent from your Lord﴾ i.e., nothing is far off or hidden from His comprehensive knowledge; and in the mention of the title of Lordship there is an indication of gentleness that is not hidden. It is also read with a kasra on the zay. ﴿is any weight of an atom﴾: the word "min" is redundant for the emphasis of the negation, i.e., nothing escapes Him that equals in weight a small ant or floating dust. ﴿in the earth or in the heaven﴾ i.e., within the sphere of existence and possibility, for the common people know of no other possible thing that is not in one of these, or connected to them. The earth is mentioned first because the discourse concerns its inhabitants, and the purpose is to establish proof of the encompassing of His knowledge, Exalted is He, over its details.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And not smaller than that, nor greater, but it is in a clear Book﴾, it is an independent statement confirming what precedes it, and "la" is negating for the genus; "asghar" is its subject, and "fi kitab" is its predicate. It is also read with a nominative (raf') as a subject and predicate. "Min" is coordinated with the wording of "mithqal dharra" and the fatha replaces the kasra due to the impossibility of declension; or it is coordinated with its position together with the preposition. The exception is made disjunctive, as if it were said: nothing escapes your Lord, but all things are in a clear Book, so how could anything of them escape Him? It was also said: the exception may be connected, and "ya'zub" is in the sense of "yabin" and "yasdur" (becomes manifest and proceeds), and the meaning is: nothing proceeds from Him, Exalted is He, except that it is in a clear Book. The "clear Book" is meant to be the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, the friends of Allah﴾ is an explanation given in the manner of good tidings and promise, concerning what is the outcome of the deeds of the believers, and the final end of what was mentioned before it: that Exalted Allah is watchful over His Prophet ﷺ and his community in all that they do and all that they leave undone, and that His knowledge, glorified is He, encompasses everything in the heavens and the earth, and that all of it is recorded in the Clear Book. This follows the mention of the terrible state of those who fabricate lies against Allah, Exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection, and of the terror that will befall them, a general allusion in the manner of threat and warning. The sentence is introduced with the two particles of alerting and affirmation (ألا and إنّ) in order to increase the firm establishment of its content. The word al-wali (الوليّ) linguistically means "the near one," and what is meant by "the friends of Allah" is the pure believers, because of their spiritual nearness to Him, glorified and exalted is He, as their explanation will make clear. ﴿There is no fear for them﴾ in either of the two abodes from the befalling of something disliked, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ over the loss of something desired. That is: nothing befalls them that would necessitate that (fear or grief). It does not mean that it befalls them but they do not fear or grieve, nor does it mean that fear and grief never touch them at all; rather they continue in vigor and joy. How could it be otherwise, since sensing fear and awe, out of magnifying the majesty and awesomeness of Allah, glorified is He, and regarding one's striving and effort in establishing the rights of servanthood as insufficient, is among the distinctive traits of the elite and the near ones? The intended meaning is: the explanation of the continuous negation of these two, not the explanation of the negation of their continuity, as might be suggested by the fact that the predicate in the second clause is a present-tense verb (يَحْزَنُونَ), in line with what has been repeatedly stated: if the negation enters upon the present-tense verb itself, it indicates continuity and permanence according to the context. Such feelings may befall them because their aim is nothing but obedience to Allah, Exalted is He, and attaining His good pleasure, which entails honor and nearness; and there is no doubt in its attainment, nor any possibility of its loss, by virtue of the promise with respect to Him, Exalted is He. As for everything else of worldly matters, which hover between attainment and loss, these are far removed from being included in the thread of their purpose, whether existing or not, so that they would fear the arrival of its harm or grieve over the loss of its benefit.

And the saying of Him, Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 63:

﴿Those who believed﴾, that is, in everything that came from Allah the Exalted, ﴿and were God-fearing﴾, that is, they guarded themselves against what must be guarded against, of deeds and abstentions, with a constant guarding, as the combination of the past and the present tense forms indicates. This is an explanation and clarification of them, and an indication of what enabled them to attain what they attained, in the manner of a resumptive clause (istinaf) built upon a question. The relative clause is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "Who are those, and what is the cause of their success with that honour?" So it was said: "They are the ones who combined faith and taqwa (God-consciousness), which lead to every good and keep away from every evil." It was also said that its position is in the accusative case, or in the nominative by way of praise, or that it is a descriptive phrase of praise for the awliya' (friends of Allah). The interposition of the predicate does not detract from this.

By taqwa is meant its third level, which encompasses what lies beneath it: the level of guarding oneself against shirk, which faith also conveys, and the level of avoiding everything that incurs sin, whether of action or of omission, that is, a person's purification of himself from everything that occupies his inner self away from the Truth and from devoting himself to it entirely. This is the true taqwa commanded in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear that is due to Him﴾. By it arise witnessing, presence and nearness, upon which the application of the name revolves. Thus was the state of those who entered under the address together with him ﷺ, in His words, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿and you do not do any deed﴾. However, they differ in the matter of devotion and purification in degrees, according to the differences in their degrees of readiness that are bestowed upon them in accordance with the will that is founded upon lofty wisdoms. The highest of these is what the aspirations of the prophets, peace be upon them, reached, so that they combined thereby the leadership of prophethood and of sainthood. Attachment to the world of forms did not hinder them from being absorbed in the world of spirits, and involvement with the interests of creation did not prevent them from devoting themselves to the presence of the Truth, owing to the perfection of readiness of their pure souls, supported by holy power. Thus the essence of the matter of sainthood is the taqwa mentioned. So the awliya' of Allah are the believers who are God-fearing.

Close to this is what was said: that they are those whom Allah guided with proof, and who undertook to uphold the right of the servanthood of Allah the Exalted and to call to Him. It does not conflict with this what was said: that they are those by whose sight Allah is remembered, on the basis of what was narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked: Who are the awliya' of Allah? He said: 'They are those by whose sight Allah is remembered.'" That is, by their bearing, their humility and their tranquillity. Nor does it conflict with what was said: that they are those who love one another for the sake of Allah, on the basis of what was narrated from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Among the servants of Allah are servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whom the prophets and martyrs will envy on the Day of Resurrection because of their station with Allah." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell us who they are and what their deeds are, so that we may love them." He said: "They are a people who love one another for the sake of Allah, not through kinship nor through wealth that they exchange. By Allah, their faces are light, and they are upon pulpits of light. They do not fear when people fear, and they do not grieve when people grieve."

What was mentioned of the goodly bearing and tranquillity that remind one of Allah the Exalted, and of loving one another for the sake of Allah, the Glorified, are worldly rulings necessary for faith and taqwa, and the particular effects of both, which deserve to be singled out for mention because of their manifestness and their nearness to people's understanding.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ related each of these according to what the situation of guidance and admonition requires, as encouragement for the questioners or others among those present, regarding what he singled out for mention there of their rulings. Perhaps those present at first needed to correct their condition in terms of words, deeds, clothing and the like, and those present at a later stage needed to have their hearts brought together and inclined toward the believers with whom they have no bond of lineage or kinship, and to reinforce the religious brotherhood that exists between them by explaining its great importance, its elevated station and its good outcome; so that they might observe its rights and abandon those of their own kin who do not agree with them in religion.

As for what was mentioned, that the prophets will envy them, it is a depiction of their good condition in the manner of a parable. Al-Kawashi said: "This is hyperbole, and the meaning is: if a people were supposed to have this description, these would be they." It was also said: the awliya' of Allah are those who take Him as their guardian through obedience, and whom He takes as His guardians through honour. And His words, may He be exalted and glorified: "those who believed and were God-fearing" have been taken as an explanation of their taking Him as guardian, and His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿لَهُمُ البُشْرى في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا وفي الآخِرَةِ﴾ [For them are good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter] is an explanation of His, exalted is He, taking them as allies (tawallīhi iyyāhum). There is no doubt that considering the final condition (al-qayd al-akhīr) as part of the concept of wilāyah (allyship) is not suitable to the context of encouraging the believers to attain it, to remain steadfast upon it, and to give them good news of its effects and results. Rather, it undermines that purpose, since attainment (al-taḥṣīl) pertains only to what is within one's power, and joyful anticipation (al-istibshār) arises only from something whose cause is known to exist. The stated condition is neither within their power, so that they could attain wilāyah by attaining it, nor known to them at its occurrence, so that they could recognise the attainment of wilāyah for themselves and rejoice in its fine effects. Rather, "taking them as allies with honour" is itself the result of wilāyah. Therefore, including it in the heading of the subject, and then informing of the absence of fear and grief, is unfitting for the dignity of the sublime revelation. What its noble composition requires is that the first (phrase) is an explanation of "the awliyā'" (allies) as has been set out, and the second is a statement of what He has granted them of the good of both abodes after the explanation of their deliverance from the evils and hardships of both. The sentence is resumptive (mustanaffah), as has preceded, as if it were said: "Is there for them, beyond that, any blessing and honour?" So it was said: "For them is what gladdens them in both abodes." The first is placed first because clearing (al-takhliyah, removal of evil) precedes adorning (al-taḥliyah, bestowal of good), along with what this contains of observing the right of contrast between the good condition of the believers and the bad condition of the slanderers.

Hastening the entry of joy by the good news of deliverance from terrors, and placing the preceding explanation between the good news of deliverance from what is feared and the good news of success in what is sought, is to show the complete care given to the explanation of "the allies," while also indicating that the absence of fear and grief is due to their guarding themselves against the causes that lead to them.

Al-bushrā is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used to mean that which is announced as good, from the immediate goods such as victory, conquest, booty and other things, and from the deferred goods, which are too great to need explanation. The choice of indefiniteness and generality is to indicate that it is beyond explanation and detail. The two adverbial phrases (al-ẓarfān) are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) concerning it, and the governing element is the sense of stability contained in the predicate, meaning: "For them is good tidings, while it is in the life of this world, and while it is in the Hereafter," that is, immediate and deferred. Or it is from the pronoun in the genitive (al-ḍamīr al-majrūr), meaning: "while they are in the life..." etc.

From the immediate good tidings is good praise, a fine remembrance, and the love of people. "On the authority of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him: I said: O Messenger of Allah, a man does a deed for Allah and people love him? So the Prophet ﷺ said: 'That is the immediate good tiding of the believer.'"

That said, it has been said: al-bushrā is a verbal noun, and the two adverbial phrases are connected to it. As for the good tidings in this world, they are the good tidings directed at the believing, God-fearing people in more than one place in the Clear Book.

And from the Prophet ﷺ: "It is the righteous dream which a believer sees or which is shown to him." And from him ﷺ: "Prophethood has departed, but the bearers of good tidings remain." And from ʿAṭāʾ: "For them is good tidings" at death, when the angels come to them with mercy. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The angels descend upon them, [saying]: "Do not fear and do not grieve, and rejoice in the Garden which you were promised."﴾

As for the good tidings in the Hereafter: the angels' receiving them as Muslims, given good news of success and honour, what they see of the whiteness of their faces, the giving of the records into their right hands, what they read in them, and other good tidings. So this is a good tiding of what will occur of the immediate and deferred good tidings, desired for their ends and not for themselves. It is not hidden that diverting the present good tiding from its primary purposes to its means is not supported by the grandeur of the noble revelation.

﴿لا تَبْدِيلَ لِكَلِماتِ اللَّهِ﴾ [There is no changing of the words of Allah]: there is no alteration of His sayings, among which are His promises given as good tidings to the believing, God-fearing people. Thus the good tidings mentioned here enter into it in the first instance, and the impossibility of their being broken is established with certainty. And on the supposition that the intended meaning of "good tidings" is the righteous dream, the meaning of the non-alteration of His words, exalted is He, is not the absence of discrepancy between them and their worldly and otherworldly results, but rather the absence of discrepancy between them and what indicates their establishment and occurrence in what will come by way of promise, in His saying, exalted is He: "For them is good tidings." So reflect.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ [That] refers to what has been mentioned, that for them is good tidings in both abodes. ﴿هُوَ الفَوْزُ العَظِيمُ﴾ [is the great triumph], beyond which there is no triumph. In it is an explanation of what was left vague earlier. That sentence and the one before it are a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) to establish the thing announced as good and to magnify its status. It is not a condition of it that what follows be connected to what precedes, or that this be a concluding clause (tadhyīl) and the earlier ones a parenthetical insertion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 65:

﴿And let not their speech grieve you.﴾ This is a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) for what he suffered from them by way of harm arising from their hateful statements, and a glad tidings to him (ﷺ) that He, Mighty and Majestic, will support him and grant him victory over them. It follows the explanation that he and his followers have security from every feared thing and success in every sought goal. It is also read as (وَلا يُحْزِنُكَ) from the verb أحزنه (ahzanahu, "to grieve someone"). In reality, this is a prohibition to him (ﷺ) against grief, as if it were said: "Do not grieve over their words, and do not care about their denial and their consultation about plotting your destruction, the nullifying of your affair, and all that they utter concerning you that contains no good." The prohibition was directed at their speech for the sake of emphasis in forbidding him (ﷺ) from grief, because a prohibition against being affected (al-ta'thir) is, in its essence, a prohibition against being influenced (al-ta'thur) and a complete negation of it. The prohibition may be directed at a necessary consequence (al-lazim), while what is intended is the prohibition of that which necessitates it (al-malzum), as in your saying: "I will not see you here." The specific mention of the prohibition against grief, despite the general negation mentioned previously covering grief as well, is because there was in him (ﷺ) no trace of fear that would warrant being forbidden from it. Perhaps some kind of grief would occasionally overcome him (ﷺ) at certain times, so he was consoled about it.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the honor⁠﻿﻿ belongs entirely to Allah⁠﻿﻿﴾ is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the prohibition, given in the form of a resumptive sentence (istinaf), meaning: the dominance and the power ﴿belong entirely to Allah⁠﻿﻿﴾, that is, within His dominion and authority, and no one possesses any of it at all, neither they nor others. So He subdues them, protects you from them, and grants you victory over them. This has indeed been the case, so it is among the immediate glad tidings. It is also read with the opening of (أنّ, "that/indeed") as a clear causal particle, meaning: because honor belongs to Allah. ﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing⁠﻿﻿﴾: He hears what they say concerning you, and knows what they resolve upon, and He will requite them for that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 66:

﴿Surely to God belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾. That is: the rational beings among the angels and the two weighty creatures (humans and jinn). Their being specified by mention is to signal that there is no need to state explicitly anything other than them, for they, despite their nobility and the loftiness of their rank, when they are servants of Him, glorified is He, subdued under His domination and dominion, then whatever else is among the existing things is more deserving of this. And it, along with what it contains of emphasis on what preceded regarding the exclusivity of might to God, Exalted is He, which necessitates the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his not caring about the polytheists and their statements, is a preparation for what follows from His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And those who call upon other than God as partners do not follow them﴾, and a proof of the invalidity of (p-162) their assumptions and the actions built upon them. The "ma" (what) is either negative, and "shuraka'" (partners) is the object of "yattabi'" (follow), and the object of "yad'una" (call upon) is omitted because it is evident, meaning: those who call upon other than God as partners do not in reality follow partners, even if they name them partners. So it has been limited to one of the two, due to the evidence of its indication of the other. It is also permissible that the mentioned term is the object of "yad'una" and the object of "yattabi'" is omitted because it is understood from His saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾, meaning: they do not follow certainty; they only follow their false conjecture. Or it is a relative pronoun conjoined to "min" (whoever), as if it were said: and to God belongs what those who call upon other than God as partners follow, meaning: and to Him belong their partners.

Their being specified by mention, despite their inclusion in what preceded, is an expression or an implication for the purpose of intensifying the explanation of the invalidity of their following and the corruption of what they built upon it, namely their assumption that their partners are worshipped, while they are servants of Him, glorified is He. Or it is an interrogative, meaning: what do they follow? That is: they do not follow anything; what they follow is only conjecture and false state, like His saying: ﴿You worship besides Him only names you have named﴾... etc.

It is also read "tad'un" (you call upon) with the "ta'", and then the interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, as if it were said: what do those whom you call upon as partners from among the angels and prophets follow? This is to affirm that they are followers of God, Exalted is He, obedient to Him, and as a reproach to them for not emulating them in that, like His saying: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek a means of access to their Lord﴾. Then the speech is turned from address to the third person, so it is said: these polytheists follow only conjecture, and they do not follow what the angels and prophets follow of the truth. ﴿And they are only guessing﴾: they lie in what they attribute to Him, glorified is He, and they conjecture and estimate that they are partners, by a false estimation.

﴿It is He who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight﴾. This is an indication of His exclusive possession of complete power and all-encompassing blessing, so that it may guide them to the Oneness of His (glory be to Him) being worthy of worship, and a confirmation of what preceded concerning the fact that all possible existents are under His power and dominion, which makes clear that might belongs exclusively to Him (glory be to Him). If the verb "ja'ala" (made) carries the sense of origination (al-Ibda', bringing into existence) and creation (al-Khalq), then "mubsiran" (giving sight) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Otherwise, "lakum" (for you) is its second object, or it is a circumstantial qualifier as in the first case, and the second object is "li-taskunu fihi" (that you may rest therein). Or the second object may be omitted, indicated by the second object of the second sentence, just as the final cause of it is omitted, relying on what is stated in the first.

The sense is: It is He who made the night for you dark, that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight, that you may move about in it for your benefits. Its parallel will come in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none who can remove it but He; and if He intends for you good, there is none who can repel His bounty﴾ ... to the end of the verse. So in each of the two sides there has been omitted what was mentioned in the other, being satisfied with what is mentioned in place of what is left out. The ascription of "giving sight" (al-Ibsar) to the day is figurative (majazi), like that in: "its day is fasting" (nahāruhu sā'imun).

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in the making of each of them as described, or in both of them. The demonstrative's sense of distance is for the announcement of the great rank of the one pointed to and the loftiness of its station. ﴿are signs﴾, wondrous and numerous, or other signs besides what has been mentioned, ﴿for a people who hear﴾, i.e., these recited signs and their likes that draw attention to those created signs, commanding reflection upon them with a hearing of contemplation and reflection, so that they act in accordance with their requirements. The specification of the signs for them, although they are set up for the benefit of all, is because they are the ones who benefit from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 68:

﴿They say: "God has taken a son."﴾ This begins the mention of another kind of their falsehoods and the explanation of its invalidity. (p-163) That is, he adopted him. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence and holiness above what they attribute to Him, and an expression of wonder at their foolish statement. ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ absolutely, in need of nothing in anything. This is the reason for His transcendence, and it indicates that taking a son is among the attributes of need.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, that is, of rational beings and others. This affirms His self-sufficiency and confirms His ownership of everything other than Himself, exalted is He. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, that is, no proof for what has been mentioned of their false saying. This clarifies its invalidity by establishing that the clear demonstration presented is free from any counter-argument. The particle ﴿مِن﴾ in His saying ﴿مِن سُلْطانٍ﴾ ("any authority") is extra, for emphasizing the negation, and it is the subject, with the preceded adverbial phrase as its predicate. Alternatively, it is in the nominative as the agent of the adverbial phrase, because the phrase depends on the negation. The phrase ﴿بِهَذا﴾ ("for this") is connected either to ﴿سُلْطانٍ﴾, because it means proof and evidence, or to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of it, or to the sense of settledness contained in ﴿عِنْدَكم﴾ ("you have"), as if it were said: "You have in this statement any authority." The shift to address (iltifat, a change from third person to second person) is for greater intensity in binding them and silencing them, and to emphasize the rebuke and reproach contained in His saying: ﴿Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾ for their ignorance and disagreement. This contains an alert that every assertion without evidence is ignorance, that beliefs must have a decisive proof, and that taqlid (blind imitation of authority) has no standing whatsoever.

ۚ"Say" (﴿قُلْ﴾): a shift in the mode of address, directing the speech to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) so that he may make clear to them the evil of their end and the gravity of their outcome. ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate lies against God﴾, meaning: in every matter, so that what we are concerned with enters by way of fabrication through attributing a son and a partner to Him, glory be to Him, entering first and foremost. ﴿will not prosper﴾, meaning: they will not be saved from any harm, nor will they attain any desired thing at all. The restriction of non-salvation and non-success to what falls under that category, namely non-salvation from the Fire and non-success in attaining Paradise, does not suit the context of emphasis in warning against fabricating lies against Him, glory be to Him.

﴿Matā'un fi al-dunyā﴾ (a brief enjoyment in this world) is a resumed statement (mustaʾnaf) brought to explain that what appears to them, outwardly, of attaining their aims and enjoying worldly pleasures in general, or within their fabrications, is far from being the kind of success (falāḥ). It is as if it were said: "How will they not succeed when they are in ease and comfort?" So it was answered: "It is a small enjoyment in this world, and not a success in attaining what is sought." Then, by His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿Then to Us is their return﴾, the absence of deliverance from what is disliked is also indicated; that is, by death.

﴿Then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾. So they remain in everlasting wretchedness because of their continuous disbelief, or because of their disbelief in the world. Then where are they from success? It has been said that the omitted subject (mubtada' maḥdhūf) is "their life" or "their turning about," and it has been said that it is their fabrication. It is not hidden that mata' (enjoyment) is applied only to what is inclined to by the soul, desired in itself, enjoyed and benefited from. The reason it is not regarded is its swift passing away. The very act of fabricating against Him, Glorified is He, is the worst of ugly deeds in the soul, let alone being inclined to by it. To count it as such is by considering the application of the ruling of what leads to it, namely their leadership through it, which has no basis. So the correct view is what was mentioned first. It is not far-fetched what has been said: that the omitted element is the predicate (khabar), that is, "for them is an enjoyment."
