The verse is either delivered from God Exalted, to establish that they will not succeed, and not included in the speech that was commanded, as the apparent sense of His words, Exalted is He, "Then to Us" and His words, Exalted is He, "Then We will make them taste," indicate; or it is included in it, on the basis that the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to convey it and relate it from Him, Mighty and Majestic is He.(p-164)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 71:

﴿And recite to them﴾, i.e., to the polytheists among the people of Makkah and others, in order to confirm what has preceded, that they will not prosper, that what they enjoy is on the wing of passing away, and that they are on the verge of the everlasting punishment.

﴿the news of Nuh﴾, i.e., his account, which is of great significance and importance with his people, who are like your people in disbelief and obstinacy; so that they may reflect upon what it contains of the cessation of what they enjoyed of bounty, and the descent of the punishment of drowning joined to the lasting punishment, so that they may be restrained thereby from the disbelief in which they are, or so that the severity of their stubbornness may be broken, or so that some of them may acknowledge the truth of your prophethood, in that they recognise that what you recite agrees with what is established among them without any contradiction between them at all, along with their knowledge that you did not hear that from anyone except by way of revelation. It also contains, regarding the confirmation of what has preceded, that everything belongs to Allah, glorified is He, and the exclusivity of might to Him, exalted is He, and the absence of fear and grief from His friends, mighty and exalted is He, all of them, and the encouragement of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his being led to disregard them, their sayings and their deeds, which is not hidden.

﴿when he said﴾: the clause is a ma'mul (object governed) of (نبأ, "news"), or a badal (substitute) from it, a badal ishtimal (substitution of inclusion). Whichever it is, what is meant is some of the account of Nuh (ﷺ), not all that took place between him and his people. The lam in His words, exalted is He, ﴿to his people﴾ is for conveying (al-tabligh, the delivery of the message).

﴿O my people, if my standing (maqam) is heavy upon you﴾, i.e., becomes great and burdensome. (Maqam) means my self, as one says: "I did it for the place (makan) of so-and-so," meaning for so-and-so; and from it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿and for him who fears the standing of his Lord﴾, i.e., fears his Lord. Or (maqam) means my standing and my remaining among you for a long period, or my standing up [to preach]. For they, when they admonished the assembly, would stand on their feet while the assembly sat, so that their condition would be made evident and their speech heard.

﴿then upon Allah I have relied (tawakkaltu)﴾ is the answer to the condition, i.e., I remain constant in restricting reliance (tawakkul, trust in God) to Him, exalted is He. It is also permissible that what is meant is the bringing about of a specific rank among the ranks of tawakkul.

﴿So resolve upon your affair﴾: it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the answer, and the fa' is for the sequence of the command to resolve upon reliance on Him, not for the sequence of the resolving itself upon it. Or it is the answer, and what preceded is an intervening clause (jumla mu'tarida). (Al-ijma', resolve) means determination. It is said that it is transitive by itself; and it is said that there is an omission and the adding of a preposition. Al-Sudusi said: "ajma'tu al-amr" (I resolved the matter) is more eloquent than "ajma'tu 'alayhi" (I resolved upon it). Abu al-Haytham said: "ajma'a amrahu" means he made it gathered after it had been scattered; its scattering is that one says at one time, "I will do this," and at another, "I will do that"; and when he determines upon one matter, he has gathered it, i.e., made it whole.

﴿and your partners﴾: with the accusative, on the basis that the waw is in the sense of "with" (ma'a), as the reading with the nominative indicates, conjoining it to the attached pronoun, treating the separation as a kind of emphasis. The attribution of resolving to the partners is in the manner of mockery (al-tahakkum). It is also said that it is conjoined to (amrakum) with an omitted modifier, i.e., the affair of your partners. It is also said that it is governed by an omitted verb, i.e., "and call upon your partners." It has been read as (kadhalika) and read as (fajma'u) from al-jam' (gathering), i.e., resolve upon your affair with which you intend against me, by seeking my destruction, and exert yourselves in it in whatever manner you are able.

﴿Then let not your affair be to you a gloom (ghumma)﴾, i.e., concealed, from (ghammahu), when he covered it; rather, let it be exposed and well known, that you proclaim it to me. For secrecy is resorted to only to close the door on seeking deliverance by flight or the like; so when that is impossible in my case, there is no point in secrecy. The Prophet (ﷺ) addressed them with this only to show his disregard for them, and that they will not find a way against him, and out of his trust in Allah, glorified is He, and in what He promised him of protection and safeguarding. So the word (thumma, "then") is for distance in rank (al-taraakhi fi al-rutba), (p-165), and the stating of the noun (amr) in place of a pronoun is for the additional confirmation required by the situation of commanding openness, which is implied by the prohibition of concealment and secrecy.

It is said: what is meant by their affair is what befalls them from his (ﷺ) side of a severe condition, hateful to them; and (ghumma) and (ghamm) are like (kurba) and (karb); and (thumma) is for temporal distance. The meaning is: let your state not be a gloom upon you, and be rid of the burden of my standing and my admonition by destroying me. It is not hidden that this is not supported by His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Then carry out your decision against me and give me no respite﴾, i.e., deliver to me, i.e., settle that affair which you intend against me, and do not delay me, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to him that affair﴾. Or, deliver to me what is due from you, which is your right with you, from my destruction, as a man pays his creditor. For interposing what occurs after the destruction between the command to resolve upon its beginnings and the command to carry it out is like separating the tree from its bark.

It has been read as (afdū) with the fa', meaning: go to your end with your evil against me, or come forth to me, from (afḍā) when one goes out into the open space (al-fadā').

**﴿Then if you turn away⦆** The fa' (فاء) here marks the turning away as a consequence of what has preceded. The meaning of the turning away may be either its continuation, or the initiation of a particular turning away. That is: if you turn away from my counsel and admonition, after having witnessed from me the signs of the truthfulness of what I say and its proofs—among which is my calling all of you to carry out what you intend against me of evil, being unconcerned about you and about what will come from you—and if you refrain from answering, knowing that I am upon the manifest truth and supported by Allah, the Mighty, ﴿then I have not asked you﴾ in return for my exhortation and admonition ﴿for any wage﴾ that you would pay me, so that this would lead to your turning away—either because you accuse me of greed and of asking, or because of the burden of paying what is asked of you—or so that your turning away would harm me by depriving me.

The first reading serves to show the invalidity of the turning away by explaining the absence of what would make it valid, while the second serves to show his ﷺ lack of concern for their existence or non-existence. On both readings, the fa' of the apodosis indicates that the conditional clause is the cause for the content of the consequent to be made known, not for itself. The meaning is: if you turn away, then know that there is nothing in me that validates it, nor any effect of it upon me.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: **﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾** encompasses both meanings together, except that on the first it is an emphasis, and on the second it is a justification for his ﷺ independence from them. That is: my reward for the admonition and reminder is only from Him, the Exalted, who rewards me for it, whether you believe or turn away. **﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾**, those who submit to His judgment, not opposing His command nor hoping for other than Him; or those who surrender to whatever affliction befalls them in obedience to Allah, the Exalted.

﴿So they denied him﴾, and persisted in the denial they were already engaged in, after he had established the proof against them and made the clear path plain to them. He also affirmed that their turning away had no cause other than rebellion and obstinacy. Therefore, undoubtedly, the word of punishment was realized against them. ﴿Then We saved him and those with him in the ship﴾, from among the Muslims, and they numbered eighty. ﴿And We made them successors﴾ of those who were destroyed. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾, that is, by the flood. The mention of the drowning is placed after the mention of the deliverance and the succession, as occurs in His words, Exalted and Majestic be He: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the cry seized those who had wronged﴾, and other noble verses. This is to show the complete care given to the one who is mentioned first, to hasten joy for the listeners, and to announce that mercy, which is among the requirements of lordship (rububiyya), precedes wrath, which is among the consequences of the crimes of the criminals.

(p-166)

﴿Then see how was the end of those who were warned﴾. This is an expression of awe at what befell them, a warning to whoever denies the Messenger (ﷺ), and a consolation for him (ﷺ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 74:

﴿Then We sent﴾, i.e., We sent, ﴿after him﴾, i.e., after Nuh (peace be upon him), ﴿messengers﴾. The indefiniteness (al-tankir) is for magnification, both in essence and in attribute, i.e., noble messengers, many in number, ﴿to their peoples﴾, i.e., to their nations. However, this does not mean that each messenger among them was sent to the peoples of all, or to any people whatsoever, but rather each messenger was sent specifically to his own people, like Hud to 'Ad, Salih to Thamud, and others, of those whose stories are related and of those whose stories are not related.

﴿But they came to them﴾, i.e., each messenger came to his specific people, ﴿with the clear proofs﴾ (al-bayyinat), i.e., the manifest miracles indicating the truth of what they said. The preposition "bi" (with) is either connected to the mentioned verb, with the meaning of transitivity, or to an elided element that functions as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "jaa'uhum," i.e., "accompanied by the clear proofs." However, this does not mean that each messenger came with one single proof, but rather with many proofs specific to him and determined for him according to what wisdom requires, for the observance of the division of the individuals into individuals applies only between the two pronouns "jaa'uhum," as has been indicated. ﴿So they were not going to believe﴾ is an explanation of the continuation of their non-belief in past time, not of the non-continuation of their belief, as its like has passed in this noble surah more than once, i.e., it was not right or proper for any of those peoples at any time to believe; rather, that was impossible for them due to the severity of their stubbornness in disbelief and obstinacy.

Then, if what is related is the final state of each people, as the narration of the people of Nuh indicates, then the intended meaning of their non-belief mentioned here is their persistence in that after the various kinds of admonition, and by what is indicated in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿(because of what they had denied before)﴾, their denial from the time of the coming of the messengers until the time of persistence and obstinacy. And this was not made the primary intended object as the first was, where it was made a relative clause for the relative pronoun, as a notification that it is clear in itself and needs no explanation; what requires explanation is their non-belief after the successive manifest proofs and the abundant striking miracles, which would have compelled them to accept if they had been people of intellect. The relative pronoun "alladhi" to which belief and denial are attached, both negatively and affirmatively, refers to all the laws that each messenger brought, its roots and its branches, and if what is related is all the states of each people among them.

So the intended meaning of what was mentioned first is their continuous disbelief from the time of the coming of the messengers to its end, and the intended meaning of what was indicated last is their denial before their coming. Therefore, the mentioned relative pronoun must refer to the roots of the laws upon which all the messengers agreed, and to which they called their nations, being the most important of matters, because it is impossible for them to change or be altered, such as the creed of Tawhid (monotheism) and its requirements. The meaning of their denial of them before the coming of their messengers is that they were not, in the time of ignorance, in a state where they had never heard the word of Tawhid at all; rather, each of those peoples would hear of it from the remnants of those before them, such as Thamud from the remnants of 'Ad, and 'Ad from the remnants of the people of Nuh (peace be upon him), and they would deny it. Then their state after the coming of the messengers was like their state before that, as if no one had been sent to them. The restriction of denial and non-belief to the mentioned roots is because the condition of the rest is evident by indication of the text, for when they did not believe in what all the messengers agreed upon, then they are even less likely to believe in what only some of them held exclusively. Not making this denial the primary intended object is because what the matter of punishment and retribution revolves around, when the deniers gather, is the denial that occurs after the call, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾. What occurred before it was mentioned only as an explanation of their deep-rootedness in disbelief and denial. In both cases, the three pronouns agree in their reference. It has been said that the pronoun in (kadhdhabu) refers to the people of Nuh (peace be upon him), and the meaning is: the people of the messengers would not believe in that which a similar thing was denied by the people of Nuh. And its strain is not hidden.

It has also been said: the "bi" is causal, i.e., because of their habituation to denying the truth and their training in it before the sending of the messengers. It is not hidden that this leads to contradicting the majority who make the verbal "ma" a noun, as is the view of al-Akhfash and Ibn al-Sarraj, so that the pronoun may return to it; and returning it to the truth by claiming that it was fixed in minds is, as is not hidden, a strained interpretation.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., in the likeness of that firmly established sealing, ﴿We seal﴾ with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), and it was read with the "ya" (third person), the pronoun referring to Allah, glorified is He, ﴿upon the hearts of the transgressors﴾, those who exceed the known limits in disbelief and obstinacy, who shun acceptance of the truth and following the path of guidance. This occurs through abandoning them and leaving them to themselves, because of their immersion in error and misguidance. And in such things is an indication that actions occur by the power of Allah Most High and the acquisition (kasb) of the servant.

﴿Then We sent﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to His saying, ﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples﴾, as the conjunction of one narrative (qiṣṣa) to another narrative. ﴿After them﴾ means: after those messengers, peace be upon them, comes Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both. Their mission was singled out for mention, and it was not considered sufficient that their account be included within the general allusion, made in summary form, to the accounts of the messengers with their peoples. The method of detailed narration (ḍarb tafṣīl) was chosen to signal the great importance of the story and the magnitude of its impact, as in the account of Noah, peace be upon him.

﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ means: to the nobles (ashrāf) of his people. Their being singled out for mention is due to their primacy in establishing affairs and important matters, and to the fact that everyone refers to them in calamities and grave difficulties.

﴿With Our signs﴾ means: accompanied by them. These are the detailed signs (al-āyāt al-mufaṣṣalāt) mentioned in Surat al-A'rāf.

﴿(But they became arrogant)﴾: al-istikbār (arrogance) is the claim of greatness without entitlement. The fa is a fa faṣīḥa (an eloquent fa, implying an omitted clause), meaning: then they came to them and conveyed the message to them, but they became arrogant toward following the two of them. This is what the accursed one said to Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for some years of your life?﴾ ... etc. ﴿And they were a criminal people﴾ is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) confirming the content of what precedes it, meaning: they were habitually committed to committing great sins. Indeed, ijrām (criminality) indicates the greatness of the sin, and from it comes al-jirm, meaning the body. Therefore they grew bold in what they dared to do, namely disdaining the message of God, the Exalted. And interpreting arrogance as refusal to accept the signs is not supported by His saying, Mighty and Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 76:

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾ This is explicit that what is meant by "their arrogance" is what occurred from them before the coming of the truth that they called magic, namely the staff and the white hand, as the context of the noble composition indicates. This was the first of the great signs that he (ﷺ) displayed. The fa' here is also an eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasihah), which expresses what has been stated explicitly in other places, as if it were said: Musa said: "I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord," up to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾ "So when the truth came to them from Us and they recognized it, they said, out of the excess of their haughtiness (p-168) and obstinacy: 'Indeed, this is clear magic,'" meaning: its being magic is evident, or it surpasses its kind, clear in comparison with its peers. It was also read as ﴿لَساحِرٌ﴾ (lasahirun, "indeed a magician").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 77:

﴿Musa said﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) built upon a question that naturally comes to mind, as if it were said: "What then did Musa say to them at that time?" So it is answered: he said, in the manner of a rebuking interrogation of denial: ﴿Do you say of the truth﴾ which is further than anything from magic, which is pure falsehood, ﴿when it has come to you?﴾ That is: at the time of its coming to you and your standing before it, or from the very beginning without reflection or contemplation. Both states are incompatible with the aforementioned statement. The object of the saying is omitted, relying on confidence in what precedes and follows it as an indication of it, and as a notification that it is something that should not be uttered even in the form of reporting. That is: "Do you say to it what you say, that it is magic?" By this is meant that it is something that no speaker could say or utter. Or "saying" is taken in the sense of blame and slander, from their saying: "So-and-so fears al-qala (gossip)," and "there is taqawul (mutual talk) among the people" when some of them say to others what displeases them. A parallel to this is the mention in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We heard a youth mentioning them﴾ ... etc. So the object is dispensed with, meaning: "Do you blame him and slander him?"

On both interpretations, His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a separate denial from his side, peace be upon him, concerning its being magic, and a refutation of their statement, and a rebuke to them for that following upon rebuke, and ignorance-charging following upon ignorance-charging. As for the first interpretation, it is evident. As for the second, the reason for choosing the denial that it is magic over the denial that it is blameworthy (by saying, for example: "Is there a flaw in it?"), as the apparent sense of the preceding denial would require, is to explicitly reply to them regarding the particular thing they found fault with, after alerting them through the preceding denial that there is not the slightest trace of any flaw in it. The sense of nearness in "this" serves to further specify the referent and to bring to mind the attributes in it that indicate that it is a dazzling sign among the signs of God, which proclaim the impossibility of its being magic. That is: "Is this magic, whose matter is clear and manifest, and whose state is observed and well known, such that no one with seeing eyes would doubt it?" The placement of the predicate first is to notify that it is the object of the denial.

Since its being magic would entail that the one who brought it is a magician, the preceding denial is emphasized, along with the rebuke and ignorance-charging it contains, by His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿and the magicians do not prosper﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of those addressed, and the connective is the waw without a pronoun, as in the saying of one who said:

"Winter has come, and I possess no provision"

and your saying: "Zayd came while the sun had not risen." That is: "Do you say of the truth that it is magic, while the state is that its practitioner does not prosper, i.e., does not attain a desired goal nor escape a disliked thing? How then could it be issued from one like me, of those supported by God the Mighty the Wise, who attain every aim and escape every danger?"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is this magic?﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the circumstantial clause and its referent, by which the preceding denial is emphasized, by explaining the impossibility of its being magic with respect to its essence, before explaining its impossibility with respect to its issuing from him, peace be upon him. As for the allowance that the whole should be the content of the saying, on the meaning: "Have you come with magic, seeking success through it, and the magicians do not prosper?", this is not at all supported by the noble composition.

Firstly, because what they said is the judgment that it is magic, without there being in it any indication of the meaning forced upon it in any way; so diverting his response, peace be upon him, from the explicit content of what they addressed him with to something not understood from it at all is what the revealed composition must be exalted above bearing.

Secondly, because mention of the non-prosperity of magicians in absolute terms is the function of one who holds fast to the manifest truth, not of disbelievers clinging to the coattails of some of them in opposing him, peace be upon him. Had that been part of their speech, it would have been fitting to restrict the non-prosperity to the one they claimed to be a magician, on the basis of the prevalence of those who bring such things among magicians.

Thirdly: because His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 78:

(p-169) ﴿They said: "Have you come to us⁠ ⁠⁠...⁠ ⁠⁠⁠" etc.⁠ — this is put forward to explain that he (ﷺ) silenced them with the stone, so they were unable to produce any statement related to his words, let alone a correct answer, and they were compelled to cling to the hem of imitation, which is the habit of every helpless one who has been refuted and the custom of every stubborn obstinate one. It is a resumption that came as a reply to what preceded it of his speech (ﷺ), following the manner of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Moses said⁠ ⁠⁠...⁠ ⁠⁠⁠⁠ etc.⁠ — as has been indicated. It is as if it was said: "What did they say to Moses (peace be upon him) when he said to them what he said?" So it was said: "They said, unable to argue: Have you come to us ﴿to turn us away⁠⁠⁠﴾, i.e., to divert us, for turning (fatl) and turning away (laft) are brothers ﴿from that which we found our fathers upon⁠⁠⁠﴾, i.e., from the worship of idols. There is no doubt that this is only possible if what was mentioned is a continuation of his speech (peace be upon him) in the manner explained, for if it were reported as coming from them, his reply (peace be upon him) would be devoid of the rebuke that compelled them to abandon the ways of argument. And there is no doubt that there is no connection between their saying "Have you come to us" etc. and his denial (peace be upon him) of what was reported from them that would make it a fitting reply to them. ﴿And that greatness may be yours⁠⁠⁠﴾, i.e., kingship, or arrogance over the people by making them your followers. It was also read (wa-yakūna) with the yā' (third person). The word "fī" in the saying of the Exalted ﴿in the land⁠⁠⁠﴾, i.e., the land of Egypt, is connected to (takūna) or to (al-kibriyā') or to the being-established in (lakumā), since it occurs as a predicate, or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier of (al-kibriyā') or of the pronoun in (lakumā), because it bears it. ﴿And we are not going to believe you⁠⁠⁠﴾, i.e., we will not give credence to what you have brought. The repetition of the pronoun in these two places, after its singular form in the earlier contexts, is by consideration of greatness being shared by both of them (peace be upon them), and because belief in one of them entails belief in the other. As for turning away (al-laft) and coming (al-majī'), since they are among the peculiarities of the Lawgiver, they are attributed to Moses (peace be upon him) alone.

"And Pharaoh said" — the verb is in the singular because the command belongs to Pharaoh; that is, he said to his chiefs, ordering them to arrange the initial steps for compelling the two of them, peace be upon them, to act, after despair of compelling them by speech: ﴿Bring me every learned sorcerer﴾ — skilled and adept in the various arts of magic. It is also read (sahhar), meaning "a great sorcerer."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 80:

﴿When the magicians came⦆ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to an implied clause demanded by the context, which has been omitted to indicate the swiftness of their compliance with the command of Pharaoh, as is the usual function of the eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasihah) in every context. The sense is: "So they brought it, and when they came..." ﴿Moses said to them﴾, but not at the very beginning of their coming; rather after they had said to him, peace be upon him, what is recounted about them in the other surahs, in their saying: ﴿"Either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw"﴾, and the like. ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾, meaning: those who will throw whatever kind of magic it may be.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 81:

﴿Then when they cast⁠﴾ what they cast of staves and ropes, and they struck awe into the people and produced a great magic. ﴿Moses said⁠﴾ to them, paying no heed to them or to what they had done: ﴿What you have brought is magic.⁠﴾ The "mā" (what) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) functioning as the subject (mubtada'), and "al-siḥr" (the magic) is its predicate (khabar). That is: it is magic itself, not what Pharaoh and his people called signs of God, glorified is He. Or it is of the kind of magic, showing them that its state is manifest and not worth regarding, as if he said: what you have brought is of the sort that should not be brought. It has also been read as "al-siḥr" in the interrogative form, so "mā" is interrogative, meaning: what is it that you have brought? Is it the magic whose state every person knows, and which no intelligent person would take up? It has also been read "mā ji'tum bihi siḥrun" and "mā ataytum bihi siḥrun." Their indication of the second meaning in the well-known reading is more evident.

﴿Indeed, God will nullify it⁠﴾ — that is, He will utterly annihilate it through what He manifests at my hands of the miracle, so that no trace of it remains at all; or its falsehood will become evident to the people. The "sīn" (sa-) is for emphasis. ﴿Indeed, God does not set right the work of the corrupters⁠﴾ — that is, the work of the category of corrupters absolutely, so magic enters into it primarily; or "your work," in which case it is an instance of placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, to brand them with corruption and to indicate the reason for the ruling. The intended meaning of not setting right their work is not that their corruption is not made into righteousness, but that it is not rewarded and not completed: that is, He does not make it firm, does not perfect it, and does not make it endure, but rather He annihilates it, destroys it, and brings ruin upon it. The sentence is an explanation of what preceded it in His saying, "Indeed, God will nullify it," and the whole is a concluding parenthetical remark (i'tiraḍ tadhyīlī). In it is evidence that magic is corruption and deception with no reality.

ﷻ"And Allah establishes the truth" is coordinated with His saying "He will nullify it" (سَيُبْطِلُهُ), i.e., He will confirm it and strengthen it. The mention of the Glorious Name (al-Ism al-Jalil) in the last two positions is for the sake of instilling awe and cultivating reverence. ﴿By His words﴾, i.e., by His commands and decrees. It is also read as (بِكَلِمَتِهِ) (bi-kalimatihi, "by His word," in the singular). ﴿Even if the criminals dislike it﴾. By "the criminals" is meant everyone characterized by criminality (al-ijram), including the sorcerers and others.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 10, Verse 83:**

﴿So none believed in Musa﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to an implied element (muqaddar) that has been spelled out in other places, namely: (Then he threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were faking) ... and so on. It was left unstated because of reliance on that, and out of preference for concision (ijaz), and to signal that His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah will surely nullify it﴾, are something that admits no falsehood at all. Its conjunction to that with the letter fa (fa', the particle of sequence) — even though the not-believing was a continuous state — is of the same kind as what is in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, and as in your saying: "I admonished him but he did not heed, and I shouted at him but he did not desist." The secret in this is that doing something after what would require abstaining from it has arrived, even if it is a continuation of that state, is nevertheless, according to its description, a new act and a fresh deed. That is: none believed in him, peace be upon him, upon seeing those overpowering signs, ﴿except a small group (dhurriyyah) of his people﴾, i.e., except some youths from among the descendants of his people, the Children of Israel. He had called the elders, but they did not respond to him out of fear of Pharaoh, while a group of their young men answered him. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Pharaoh, and the dhurriyyah is a group of his youth who believed in him, peace be upon him, or the believer of Pharaoh's family, his wife Asiya, his treasurer and his wife, and his hairdresser; but this is far-fetched. ﴿In fear﴾, i.e., existing in great fear ﴿of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾. The pronoun refers to Pharaoh, and the plural is used according to the customary usage for the pronouns of the great, and the context of explaining his exaltedness in corruption, his extremity in evil, and his domination over the servants does not preclude it. Or it refers to his household, as one says "Rabi'ah and Mudar" (the names of tribes used for their collective lineage). Or it refers to the dhurriyyah, or to the people, i.e., in fear of Pharaoh and of the nobles of the Children of Israel, for they used to prevent their descendants out of fear of Pharaoh's harm to them and to themselves.

﴿that he would persecute them﴾ (p-171), i.e., that he would torment them. It is a substitutive of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), or an object of "fear" (khawf), since the operation of an indefinite verbal noun (mașdar munakkar) as a governing element is common, as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ ... ﴿an orphan﴾. Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) after the omission of the preposition lam (lam al-ta'lil, "for"). The attribution of the verb to Pharaoh specifically is because he is the one who commands the torment.

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh was haughty (la-'al) in the land﴾, i.e., truly dominant in the land of Egypt, ﴿and indeed he was among the extravagant (al-musrifin)﴾ in wrongdoing and corruption through killing and the shedding of blood, or in arrogance and tyranny to the point that he claimed lordship and enslaved the descendants of the prophets. The two sentences are an concluding parenthetical insertion (i'tiraq tadhyili) that confirms the content of what preceded.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 84:

﴿And Moses said﴾ when he saw the fear of the believers of him: ﴿O my people, if you have believed in Allah﴾ i.e., you have affirmed Him and His signs, ﴿then in Him put your trust﴾ and place your reliance upon Him, and do not fear anyone other than Him, for He is sufficient for you against every evil and harm, ﴿if you are Muslims﴾ submitting to the decree of Allah the Exalted, sincere toward Him. This is not a case of attributing a ruling to two conditions (ta'lil al-hukm bi-shartayn), for the ruling that is causally linked to faith (al-ta'lil bi-l-iman) is the obligation of reliance upon Him, the Exalted, since faith is what necessitates it, while the thing conditioned upon Islam (al-mashrut bi-l-Islam) is its existence, since it is not realized alongside corruption (al-takhlit). Its parallel is: "If Zayd does good to you, then do good to him, if you are able to."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 85:

﴿Then they said﴾, answering him (peace be upon him) without any hesitation in that matter: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, because they were believers, sincere (mukhlisin). Then they called upon their Lord, saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial﴾, i.e., a target of trial ﴿for the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., do not give them power over us so that they torment us, or tempt us away from our religion, or are tempted by us and say: "Had these people been upon the truth, they would not have been afflicted."

And His, exalted is He, statement:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 86:

﴿And deliver us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.﴾ This is a supplication from them for deliverance from the evil of their (the wrongdoers') company, and from the ill effect of associating with them after being delivered from their oppression. For this reason they are described as "the disbelieving" after having been described as "the wrongdoers." And in the ordering of the supplication after reliance upon God (tawakkul) there is a hint that the one who supplicates ought to base his supplication upon reliance upon God Most High.

﴿And We revealed to Moses and his brother, "Settle your people in Egypt in houses"﴾ **أنْ** (an) is explanatory (*mufassirah*), because revelation (*al-wahy*) contains the sense of speech, meaning: take a dwelling place (*mubaah*) ﴿for your people in Egypt, houses﴾ in which you will live and to which you will return for worship. ﴿And make﴾ you and your people ﴿your houses﴾ those ﴿a direction of prayer (*qiblah*)﴾, meaning a place of prayer (*musalla*). It was also said: mosques facing the *qiblah*, which is the Ka'bah, since Moses, peace be upon him, used to pray toward it. ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, that is, in them. They were commanded to do this at the beginning of their affair, lest the disbelievers gain dominance over them, harm them, and tempt them away from their religion. ﴿And give good news to the believers﴾ of victory in this world, in answer to their supplication, and of Paradise in the next. The pronoun was dualized first because settling a people and taking places of worship are matters that the leaders of the people arrange by consultation. Then it was made plural, because making the houses mosques and praying in them is something every person does. Then it was made singular, because giving good news to the community is the task of the bearer of the law. Placing "the believers" in the position of the pronoun of the people is to praise them for their faith, and to indicate that faith is the basis of receiving good news.

(p-172) ﴿And Moses said: Our Lord, You have indeed given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment﴾, i.e., what is adorned with, of clothing, mounts, and the like, ﴿and wealth﴾ and many kinds of property ﴿in the life of this world. Our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way﴾. This is a supplication against them in the form of an imperative, with what is known from observing their conditions that it will not be otherwise, like your saying: "May God curse Iblis." It has also been said that the *lam* is the *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence), connected to "You have given," or it is the *lam al-'illah* (the lam of cause), because giving blessings to those who disbelieve is *istidraj* (gradual lure) and a reinforcement of misguidance. Also, because they made these things a *dhari'ah* (means or pretext) to misguidance, it is as though they were given them so that they would go astray. Thus "Our Lord" is a repetition of the first, as emphasis or as an alert that the intent is to present their misguidance and ingratitude, as a preface to His saying: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾. *Al-tamsu* is erasure (*al-mahw*), and it was read with a *damma* on the *mim*, meaning: destroy it. ﴿And harden their hearts﴾, i.e., make them hard, and seal them so that they do not open to faith, as is the nature of their condition. ﴿So they will not believe﴾ is either the answer to the supplication, or a supplication in the form of a prohibition, or a conjunction with "so that they may lead astray," with what lies between them being an intervening supplication. ﴿Until they see the painful punishment﴾, i.e., they witness it and become certain of it, to the extent that this will not benefit them at that time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 89:

﴿He said: "Your supplication has been answered."﴾ That is, Moses and Aaron, upon them be peace, because he (Moses) used to say "Amin" (Amen) to it, as is indicated by the attribution of "Lord" to the pronoun of the first person plural in the three places. ﴿So go straight﴾ meaning: remain steadfast in the state you are in, of calling (to the truth) and of establishing the proof against them, and do not be hasty, for what you have requested will certainly occur at its appointed time. It is related that he remained among them for forty years after the supplication.

﴿And do not follow the path of those who do not know﴾, that is: the ways of God, glorified is He, in linking matters to wisdoms and benefits; or the path of the ignorant in being hasty, or in not trusting in the promise of God, exalted is He. It is also read with the light nun and with its kasra because of the meeting of two quiescent letters (wa-la tattabi'anna), and (wa-la tatbi'an) from tabi'a, and (wa-la tattabi'an) likewise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 90:

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾. It is from jawaza al-makan, when one passes over a place and leaves it behind, and the ba' is for transitivity (ta'diyah). That is, We made them cross the sea, by making it dry (yabasan) for them, and We preserved them until they reached the shore. It is also read (jawwaznā), which is from tajwiz, synonymous with mujawazah (crossing over), not from what carries the meaning of tanfidh (carrying out), such as what occurred in the verse of al-A'sha:

؎ kama jawwaza al-sakkiyya fi al-bab fayataq

Otherwise it would have been said: "We made the Children of Israel pass through the sea," and the noble composition would have been devoid of the indication of their separation from the sea, and of the accompaniment of divine care for them at the time of crossing, as is well known in the distinction between adhhabahu and dhahaba bihi.

﴿So Pharaoh followed them﴾. It is said: tabi'tuhu hatta atba'tuhu when he had preceded you and you caught up with him, that is, he overtook them and caught up with them, ﴿Pharaoh and his hosts﴾, until the two groups came into view of each other and the two companies nearly met, ﴿in rebellion and transgression﴾: in injustice and aggression (p-173). That is, transgressing and aggressing, or for rebellion and enmity. It is also read (wa-'aduwwan). The reason is that Musa, peace be upon him, left with the Children of Israel at a moment of Pharaoh's heedlessness. When he heard of it, he followed them until he caught up with them and reached the coast, while they had already come out of the sea, and their path remained dry as it was. So he entered it with all his hosts, and when the last of them had entered and the first of them were about to come out, the sea overwhelmed them with what overwhelmed them.

﴿Until, when drowning overtook him﴾: that is, it reached him and gripped him. ﴿He said: I believe that He﴾: that is, that He; the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n). It is also read (innahu) as a resumption (isti'naf) instead of (amantu), and as an explanation of it: ﴿there is no god but He in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾. He did not say as the magicians said: (﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾), but rather He, may He be exalted, expressed him by the relative pronoun, and made its relative clause the belief of the Children of Israel in Him, may He be exalted, to indicate his return from obstinacy and his following of those who had been leading them, out of hope of acceptance and of being included with them in the line of salvation.

﴿And I am among the Muslims﴾: that is, those who submitted their souls to God, that is, made them sound and devoted exclusively to Him, may He be exalted. By them he meant either the Children of Israel specifically, or the category in general, and they are included in it at the first level of inclusion. The clause, according to the first interpretation, is coordinated with (amantu), and the choice of the nominal sentence is to claim permanence and continuity. According to the second, it may also be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the speaker, that is: I believe, sincere to God, included in the line of those firmly rooted in Him. The one meaning has been repeated in three expressions, out of eagerness for acceptance leading to salvation, and how far away, how far away, after what has passed has passed and what is to come has come.

And His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 91:**

﴿Now?﴾ is a quoted utterance (maqul) for an implied saying coordinated with "qala" (he said). The meaning is: "Then it was said: Now?" From here up to His words, may He be exalted, ﴿a sign﴾, this is a report of what God, glory be to Him, did in anger at the one who was forsaken. Setting what he had shown against the rejection, in the form of a reproachful denial, is a rebuke for his delay and a censure for his disobedience, corruption, and other things. Omitting the verb mentioned and presenting the reported statement in the form of a command (insha') indicates the greatness of the wrath and the severity of the anger, as is clear. This is confirmed by what is reported, that Gabriel (Jibril) at that moment pushed the mud of the sea into his mouth and stopped it up with it. This is a confirmation of the verbal rejection by the practical rejection. It is not contradicted by his (Pharaoh's) stated reason, fear that mercy would reach him, as it is reported that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you had seen me, O Muhammad, while I was taking the mud of the sea and stuffing it into his mouth, fearing that mercy might reach him." For the intended mercy is worldly mercy, that is, deliverance, which is what the forsaken one sought. Attaining it does not necessarily require sound faith, as in the case of the people of Yunus (peace be upon him), so that his (Pharaoh's) aversion would entail what cannot be imagined concerning Gabriel (peace be upon him), namely approval of disbelief. For there is no impossibility in this mercy being bestowed merely upon uttering the word of faith, even if that occurs in a state of distress and despair. Thus his (ﷺ) stuffing is interpreted as closing the door on a remote possibility, due to the completeness of the rage and the intensity of the fury. Reflect on this. And God is the Granter of success.

The governing element of the adverbial (zarf) should properly be taken as deferred (muakhkhar), so that the denial and rebuke are directed at the delay of faith to a point where its acceptance becomes impossible. That is: "Now you believe, when you have despaired of life and become certain of death."

His (glorified and exalted) words ﴿and you had disobeyed before﴾ form a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of the implied verb. It is brought in to intensify the rebuke and censure for delaying faith until this moment, by showing that the delay was not due to the call not having reached him, nor to his reflecting on and pondering its proofs and signs, nor to any other thing that might be considered an excuse for delay. Rather, it was in the manner of rejection, defiance, and corruption. For His words, may He be exalted, ﴿and you were among the corrupters﴾ are coordinated with "you disobeyed" (عصيت) and fall within the scope of the circumstantial clause. That is: "and you were among those who went to extremes in misguidance and in leading others astray from faith." This is like His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred [others] from the way of God — We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment for what they used to corrupt.﴾ This expression refers to his corruption, which returns to himself and spreads to others in the form of injustice and transgression, and in barring the Children of Israel from faith. The first refers to his particular disobedience.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 92:**

﴿Today We will save you﴾, that is, We will bring you out from what your people fell into, from the depths of the sea, and We will make you float. The expression "saving" (al-tanjiyah) hints that his intention in faith was salvation, as has passed, and it mocks him. Or, "We will cast you upon a high shore (najwah) of the earth so that the Children of Israel may see you." It is also read as (nunjīka), from ījā' (rescue), and as (nunaḥḥīka), with the letter ḥā', from al-tanḥiyah (removal), meaning: We will cast you to the side of the shore. ﴿in your body﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject) from the pronoun of address, meaning: We will save you clothed only in your body, not with your soul, as you desired. This is a disappointment for him and a complete cutting off of his hopes. Or, "naked of clothing," or "whole and sound." Or, "with your armour," for he had a golden armour by which he was known. It is also read as (bi-abdānika), meaning with all the parts of your body, as in their saying "he fell with his limbs (bi-ajramihi)." Or (bi-durū'ika), with your armours, as if he had been displaying them.

﴿So that you may be a sign for those who come after you﴾, a sign (āyah) and a mark for those behind you, who are the Children of Israel, since his greatness was in their souls to the extent that they imagined he could not be destroyed. It is even reported that they did not believe Musa (peace be upon him) when he informed them of his drowning until they saw him cast up on their passage from the shore. Or, it may be a lesson (ʿibrah) and a deterrent (nakāl) from tyranny for those who come after you from the nations, when they hear the outcome of your affair from those who witnessed you. Or, it may be a proof showing them that a human being, however far he reaches the utmost degree of greatness of rank, height of pride, and strength of authority, is a subject, overpowered, far from the places where lordship (rubūbiyyah) is due. It is also read as (li-man khalafaka), as a past verb, meaning: for those among the tyrants who succeeded you. It is read as (li-man khalaqaka), with the letter qāf, meaning: that it may be a sign to your Creator like the rest of the signs. For His singling you out, glorified is He, by casting you onto the shore is evidence that this was intended by Him to expose your fabrication and remove doubt about your affair, and a clear proof of the perfection of His knowledge, power, wisdom, and will. This interpretation is also possible on the well-known reading. In explaining His saving him with what has been mentioned, there is an indication that this was not for his honour, or for some other benefit returning to him, but for the complete belittling of him and the exposing of him before the eyes of all witnesses, and for increasing the horror of his condition, like one who is killed and whose body is then dragged through the markets, or paraded with his head through the lands. The first lām is connected to "We will save you," and the second is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from (āyah), meaning: being a sign for those behind you.

﴿And indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs﴾, not reflecting upon them, nor taking heed from them. This is a concluding parenthetical remark (i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī), brought in at the point of narration to confirm the meaning of the speech being related.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 93:

﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel﴾ is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought in to explain in summary the abundant blessings bestowed upon them following the blessing of deliverance, and their failure to give thanks for them and to fulfil their rights. That is: We settled them and lodged them after We had delivered them and destroyed their enemies. ﴿A firm abode of truth﴾, i.e., a good and pleasing dwelling place, namely al-Sham (Greater Syria) and Egypt, which they came to possess after the Pharaohs and the Amalekites, and they became firmly established in their regions, as indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land, which We had blessed﴾.

﴿And We provided them with good things﴾, i.e., delicacies, ﴿but they did not differ﴾ regarding the matter of their religion ﴿until knowledge had come to them﴾, i.e., only after knowledge had come to them through their reading of the Torah (al-Tawrah) and their knowledge of its rulings. Or [it means] regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ): they did not differ except after they had known the truthfulness of his prophethood and the manifest evidence of his miracles. Thus, those who differed are their descendants who lived in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, distinguishing between the one in the right and the one in the wrong by reward and punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 94:

﴿If you are in doubt﴾: that is, in a doubt that is merely assumed for the sake of supposition and estimation. The content of a conditional proposition (shartiyyah) is only the linking of one thing to another, without any implication about the possibility of either of them. How could it imply that, when both may be impossible, as in His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you were to associate partners with Allah, your deeds would surely be lost﴾, and their like? ﴿Of what We have sent down to you﴾, which includes the stories, among them the story of Pharaoh and his people, and the reports about the Children of Israel. ﴿So ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾: for that is established among them and confirmed in their books, as We have revealed to you. The purpose is to demonstrate his prophethood (ﷺ) through the testimony of the rabbis, as it is written in their books, even if there is no need for this at all. Or it describes the People of the Book as firmly grounded in knowledge of the soundness of his prophethood (ﷺ). Or it is meant to stir him (ﷺ) and increase his steadfastness in the certainty he already has, not to permit that doubt could come from him (ﷺ). For this reason he (ﷺ) said: ﴿I do not doubt, nor do I ask﴾. It has also been said that the relative pronoun refers to the believers among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Tamim al-Dari, Ka'b, and their like.

It has also been said that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the intended meaning is his community, or it is addressed to everyone who hears, meaning: If you, O listener, are in doubt about what We have sent down to you through the tongue of our Prophet. In this there is a warning that whoever is troubled by a doubt in religion should hasten to resolve it by turning to the people of knowledge. It was also read as (فاسألِ الَّذِينَ يَقْرَءُونَ الكُتُبَ) "so ask those who read the Books" (the plural accusative form).

﴿The truth has certainly come to you﴾, which cannot be turned away from, and about whose truthfulness there is no doubt, ﴿from your Lord﴾. This was made manifest through the decisive verses, around which no trace of doubt can hover. In mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ) there is an honour that is not hidden. ﴿So do not be among those who waver﴾, by being shaken from the firmness and certainty you are upon. Persist in that as you were before.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 95:

﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah﴾. This is by way of incitement and stirring up (al-tahyij wa'l-ilhab), and what is meant by it is to inform that denial is of such ugliness and grave prohibition that one should be forbidden from it even if it is inconceivable that he would commit it, so how much more so one for whom it is possible to be characterized by it. It also serves to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers. ﴿And [then] you would be﴾ thereby ﴿among the losers﴾, in souls and in deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 96:

﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justly decreed﴾ begins an explanation of the secret behind the obstinacy of the disbelievers in what they are upon of disbelief and misguidance; that is: it has been established and made binding in accordance with the will that is founded upon consummate wisdom, ﴿the word of your Lord﴾, meaning His judgment and decree (p-176) that they will die upon disbelief and be abiding in the Fire, like His Exalted saying: ﴿But the word from Me has been realized: I will surely fill Hell﴾ to the end of the verse, ﴿will not believe﴾ ever, since His speech is not false and His decree cannot be overturned. That is: they will not believe a beneficial faith that takes place at its proper time. Thus included among them are those who believe at the witnessing of the punishment, like Pharaoh, who remained [in his state] at the time of death; and thus the apostates are included among them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 97:

﴿Even if every sign should come to them﴾ whose indication is clear and which is acceptable to the intellects, [they would not believe], because the cause of their faith, namely the connection of His (exalted is He) will to it, is absent. Yet its absence is not due to any prevention on His part (glorified is He), given that they deserve it, but rather due to their bad choice, which branches off from their lack of readiness for that, ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾, like the fate of the family of Pharaoh and their like.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 98:

﴿Then why was there not⦆ a resumptive statement serving to confirm what preceded regarding the impossibility of faith for those upon whom Allah's word had been fulfilled, because of their poor choice, while they had the ability to make amends. Accordingly, the exception that follows serves as an explanation that the people of Yunus, peace be upon him, were among those upon whom the word was not fulfilled, because they were guided to make amends in their time. "Lawla" here means "halla" (why not). It is also read as "kadhalika" (thus), meaning: "Then there was never a town of the destroyed towns ﴿that believed⦆ before witnessing the punishment, nor did it delay its faith until the moment of witnessing it, as Pharaoh and his people did. ﴿So its faith benefited it⦆, in that Allah would accept it from them and remove the punishment from them because of it. ﴿Except the people of Yunus⦆: this is a disconnected exception, meaning: but the people of Yunus ﴿when they believed⦆ as soon as they saw the signs of the punishment, and did not delay until it descended ﴿We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world⦆ after it had overshadowed them and was about to befall them. It is also permissible that the sentence carries the sense of negation, as the particle of restriction makes clear, in which case the exception is connected, since by "towns" is meant their inhabitants. It is as if it were said: No group of the disobedient nations believed so that their faith benefited them, except the people of Yunus, peace be upon him. Then Allah's words ﴿(when they believed)⦆ are a resumption explaining the benefit of their faith. This is supported by the reading in the nominative case as a substitution. ﴿And We gave them enjoyment⦆ of worldly provision after the punishment was removed from them ﴿for a term⦆ determined for them in Allah's knowledge, glory be to Him.

It is narrated that Yunus, peace be upon him, was sent to Nineveh in the land of Mosul, and they denied him, so he departed from them in anger. When they lost him, they feared the descent of the punishment, so they wore sackcloth and cried out for forty nights. It was also said: Yunus, peace be upon him, told them: "Your term is forty nights." They said: "If we see the signs of destruction, we will believe in you." When thirty-five nights had passed, the sky became overcast with a dense, terrifying black cloud that smoked with intense smoke, then descended until it enveloped their city and blackened their rooftops. They wore sackcloth and went out to the open ground, themselves, their women, their children, and their animals, and they separated the women and children from one another, and the animals from their young. So the animals yearned for one another, the voices rose high, and the wailing grew. They displayed faith and repentance and humbled themselves before Allah, the Exalted, and He had mercy on them and removed it from them. That day was the Day of 'Ashura', a Friday.

And from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: Their repentance reached the point that they returned the wrongful takings, so that a man would pull out a stone, which he had placed as the foundation of his building, and return it to its owner. It was also said: They went out to an elder from among the remnants of their scholars, and they said: "The punishment has descended upon us; what do you think?" He said to them: "Say: O Living when there is no living, O Living who gives life to the dead, O Living, there is no god but You." So they said it, and it was removed from them.

And from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, they said: "Our sins have grown great and magnificent, and You are greater and more magnificent than them. Deal with us as You are worthy of, and do not deal with us as we are worthy of."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 99:

﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would all have believed﴾. This is a confirmation that the faith of all the responsible beings (mukallafun) revolves, in existence and in non-existence, around the pivot (qutb) of His will, exalted is He, absolutely, following the statement that the disbelief of the disbelievers is subordinate to His word. The object of the will (maf'ul al-mashi'ah) is omitted, because there exists what requires it: its occurrence as a condition (shart), the object of it being the content of the apodosis (jaza'), and that its being connected to it is not strange, as is well known. That is: if Allah, glorified is He, had willed the faith of those on earth of the two weighty ones (jinn and humankind), they would all have believed, such that not one of them would deviate from it, "all together", gathered upon faith, not differing concerning it. But He does not will it, because it contradicts the wisdom upon which the foundation of creation and legislation (al-takwin wa-al-tashri') is built. In this is an indication that whomever Allah, exalted is He, wills to have faith will certainly believe.

﴿Will you then compel the people﴾ to what Allah has not willed of them, as the particle of negation in the conditional sentence indicates. The fa' (then) is for coordination (al-'atf) upon an implied element that the speech is drawn into, as if it were said: "Does your Lord not will that? Then you compel them ﴿until they become believers﴾." So the rebuke is directed at the ordering of the mentioned compulsion upon the non-willing of Allah, exalted is He. It is also permissible that the fa' be for the ordering of the rebuke upon His non-willing, exalted is He, on the basis that the hamzah (interrogative particle) is posterior in consideration, though it was placed first because it demands initial position (al-sadarah), as is the view of the majority. In any case, the will is taken in its unrestricted sense, since there is no benefit otherwise; indeed, there is no justification for considering the non-willing of coercion specifically in the rebuke's ordering upon it or the ordering of the rebuke upon it. And the placement of the noun after the interrogative particle is a notice that compulsion is a possible matter, but the concern is who the one compelled is, and that it is none other than Him alone, without partner in it; for He is the One capable of doing in their hearts what compels them to faith, and that is not attainable by human beings. In this is also a notice that compulsion is considered within the will, as has been pointed out.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 100:

﴿And it is not for any soul﴾ is an explanation that the faith of believing souls depends on the will of God, the Exalted, in existence, after the explanation that the general rule of His will applies to them in existence and non-existence. That is, it is not valid or proper for any soul among those whom God, the Exalted, knows will believe ﴿to believe except by the permission of God﴾, that is, by His facilitating it and granting it the subtle gifts of grace (alṭāf, sing. luṭf, divine grace that draws a person to obedience). The soul was specified as the one mentioned, and this was not treated in the same way as His words, ﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by the permission of God﴾, because the exception is an incomplete exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh, an exception whose excluded element is left unstated, so the sense is determined by the context) drawn from the most general of conditions. That is, it is not for any soul to believe in any of its states except in a state in which it is connected to His permission, the Exalted. Therefore, faith must be something that its state will come to. Just as death is the destination of every soul, from which there is no escape, the soul must be specified as the one mentioned. The souls that God knows will not believe have no state in which they believe, so that this state could be excepted from the others.

﴿And He places the abomination (rijs)﴾, that is, disbelief, by the context of what precedes it. It is expressed by rijs, which is an expression for what is ugly, loathsome and detestable, because disbelief is a sign (ʿalam, a recognized marker) of ugliness and repugnance. It was said that rijs is punishment, or the abandonment (khidhlān) that leads to it. It was read with the plural-of-majesty nūn (nujʿalu), and it was read with the zāy (rizz, "He causes to sink"), that is, He places disbelief and keeps it in place ﴿upon those who do not use reason﴾, who do not employ their minds by considering the proofs and signs, or who do not comprehend His indications and rulings because of the seal (ṭabʿ) upon their hearts. Thus the guidance that is expressed by permission does not come to them, and they remain submerged in the foulness of disbelief and misguidance, or subdued by punishment and retribution. The sentence is coordinated (maʿṭūfah) with an implied clause which the noble wording implies, as if it were said: "So He grants them permission by bestowing the subtle gifts of grace, and places…" etc. (p-178)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 101:

﴿Say﴾, addressing the people of Makkah, as an urging for them to reflect upon the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth and what is in them of the wondrous signs, both those within the selves and those on the horizons; so that it becomes clear to you that they are among those who do not understand, and the Word has become due against them. ﴿Look﴾, i.e., reflect. It is also recited with the movement of the hamza transferred onto the lam of ﴿qul﴾. ﴿What is in the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., what marvellous thing there is in them of the wonders of His creation that point to His oneness and the perfection of His power. On the basis that (ma dha) is made, by composition, a single noun in which the interrogative sense has predominated over the demonstrative sense, so it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is the adverbial phrase (zarf). It is also permissible for ma to be the subject, and dha to mean "alladhi" (who/which), with the adverbial phrase as its relative clause (silah), and the sentence is the predicate of the subject. On both of these readings, the subject and predicate are in a position of accusative (nasb) by the removal of the governing preposition, and the verb of looking (al-nazar) is suspended by the interrogative.

﴿And the signs do not avail﴾, i.e., do not benefit, and it is also recited with the masculine form (al-tadhkir). ﴿The signs﴾, which are what is expressed by His words, exalted is He: (what is in the heavens and the earth). ﴿And the warnings﴾, the plural of nadhir, on the basis that it is an agent noun in the sense of mundhir (warner), or on the basis that it is a verbal noun (masdar), i.e., the signs do not avail, nor do the warning messengers, or the warnings (al-indharat), ﴿for a people who do not believe﴾ in the knowledge and judgment of Allah, exalted is He. So "ma" is a negation particle, and the sentence is either a circumstantial clause (hali) or a parenthetical clause (i'tirazi). It is also permissible for "ma" to be an interrogative of denial in a position of accusative on the basis of it being a verbal noun (masdariyyah), i.e., "what kind of benefit do the signs avail..." etc., in which case the sentence is then parenthetical.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 102:

﴿Are they waiting for anything but like the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ That is: the polytheists of Makkah and their likes. ﴿Only a day like the days of those who passed away before them﴾, that is: only a day like the days of those who passed away before them, ﴿from among the polytheists of the earlier nations﴾, meaning like their events and the descent of God's punishment upon them, since they deserve nothing else. From their saying: "ayyam al-'Arab" (the days of the Arabs), referring to their battles. ﴿Say﴾ as a threat to them: ﴿Then wait﴾ to see what your outcome will be; ﴿indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ for that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 103:

﴿Then We save Our messengers﴾ with the doubled consonant (tashdid); it is also read with a single consonant (takhfif). It is coordinated (ʿatf) with an implied element indicated by His saying: ﴿like the days of those who passed away before them﴾. What lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD) brought in for the sake of hastening to the threat and emphasizing the severity of the warning, as if it were said: "We destroyed the nations, then We saved Our messengers who were sent to them and ﴿those who believed﴾." The form of the future tense (istiqbal) is used to narrate past circumstances, in order to magnify their gravity by bringing their images to mind. The narration of the deliverance is delayed past the narration of the destruction, contrary to what occurs in His saying: ﴿So We delivered him and those with him in the ark﴾ ... and similar passages that occur in many places, so that His saying, mighty and majestic is He, may connect to it: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that deliverance, ﴿it is a right upon Us﴾ is a parenthetical interjection between the operator and the operand, meaning: that right is a truth; and it has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the omitted element that "thus" stands in for, meaning: deliverance like that is a truth. The particle "ka" (thus) is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We save the believers﴾, that is, from every hardship and punishment. The sentence is a concluding summary (tadhyil) of what precedes it, confirming its content. By "the believers" is meant either the category that includes the messengers, peace be upon them, and their followers, or the followers alone. The deliverance of the messengers is not mentioned because it is understood that they have no need of it. In either case there is (p-179) an indication that the basis of salvation is faith.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 104:

﴿Say﴾ to the bulk of the polytheists, ﴿O mankind﴾. The address is made by the generic noun, introduced with the particle of alerting (ḥarf al-tanbīh), in order to generalize the delivery of the message and to show complete concern for what has reached them. ﴿If you are in doubt about my religion﴾, which I worship God, Exalted and Majestic is He, by, and to which I invite you, while you do not know what it is or what its description is, ﴿then I do not worship those whom you worship besides God﴾ at any time whatsoever.

﴿But I worship God, who causes you to die﴾, and then does to you what He does of the various kinds of punishment. That is, know that: the restriction of worship to Him, and the renunciation of worshipping anything other than Him, such as idols and others, which you worship out of ignorance. The mention of abandoning the worship of others before the worship of Him, Exalted is He, is due to the precedence of emptying (al-takhliyah) over adorning (al-tahliyah), as in the statement of monotheism (kalimat al-tawhid), and to signal opposition from the very beginning of the matter. Or, if you are in doubt about the soundness and rectitude of my religion, then know that its essence is the sincere devotion of worship to the One in whose hand is bringing into existence and annihilation, not what is far removed from both of them, namely the idols. So present it to your intellects, turn your thoughts over in it, and look into it with the eye of fairness, so that you may know that it is the truth about which there is no doubt. In specifying the causing of death as the mention connected to them, there is an intimidation that is not hidden. And the expression of what they are in with the word "doubt" — although they are certain of its invalidity — is to signal that the furthest a rational person can come to in this matter is doubt about its soundness, whereas certainty about its invalidity is something for which there is no path. Or, if you are in doubt about my steadfastness in the religion, then know that I will never abandon it.

﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾, in accordance with what reason indicates and revelation has spoken, and this is an explicit statement that what he is upon of the religion of monotheism is not by way of pure reason alone, but by heavenly support and divine guidance. The omission of the preposition from (an) may be either of the regular kind of omission with (an), or it may be specific to the imperative verb, as in his saying:

*I commanded you the good, so do what you have been commanded.*

And that you set your face toward the religion, upright (ḥanīfan)... 

Let me be careful: the passage is a translation task. Here is the translation:

"And that you set your face toward the religion" is coordinated with "that I should be" (an-akūna) above, except that the relative clause of "an" is in the imperative form, and there is no harm in that. The reason is that the criterion for permissibility of connecting it with verb forms is that it signifies the verbal noun, and that does not differ between the declarative and the imperative. The requirement that the relative clause be declarative in the substantive relative pronoun is only for the purpose of describing definites with sentences, and they are described only by declarative sentences. The literal relative pronoun is not so, i.e., "and I have been commanded to be upright in the religion and to be independent in it by performing what is commanded and refraining from what is forbidden, or by facing the qibla in prayer and not turning to right or left" (ḥanīfan) is a circumstantial clause from "the religion" or "the face," i.e., inclining away from the false religions.

"And do not be among the polytheists" is coordinated with "set" (aqim) and falls under the command, i.e., do not be among them in belief or in action.

And His saying, Mighty and Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 106:

﴿And do not call upon﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) with His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Say: O mankind﴾. It is not included under the command. It was also said that it is conjoined to the prohibition preceding it, but the first view is the correct one, because the sentences that follow it, up to the end of the two verses, are coherent, and it is not possible to separate some of them from others, as you see. There is no basis for including all of them under the command, while it is a confirmation of the prohibition mentioned and an elaboration of what was stated in summary in it, to show the completeness of the concern with the matter and to uncover the reason for the falsity of what the polytheists hold. That is: do not call upon, apart from God, either alone or in association, that which cannot benefit you if you call upon it to repel a harm or to bring about something beloved.

﴿And that which cannot harm you﴾ if you abandon it, by withholding what is beloved, whether by preventing or removing it, or by inflicting something hateful. The mention of benefit before harm needs no explanation of the reason.

﴿But if you do﴾ — that is, what you were forbidden from, calling upon what neither benefits nor harms — it is referred to in this manner as an honouring of his status (ﷺ) and an alerting to the exalted rank of his station, lest the worship of other than God, the Glorified, be attributed to him, even implicitly within the conditional clause.

﴿Then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is the consequence of the condition and an answer to the question of one who asks about the liability for what was forbidden.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 10, verse 107:**

﴿If Allah touches you with harm﴾ is a confirmation of what was mentioned within the relative clause's scope (*hayyiz al-silah*) regarding the idols' lack of benefit, and a depiction of His exclusive possession of this, glorified is He. ﴿There is none to remove it﴾ from you, whoever or whatever it may be, ﴿except Him﴾ alone. Thus the idols' inability to remove harm is established through a demonstrative method (*al-tariq al-burhani*), and this is a clarification of their lack of benefit by removing what is disliked, which necessarily implies their lack of benefit in bringing what is loved, by an apparent implication. For the removal of what is disliked is the lowest degree of benefit, so when it is negated, benefit is negated entirely.

﴿And if He intends for you good﴾ is a verification of the negation of harm mentioned within the relative clause's scope; that is, if He intends to afflict you with good, ﴿there is none to repel His favor﴾, of which what He intends for you of good is part. This is evidence for the response of the conditional (*jawab al-shart*), not the response itself. It also contains an indication that the outpouring of good from Him, exalted is He, is by way of grace (*tafaddul*), without any obligation upon Him, glorified is He. That is, none is able to repel it, whatever it may be, so the idols are included in this by primary inclusion. This is a clarification of their inability to harm by repelling what is loved before it occurs, which necessarily implies their inability to harm by removing it, or by inflicting what is disliked by clear implication. Perhaps the mention of intending (*al-irada*) with good and touching (*al-mass*) with harm, despite the two matters being mutually implicated, is to indicate that good is intended in itself, and that harm only touches whoever it touches because of the external motives it entails, not by primary intention. Or it may be that the meaning of both verbs is intended in each of harm and good, and that there is no repeller of what He wills of either, nor any remover of what He afflicts with either. So the speech was made concise by mentioning touching in one and intending in the other, so that what is mentioned on each side indicates what was left out on the other side. [This is also] to show that affliction was explicitly stated when it was said: ﴿He afflicts with it﴾ (*yusibu bihi*), displaying full concern for the side of good, as is indicated by the omission of the exception in it. That is, He afflicts with His vast grace, which encompasses what He intends for you of good. Making "grace" (*al-fadl*) a reference to that very good itself, on the basis that it is a case of placing the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun (*wad' al-muzhar fi mawdi' al-mudmar*), for the benefit mentioned, is refuted by His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿to whomever of His servants He wills﴾, for that calls out to the generality of the grace.

His saying, mighty and majestic, speaking: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is an appendage (*tadhil*) to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He afflicts with it﴾... etc., confirming its content. The whole is a concluding appendage (*tadhyil*) to the last conditional sentence, verifying its content.

"Say," addressing those disbelievers after you have conveyed to them what was revealed to you: ﴿O mankind, the truth has certainly come to you from your Lord﴾, namely the Glorious Qur'an, which comprises the excellent rulings, among which are the fundamentals of the religion mentioned just before, and you have become aware of the clear proofs and guidance contained within it, and you have no excuse left. ﴿So whoever is guided﴾ by believing in it and acting upon what it demands, ﴿then he is only guided for his own self﴾, i.e., the benefit of his guidance accrues to him alone. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ by disbelieving in it and turning away from it, ﴿then he only goes astray to his own harm﴾, i.e., the burden of error is confined to himself. The intent is to clear the honor of the Messengership from any taint of a purpose returning to him ﷺ, such as bringing benefit or repelling harm, as is hinted at by attributing the coming to the truth without indicating that it was through his mediation. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾, i.e., a keeper to whom your affairs have been entrusted; rather, I am only a bringer of good tidings and a warner.

﴿And follow﴾ in belief, action, and conveying, ﴿what is revealed to you﴾ in a manner of constant renewal and continuity, from the truth mentioned, which is affirmed day after day. The expression of its reaching them by "coming" and of its reaching him (ﷺ) by "revelation" is a reminder of the distance between the two ranks. ﴿And be patient﴾ with what afflicts you of the hardships of conveying (the message), ﴿until God judges﴾ by giving victory over them, or by commanding fighting against them, ﴿and He is the best of judges﴾, since error is impossible in His judgment, because He knows the inner secrets (al-sara'ir) as well as He knows the outward appearances (al-zawahir).

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): «Whoever recites Surah Yunus, he is given ten good deeds as reward for each person who believed in Yunus and each person who denied him, and for each person who drowned with Pharaoh.»

And praise belongs to God alone.
